The silk it produced helped to pay for Japan's industrialisation, and the surrounding region was, for decades, one of the world's great silk-growing districts. The pin sits close by, between Yoshii and Tomioka, in the western part of the prefecture, where the Kantō plain meets the first line of the mountains.

The mountains are the other draw. Mount Myōgi, to the west of the town, is a jagged ridge of grey volcanic rock, with strange pinnacles and cliffs that have long made it a place of pilgrimage and a favourite with climbers, and its shrine, tucked under the cliffs, is an atmospheric place. To the north-east, the great volcanoes of Mount Haruna and Mount Akagi rise above the plain, and on a clear day the whole line is visible. Nearby Shimonita is famous for its konnyaku, the firm, jelly-like food made from a root and used in countless Japanese dishes.

Riding here is good. The roads wind up into the hills past orchards, pine woods and small farms, with views over the plain and the mountains, and the surface is mostly smooth. Traffic is moderate, though weekends see more cars and bikes headed for the mountains. The weather is changeable: summer afternoons can bring sudden thunderstorms, and winter mornings can be icy in the shade, while the long dry winter wind from the north is known locally as the karakkaze, cold and fierce.

Tomioka, with nearly fifty thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and Fujioka and Yoshii are also well served. Look for local specialities like shimonita negi, a thick, sweet leek, and the various noodle dishes that the region is known for.

The ride is the Boso Peninsula in Chiba, which is on the other side of Tokyo, but the pin sits well to the north-west. Early morning, with mist in the valleys and the first light on the Myōgi cliffs, is a lovely time for photographs.
t.mount haruna and ikaho onsen photo pull:
The Kantō plain is the biggest flat area in Japan, and east of the Tone river it feels like a green, endless table, with rice paddies, tidy villages, long straight canals and not a hill in sight. The pin sits in the heart of it, near Satte, Sugito and the little town of Sakai across the prefectural border, in a landscape that rewards a slow pace and a long view. On a very clear winter day, Mount Tsukuba, with its twin peaks, rises on the eastern horizon, and the white cone of Mount Fuji and the Nikkō mountains can be seen to the west and north.

Satte is known for the Gongendō embankment, a long strip of cherry trees along the Gongendō river, which in early April make a tunnel of pink above the water, and in the same season rape flowers, a bright yellow carpet, spread out below the blossom. Sugito is the home of Tōbu Zoo, a large animal park popular with families. The landscape is crossed by old rivers and levees, some of them centuries old, which have shaped the farmland and the towns, and flooding is a known danger in heavy typhoon rain.

The riding is flat, straight and easy, with long levee roads, bridges and rows of power lines. It is not a ride for thrills, but it is peaceful, with big skies and wide views, especially at sunrise or sunset when the light is low and the haze glows orange. Traffic is moderate, but delivery trucks, farm vehicles and cyclists are common, and the roads are often narrow with a drop at the edge, so stay focused. Wind from the north in winter is strong and cold, and in summer the humidity is high.

For food and fuel, Satte and Sugito have supermarkets, convenience stores and family restaurants, and the local fare is simple and good: udon noodles, tempura, grilled eel from the nearby rivers, and in the region the rice, grown in the rich alluvial soil, is excellent. A bowl of hot noodles and a flask of green tea make an excellent break.

The ride is the Mount Haruna and Ikaho Onsen route, in the mountains of Gunma to the north-west, and the pin is the plain from which the mountains rise. Choose a clear morning, and you may see the line of peaks on the horizon, including Haruna and Akagi.
t.okutama and chichibu forest roads photo:
Hadano sits in a basin of its own, ringed by the Tanzawa mountains to the north and Mount Ōyama to the east, and the water that drains from those hills has made the town famous. The Hadano Basin springs are on the national list of remarkable waters, and locals queue at public taps to fill bottles with soft, cold mountain water. The pin lies close to the town, with Ninomiya and the seaside town of Ōiso a short ride south, in the western part of Kanagawa prefecture, an hour or so from Tokyo and a world apart from the crowded city.

Mount Ōyama, a distinctive, cone-shaped peak of 1,252 metres, has been a pilgrimage site for centuries, with a shrine called Afuri at its summit and a cable car that carries visitors to a temple halfway up. The cooking at the base of the mountain is renowned for its tofu, served in elaborate multi-course meals, and the tofu restaurants of the village are popular with day-trippers. Ōiso, on the coast, was the first sea-bathing resort in Japan, established in the 1880s, and a number of politicians and writers kept villas there.

Riders know this area for Yabitsu Pass, a winding road that climbs from the Hadano side into the Tanzawa mountains, with tight hairpins, thick forest and good views. It is popular at weekends, and the police keep an eye on it, so ride within the limits. The surface is mostly smooth but can be damp and strewn with needles and leaves in the shade. Early mornings are best, before the traffic, and autumn is lovely, with the maples turning red.

The label refers to Okutama and Chichibu, which are in the mountains to the north-west of Tokyo, so this stop is a different, more southern entrance to the hills. Hadano has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, and it is a convenient place to prepare for a day in the mountains. Look for local peanuts, a speciality of the area, and a bowl of noodles with locally grown vegetables.

Take a moment at the springs, fill a bottle, and taste the water. It is cold, clear and sweet, and it sets you up for the climb.
t.shosenkyo gorge and lake kawaguchi sceni:
Hino is the hometown of Hijikata Toshizō, the deputy commander of the Shinsengumi, the swordsmen who policed Kyoto in the last years of the shogunate, and the old post town still honours him with a museum and a small shrine. The pin sits between Hino and Hachiōji, on the terraces beside the Tama river in the western part of Tokyo, where the city's suburbs spread across a landscape of low hills and river plains. It is not the most scenic part of the capital, but it has history, and the mountains rise just beyond.

Hachiōji, with nearly six hundred thousand people, was once the silk capital of the region. Raw silk from the mountain villages was collected here and sent down the old silk road to the port of Yokohama, and the merchants of Hachiōji grew rich on it. Mount Takao, to the west, is the city's favourite hill, a forested peak of 599 metres with a temple, a cable car and trails, and it is among the most visited mountains in the world, thanks to its closeness to central Tokyo. Hino has the Tama Zoological Park, with lions, koalas and an insect house, and the Tama river, wide and shallow, has gravel banks and cycling paths.

The riding is a mix of urban and rural. The Kōshū Kaidō, once the old highway from Edo to the west, is now a busy road with heavy traffic, but the hills beyond Hachiōji offer winding roads into the Okutama area, with good surfaces and forested bends. In the city, the roads are crowded with signals, cameras and delivery vans, so the best plan is to leave early and aim for the hills. Autumn colours, around the end of November, and the cherries in early April are the high points.

Everything is easy. Hachiōji has fuel, restaurants, supermarkets and convenience stores on every corner, and the local food includes Hachiōji ramen, a soy-based soup topped with finely chopped onions. Hino and Machida are well served too, and a bowl of hot noodles by the station is a good quick lunch.

The label refers to Shōsenkyō Gorge and Lake Kawaguchi, in Yamanashi, which lie over the mountains to the west, so this stop works as the start of the ride. The highways west, including the old Kōshū road, head straight for the hills, and by mid-morning the city is behind you.
t.tokyo kanto rides@35.7,138.9:
Yamanashi is a prefecture of mountains, fruit and wine, and the pin sits in the middle of it, in the steep country north of Ōtsuki, where the Kōshū mountains rise toward the Okutama range. The Katsura river runs below, cutting a gorge near Ōtsuki that is crossed by Saruhashi, the Monkey Bridge, one of Japan's three great strange bridges, a wooden cantilever construction that has been rebuilt many times since the Middle Ages. Enzan, to the north-west, is the gateway to the Daibosatsu mountains and the Chichibu-Tama-Kai National Park.

This is a landscape of terraced orchards, with grapes, peaches and persimmons ripening along the slopes. The Kōshū grape, grown here for over a thousand years, makes the white wine of Katsunuma, and the vineyards have given the area a growing reputation among wine lovers, with tasting rooms open to visitors. The old Kōshū Kaidō, the road from Edo to Kōfu, ran through here, and Sasago Pass, a long climb to the east, was one of its steepest sections, with checkpoints and inns that have mostly vanished. Mount Fuji appears on the southern horizon from many viewpoints, a huge white shape above the lower hills.

The roads are a pleasure. From Ōtsuki, routes climb the valleys toward Kosuge and Lake Okutama, with sharp bends, narrow sections and a thick cover of forest, and the Matsuhime road in particular has a fine reputation among riders. The surface is mostly good, but narrow in places, and rockfalls, wet leaves and fallen branches are common. In winter, ice persists in the shade, and snow can close the higher roads. Autumn is the best time, with the orchards and forests in colour, and spring brings blossom in the valleys.

Fuel and food are easy in Ōtsuki, Enzan and the Kōfu basin, with convenience stores and restaurants along the main roads. The local dish is hōtō, a thick noodle soup of flat wheat noodles, pumpkin and vegetables, served in an iron pot and perfect for a cold day. Fresh fruit is for sale at roadside stands in season.

The pin is marked for swimming, and the mountain streams are clean and cold, but be careful of strong currents after rain. The label mentions Bandai Azuma and Shōsenkyō, but the mountains here have their own appeal, quieter and little known to visitors.
Zushi is the sort of place that looks as if it has been designed for a very long, very slow Sunday. A small seaside town on the east side of Sagami Bay, it has a marina, a long pale beach and a lot of cafés, and it sits beside Hayama and Kamakura, the other two members of an unofficial trio of Japanese seaside towns where Tokyoites go to escape the heat and the crowds. The pin is right on the coast, and on a clear day Mount Fuji rises beyond the bay, a faint blue cone at the end of the sea.

Kamakura is the one with the history. From the late twelfth century it was the seat of the first shogunate, and for about a hundred and fifty years the warrior government ruled Japan from here, in a town enclosed by hills and the sea. The great bronze Buddha, cast in the thirteenth century and about thirteen metres tall, sits in the open air after the building that housed it was washed away by a tsunami, and the Tsurugaoka Hachimangū shrine at the end of a long, tree-lined avenue is one of the major shrines of eastern Japan. Hayama, just south of Zushi, has an imperial villa and an air of quiet money.

Riding along this coast is a slow business. Route 134 follows the shore with views of the sea and Enoshima, the little island with its shrine, but the traffic is dense at weekends, and you can spend an hour crawling a few kilometres. The hill roads above are narrow and twisty, with a sort of village-lane feel, and one must be careful of walkers, cyclists and tour buses. Weekdays and early mornings are much better, and the light on the water at sunrise is lovely. Summer is hot and humid, with crowded beaches, so spring and autumn are best.

The marked swim is in the sea, and the beaches here are popular, with lifeguards and facilities in summer, but watch out for jellyfish in late summer. Fuel, food and coffee are all easy, and the seafood, especially shirasu, tiny whitebait served raw or boiled over rice, is the local speciality and best eaten at a beach restaurant.

The ride is Shōsenkyō Gorge in Yamanashi, which is well inland, and the Bandai Azuma Skyline in Fukushima, far to the north, so this is a gentle start by the sea. Take time to walk along the shore, and watch the surfers.
t.ashinoko skyline short attack@35.4,138.8:
On the northern flank of Mount Fuji, above Fujiyoshida, the land changes from town to forest, and the pin sits right on the border. The Fuji Subaru Line, the toll road that climbs to the fifth station on the mountain's flank at about 2,300 metres, begins a little higher up, and to the west the dense, dark woods of Aokigahara spread across an old lava flow, a forest that grows on rock so porous that no streams run through it. The town itself, with about forty-nine thousand people, is strung along a long main street with a view straight up the mountain.

Fujiyoshida has a long history as the base for pilgrims climbing Fuji. For centuries, groups of devotees called kō came here to purify themselves before the ascent, and the old lodging houses along the street still stand. The Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen shrine, in a grove of huge cedars, is the traditional start of the pilgrimage, and the Arakurayama Sengen park, with its small red pagoda against the snow-capped cone, is the photograph that appears in every guidebook. The fire festival of Yoshida, held at the end of August, lights up the whole town with giant torches.

The riding here is terrific, though the roads are busy. Climbing toward the Fuji Subaru Line, the road passes through thick forest, with wide curves, long straights and the huge mountain filling the view. The weather changes quickly, with fog, rain and cold at any season, and the temperature falls steeply with altitude. Lava caves in the area, such as the wind and ice caves, are worth a stop. Traffic builds on summer weekends, especially in the climbing season of July and August, so go early.

This is also a food stop, and Fujiyoshida has a famous dish: Yoshida udon, a thick, firm noodle with a strong chew, served with cabbage and slices of horse meat or a spicy paste, and available at dozens of small restaurants. It is cheap, filling and a perfect meal before a ride. The town has fuel, supermarkets and convenience stores, so fill up before the mountain roads.

The title mentions Ashinoko, which is Lake Ashi in Hakone, on the other side of the Fuji range, and this stop makes a good start for the short run over. Eat well, check the weather on the mountain, and expect a ride that is as much about patience as speed.
t.tomiura to nojimazaki cape loop photo pu:
Mount Fuji is hard to hide, and from the foothills above the Kōfu basin, it fills the southern sky on a clear day. The pin sits in the mountains north-west of Ōtsuki, on a quiet road with orchards below and forests above, in the rugged backcountry of eastern Yamanashi. Enzan, now part of Kōshū, lies in the valley at the foot of the hills, and the Kōfu basin beyond is Japan's best-known fruit-growing region, a place where grapes, peaches and cherries ripen in turn from late spring to autumn.

The Kōfu basin is the old heartland of the Takeda clan, the warlords of the sixteenth century, whose lord Takeda Shingen is still a regional hero. His domain was a self-contained world of mountains, with the basin protected by passes, and the terrain explains his reputation for strategy. The wine industry is much newer but already substantial, with Katsunuma at its centre, and its wineries often have tasting rooms with a view of the fruit orchards. Further north, the great peaks of the Chichibu-Tama-Kai park run from Mount Daibosatsu toward Saitama, a wilderness that most Tokyo residents never see.

The riding is steep and rewarding. Narrow roads climb out of the valley, with hairpins and tight bends, to ridges with spectacular views, and the surface is mostly good, though patchy in places. Traffic is light, apart from fruit trucks in the harvest season and weekend visitors in autumn, and the quiet is striking after Tokyo. Mist and cloud can come down quickly, and the temperature at height is much lower than in the valley, so carry an extra layer.

Enzan has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and the larger town of Kōfu, a short distance south, has everything. In the fruit season, roadside stands sell peaches, grapes and persimmons at modest prices, and the sweetness of a Yamanashi peach in July is one of the pleasures of Japan. A bowl of hōtō noodle soup is the local meal for colder days.

The label talks of Tomiura and Nojimazaki Cape in Chiba, which are on the Pacific coast far to the east, but here the sea is a long way off, replaced by mountains, orchards and distant Fuji. Time the stop for early morning, when the mountain is often visible and the air is clear.
t.gunma three mountain day photo pull off@:
The northern edge of Saitama prefecture is flat farmland, laced with canals and levees, and from here the mountains of the Kantō seem a long way off. The pin sits near Kuki, Shiraoka and Shōbu, where the plain runs out toward the Tone river and Gunma beyond. In winter, when the air is dry and clear, Mount Tsukuba shows up to the east and the Nikkō mountains to the north, and on the very best days you can see the white shoulder of Mount Fuji far to the south-west.

Kuki is known beyond Japan for Washinomiya Shrine, an old shrine with a distinctive kagura dance tradition, which became a place of pilgrimage for fans of an anime series set in the town, and the little streets beside the shrine are decorated accordingly. Shōbu, now part of Kuki, was a post town on an old highway, and its plain, tidy streets hint at the past. The local landscape is mostly farmland, with rice, wheat and vegetables, and the old riverbeds and irrigation channels still shape the pattern of the fields.

The riding is easy and uneventful, with long straight roads, level crossings and the occasional cluster of warehouses. It is not a ride for sharp bends, but for covering ground, and the best moments come at dawn and dusk, when the light is soft and the haze turns the horizon pink. Traffic is moderate, though lorries and commuters add to the noise on weekdays. Strong winds are common in winter, and a wet day can make the flat landscape feel flat indeed.

Kuki, with seventy-three thousand people, has supermarkets, fuel, restaurants and shops, and Shiraoka is similar. A small restaurant that serves udon or soba with tempura makes a good simple meal. Convenience stores are on every corner, with hot drinks and snacks, and rest areas along the highways have clean toilets and local souvenirs.

The ride is the Gunma three mountain day, a trio of volcanoes to the north-west, Haruna, Akagi and Myōgi, and this is the gentle beginning of the journey. Use the stop to check the bike, fill the tank and look at the horizon, where the first line of hills should be rising. It may not be the most dramatic place, but it suits an early start.
t.tomiura to nojimazaki cape loop scenic r:
The Tone is the biggest river in the Kantō plain, and the pin sits on the flat ground south of its lower reaches, close to Ishige, Sakai and Iwai in Ibaraki prefecture. The landscape is huge and open, with rice paddies, lotus ponds, long straight canals and wide skies, and the only relief is the twin-peaked shape of Mount Tsukuba, which rises like a lone hill on the eastern horizon. It is flat enough that the horizon seems to curve, and on a clear day the Nikkō mountains float on the northern edge of the sky.

The region has a dramatic past. In the tenth century, a warrior named Taira no Masakado rebelled against the court in Kyoto, based himself at Iwai, now part of Bandō, and proclaimed himself the New Emperor in 939. His revolt lasted only a few months, but he became a legendary figure, and his shrine in Tokyo is still revered. Iwai has a museum to Masakado, and the rice fields around the town are said to have been the scene of his battles. The slow, wide rivers and marshes of the plain, which once made travel difficult, were an advantage to a rebel.

The roads here are flat, wide and simple. Levee roads follow the river for long, uninterrupted distances, with a view over the water on one side and the fields on the other, and the straight farm roads connect small towns and clusters of warehouses. It is not a ride for thrills. The charm lies in the light, especially at sunrise and sunset, when the paddies reflect the sky and the long shadows of the trees stretch across the road. Wind is a nuisance in winter, and the humidity in summer is heavy.

For fuel and food, the towns of Bandō, Jōsō and Koga have supermarkets, restaurants and convenience stores, and the local produce includes rice, lotus root, melons and sweet potatoes. A bowl of hot noodles after a cold morning is as good as it gets.

The label mentions Tomiura and Nojimazaki Cape, which are on the Bōsō peninsula far to the south, and this stop is not a scenic route but a place on the way. It rewards those who like the simple pleasure of a long, flat road and big skies.
t.hakone@35.2,139.1:
Hakone is where Tokyo goes to get away from itself. The mountain resort sits in the caldera of an old volcano southwest of the capital, about an hour and a half by road without traffic, with Lake Ashi in the middle and Fuji looming to the northwest on a good day. Odawara, on the coast below, is the practical town, with its castle and its fish markets, while the hot-spring villages scattered through the hills have catered to travellers for centuries. The old Tokaido highway crossed these mountains, and you can still walk stretches of its stone-paved surface and see a reconstructed checkpoint beside the lake, where officials of the Tokugawa shogunate once inspected every traveller's papers.

On a bike, the draw is the mountain road. The Hakone Turnpike climbs from the coast in a long run of bends, open and smooth, with good visibility and a toll that keeps heavy trucks away. The Skyline and the roads around the crater rim offer views over the lake and the Pacific. Expect weekend crowds of cars and motorcycles, especially on fine autumn days, and be careful in fog, which rolls into the caldera quickly and can drop the temperature several degrees. Winter mornings can bring ice on the higher sections.

Landscape matters here as much as the road. Owakudani, the steaming valley of sulphur vents above the lake, is the remains of a violent eruption roughly three thousand years ago, and the smell of rotten eggs drifts across the road. Locals boil eggs in the hot pools there until the shells turn black, and tell you each one adds seven years to your life. The pampas grass fields of Sengokuhara turn silver in autumn, and the cedar avenue along the old highway is cool and dark even in midsummer.

Fuel is straightforward, with stations in Odawara and along the main road up the valley, but the mountain sections have fewer, so fill at the bottom. Konbini stores at the lakeside and along the turnpike sell hot drinks and snacks. A cup of coffee at a mountain cafe, with the lake and the trees outside, is a decent reward after the climb.

Come on a weekday if you can, and early. By midday the lake road is slow, and by evening the mist often comes back down.
t.kanazawa@36.6,136.7:
Kanazawa escaped the bombs of the Second World War and kept its old quarters, which is a large part of its charm today. The city sits on the Sea of Japan coast of Ishikawa Prefecture, between two rivers and a hill, and for centuries it was ruled by the Maeda clan, the second richest domain in feudal Japan. Their money went into art and craft, and Kanazawa is still known for gold leaf, lacquerware, ceramics and tea ceremony. Kenroku-en, the garden the clan laid out over generations, is counted among the three great gardens of Japan, with its pines held up by rope umbrellas against the heavy winter snow.

Here you can wander the old samurai district, with its mud walls and narrow lanes, and the geisha quarter of Higashi Chaya, where wooden teahouses face each other across stone-paved streets. The fish market near the station, Omicho, sells crab, sweet shrimp and sushi in season, and the sea is close enough that the catch is always fresh. Winter brings snow crab and heavy grey skies, and the city's cuisine has a deep reputation across Japan.

As a place to start a ride, Kanazawa is a city with all the usual urban frictions. The ring road and the main avenues are busy, and traffic lights are frequent, so the early miles are a matter of patience. Once you leave, the Noto Peninsula to the north offers a long, quiet coastal road, with the sea on one side and low hills and rice paddies on the other, small fishing harbours, salt farms and terraced fields. The surface is generally good, speeds are low and drivers are polite. Winter brings snow and ice to the area, and the best months to ride are late spring and autumn.

Fuel is easy around Kanazawa, a city of nearly half a million, with self-service pumps everywhere. Nonoichi and Matsuto, the neighbouring towns, are also well stocked. On the peninsula, stations thin out, especially in the evening, so fill up before heading north. Convenience stores sell a decent coffee and a rice ball at any hour.

Give yourself a morning or an evening in town, if you can. The gardens and the old districts reward slow walking, and Kanazawa is a lot more interesting than most places that serve merely as a start line.
t.izu skyline and jogasaki coast photo pul:
The Shonan coast and the hills behind it are a quirk of the Kanagawa map: Fujisawa, Kamakura and Zushi lie within a few kilometres of each other, yet each has its own character. The pin sits in the hills between the first two, near the Ofuna area, in a landscape of wooded ridges and steep valleys cut by small streams, with houses wedged between them. The label mentions the Izu Skyline, which is a long way south-west, so this is more of a gentle local pass than a mountain road.

Kamakura is the headline. For about a century and a half, from 1185, it was the seat of the shoguns, the military rulers of Japan, who chose the site because it was easy to defend, with the sea on one side and steep hills on the other. The only ways in were narrow cuttings through the hills, called kiridoshi, and several are still used as roads today. The Great Buddha, a bronze figure more than eleven metres tall, cast in the thirteenth century, sits in the open air at Kotoku-in, and the hillsides are scattered with temples and shrines.

The riding here is slow and winding. The roads are narrow, often one lane with passing places, and are lined with houses, walls and temples, and traffic is thick at weekends, especially around Kamakura station. The coastal Route 134, on the other side of the hills, runs beside the sea with views of Enoshima island and, on a clear day, Mount Fuji, but it too is crowded, so go early. Surfaces are smooth, but speed limits are low and strictly enforced.

Fuel is easy in Fujisawa, a city of nearly four hundred thousand people. Kamakura has restaurants for every taste, and the small shops sell shirasu, tiny whitebait, served on rice. A visit to a temple in the early morning, before the crowds arrive, is a calm way to begin. Spring, with cherry blossoms, and autumn, with red maples, are beautiful but crowded, while winter, with clear air and sharp views of Fuji, is the best time for photographs. The rainy season in June brings hydrangeas, a Kamakura favourite, but also damp roads.
t.okutama and chichibu forest roads high p:
Chiba's hills are the unsung part of the Kanto, a rumpled country of forest and rice terraces that tops out at about four hundred metres, and this spot, between Kimitsu and Kisarazu, is on the way in. The pin sits among low ridges and valleys, in the part of the Boso peninsula known as Kazusa, where the road follows the valleys and rises over small, wooded passes. They are not dramatic, but they are quiet, and quiet is hard to find so close to Tokyo.

The hills here have a distinct character, because of the way they were cut. The soft sandstone and mudstone erode easily, and over centuries people dug cuttings and tunnels by hand through the ridges, to connect villages, and many of these old tunnels, with rough, chiselled walls, are still in use. The streams between them are small and clear, and in some of the valleys you will find waterfalls, hot-spring baths and stands of cedar. The landscape is gentle, with terraced rice fields, bamboo groves and small shrines tucked among the trees.

Kimitsu has a different side. Its great steelworks, one of the biggest in Japan, lies on the shore, and the sight of its chimneys and tanks against the hills is part of the landscape. It is a reminder that the Boso peninsula has been at the heart of Japan's industrial growth, even as its hills stay rural. The contrast is striking, and it is possible to ride from heavy industry to forest in a few minutes.

Fuel is available in Kimitsu, with more than ninety thousand people, and in Kisarazu, with convenience stores and restaurants along the main roads. The roads in the hills are narrow and winding, with sharp bends and patches of moss or fallen leaves, so a measured pace is wise. Traffic is light on weekdays. In spring the hills glow green and pink with wild cherry, in early summer the paddies are flooded and the frogs start up, and in late autumn the maples turn red, though the colours come later here than in the mountains. In midsummer, expect humid heat and sudden rain.
t.okutama and chichibu forest roads scenic:
Tokyo Bay narrows here, and on a clear day you can see the far shore, with the city's towers rising across the water. Kisarazu lies at the heart of this stretch, and the pin sits close to the town, on the plain between the shore and the hills. The scenic road leads toward the waterfront and the artificial island called Umihotaru, a parking area built on the Aqua-Line crossing, from which the view takes in the bay, the bridge and the city beyond.

This is a coast of reclamation. Over the past half century, large areas of shallow seabed were filled in to make land for factories, ports and housing, so the shoreline has been pushed out and straightened, and the old fishing coast is hard to find. But traces survive, and the small harbours and tidal flats of the Kisarazu area still produce clams and seaweed. The city is also home to a huge outlet shopping centre, which draws crowds from Tokyo at weekends.

The riding is easy and flat, along broad roads with traffic lights and convenience stores, and a few quieter lanes through farmland. It is not a thrilling route, but it is a good one for a calm end to a day, particularly in the evening, when the sun sets behind Mount Fuji and the bay is lit orange. In winter, on a cold, clear day, the cone of Fuji stands out against the sky, and the sight is worth the cold.

Fuel and food are plentiful, since Kisarazu has more than a hundred and twenty thousand people. Try local clam dishes or a bowl of rice topped with anago, the conger eel that is a speciality of Tokyo Bay. The toll on the Aqua-Line is high, but it saves a long drive around the bay, and the bridge and tunnel are a ride in themselves. Spring and autumn offer the clearest air, and the best chance of seeing Fuji, while in summer humidity often hides it. The roads can be crowded on summer weekends, so a weekday is better.
t.lake ashi view@35.2,139.0:
Lake Ashi fills the caldera of the old Hakone volcano, at 720 metres, and it is one of the most visited places in Japan, partly because of the view. On a clear morning, particularly in winter, the cone of Mount Fuji rises above the water in perfect symmetry, and the red torii gate of Hakone Shrine stands in the lake in the foreground. The pin is on the shore, close to the town of Hakone, and a stop here is a rite of passage for riders on this route.

Hakone has been a travellers' stop for centuries. In the Edo period, the Tokaido, the great road between Edo and Kyoto, crossed the mountains here, and the shogun kept a checkpoint on the shore of the lake to control the passage of weapons and women. The checkpoint has been reconstructed, and a stretch of the old road, lined with huge cedars planted in the seventeenth century, still runs beside the lake. Pirate-style tourist boats cross the water, and the sulphurous steam of Owakudani, the volcanic valley above, drifts in the breeze.

The ride up to the lake is the thing. The roads climb from the coast in a series of tight bends, with hairpins, tunnels and views, and the road around the lake itself is a smooth, winding ribbon. This is a famous place for riders, and on fine weekends the roads are packed with motorbikes, cars and tour buses, so a weekday or an early start is wise. The weather can change in minutes, with fog and rain rolling in from the sea, and in winter ice can form on the upper roads. A few of the scenic roads are toll roads.

Hakone has more than thirteen thousand people, with fuel, restaurants and souvenir shops, and hot-spring baths, onsen, are everywhere. After a day in the saddle, there is nothing better than a hot soak with a view of the mountains. The best time for views of Fuji is early on a cold, clear morning in winter, but spring and autumn are lovely, with cherry blossoms and red maples. The summer is hazy, and the rainy season in June brings hydrangeas but little view.
t.myogi mountain and karuizawa@35.1,139.7:
Misaki is the tip of the Miura peninsula, the south-facing fingertip of Kanagawa, and the pin sits on the plateau just inland, among cabbage fields, radish patches and the rooftops of small farming villages. The land here is a mild, sunny upland, a few tens of metres above the sea, with the sea visible in several directions, and it grows some of the best vegetables in the Tokyo area. The Miura radish is a local pride, a fat, sweet white root, and in winter the fields are full of them.

The label points to Myogi and Karuizawa, which lie far to the north-west in Gunma and Nagano, so think of this as a different kind of ride, a coastal one. The nearby fishing port of Misaki is known throughout Japan for its tuna, and the little streets around the harbour are lined with restaurants serving it as sashimi, sushi or grilled collar. The best place to eat is near the harbour, with a view of the boats, and a bowl of tuna on rice is a classic after a morning in the saddle. There is a small lighthouse on the headland, and a walk along the coast shows rocky shores, tide pools and views across Sagami Bay to Mount Fuji on a clear day.

The roads here are narrow and winding, running between fields and over low ridges, with few straight stretches, and the traffic is local and moderate, though weekends see more cars heading for the beach and the harbour. The surface is generally good, but sandy dust from the fields and cabbage leaves on the corners can catch you out. The wind from the sea is strong in winter and spring, so be ready for gusts on the exposed sections.

Miura, seven kilometres away, has more than fifty thousand people and plenty of fuel and convenience stores, and the villages have small restaurants. The best seasons are autumn and winter, when the air is clear, the radishes are in the fields and the views of Fuji are good, though the sea breeze can be cold. Spring brings fresh green and rape blossom, and the early summer is damp with the rainy season. Midsummer is hot and crowded near the beaches, but the hills are cooler.
t.shosenkyo gorge and lake kawaguchi@36.1,:
Kurihashi sits on the flat, northern edge of Saitama, where the Kanto plain stretches in every direction and the horizon is a line of trees and power pylons. The pin lies in a countryside of rice fields, vegetable plots and canals, near the Tone river, which here marks the boundary with Ibaraki. The label talks about Shosenkyo gorge and Lake Kawaguchi, which are in the mountains of Yamanashi, far to the south-west, so this stop is an easy flat one, used as a place to eat and start.

The old road through Kurihashi was the Nikko Kaido, the route that Edo-period travellers and the shogun's own processions took to the shrines of Nikko, and the town was a post station with a checkpoint on the river, an important one on the highway. A reconstruction of it is in a small museum. Nearby Kazo is known for one remarkable event: each year in early May, a huge carp streamer, one of the largest in the world, is hoisted over the Tone river for the Children's Day festival, a stunning sight with its bright scales.

The riding is flat, straight and a little monotonous, on roads that run along dykes and canals with long views over the fields, and it is a good place to warm up. The most important feature is the wind, which blows across the plain with nothing to stop it, particularly in winter, when the dry north-westerly, known as karakkaze, whips dust and snow off the Kanto fields. A strong crosswind on an exposed bridge needs respect.

Fuel, food and rest are easy. Kurihashi has nearly twenty-eight thousand people, Kazo and Kuki are bigger, and there are convenience stores, family restaurants and ramen shops at every junction. For a local flavour, ask for udon, which is a speciality of the area, or fresh vegetables from a farm stand. Spring brings cherry blossoms along the riverbanks, and in summer the paddies are bright green. The best season is autumn, with clear skies and golden rice. In the rainy season and the humid heat of July and August, the plain is hard going, so start early.
t.shosenkyo gorge and lake kawaguchi high:
It is worth being honest about this one: the pin falls in the commuter belt north of Tokyo, in the flat plain of Saitama, between Shiraoka, Hasuda and the big city of Ageo, and there is no pass and no water to swim in. What you find is the other Japan, the practical one, with rice fields squeezed between housing estates and factories, and a railway line every few kilometres. It is where millions of people live and from where they commute to Tokyo.

Yet there is more to the area than meets the eye. The plain was once a vast marshland, and since the Edo period its farmers have drained and tilled it. Small shrines stand on every corner, and farms still grow rice, vegetables and flowers in the gaps between the estates. To the west, about twenty kilometres away, lies the old castle town of Kawagoe, known as Little Edo for its row of black-tiled warehouses and a wooden bell tower that rings out the hours, a good place to spend an afternoon.

The roads here are busy, with traffic lights every few hundred metres and trucks on every route, so they are best crossed early on a weekend. Quieter lanes follow the old irrigation channels and the Arakawa river, with stretches of dyke road lined with cherry trees, and these make a pleasant way to wind through the suburbs. A few small parks have ponds and rice terraces, and in spring the fields are bright with rapeseed.

Fuel and food are no problem. Ageo has more than two hundred thousand people, and every junction has a petrol station, a convenience store and a family restaurant. The best idea is to use this place as a launch pad: fill the tank, grab a canned coffee and a rice ball, and head west towards the hills of Chichibu or north towards Gunma, where the roads begin to climb. Early morning on a weekend in spring or autumn is the best time. In summer the heat is heavy, and in winter the dry wind from the mountains blows across the plain.
t.myogi mountain and karuizawa scenic road:
Noda is soy sauce country. The town stands at the point where the Edo river splits from the Tone, on the edge of Chiba, and for about four hundred years its brewers have turned soybeans, wheat and salt into the sauce that flavours Japanese cooking. The big factory of the best-known brand is here, and a museum tells the story of the craft. On a still day, you can smell the sweet, salty aroma as you ride past the brewery walls, a smell that is somehow comforting.

The scenic road follows the levee of the Edo river, which runs straight and flat between fields, with the water on one side and farmland on the other. The Edo is a man-made channel, dug in the seventeenth century by the Tokugawa shoguns to control the Tone's floods and to open a shipping route to Edo, and the soy sauce was carried to the city by boat along it. The levee roads are a cycling route and suit slow, relaxed riding.

From the top of the bank, the view across the plain is huge, and in winter, on a clear day, you can see Mount Fuji and the mountains of Chichibu, white with snow, floating above the rooftops. Along the banks, rows of cherry trees bloom in April, and in summer the grass is high and loud with insects. Herons and egrets feed in the shallows. The wind is strong on the levee, especially in winter, so a windproof layer is welcome.

Noda has more than a hundred and twenty thousand people, so fuel, shops and restaurants are plentiful, and Moriya and Mitsukaido are nearby. For a local meal, try a plate of eel or a bowl of noodles with a dash of fresh soy sauce, and compare it with the commercial kind. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm days and clear light. The summer is hot and humid, and a typhoon can bring heavy rain, but at the end of a day the sunset over the levee is something special.
t.myogi mountain@35.6,139.3:
Hachioji sits where the Tokyo plain finally runs into the hills, a city of well over five hundred thousand people at the foot of the Tama mountains, and the Myogi ride comes back to it as to a front door. In the old days it was a post town on the road to the western provinces, famous for silk, and merchants carried raw silk down the Hachioji road to the ports of Yokohama for export. That trade made the city rich, and the old route is still remembered as the Silk Road of Japan.

The mountain that dominates the skyline is Takao, a modest peak of about six hundred metres with a Buddhist temple, Yakuo-in, on its slopes. The temple is a pilgrimage site and the mountain a favourite weekend hike for Tokyoites, who ride the cable car and eat soba in the shops on the way up. The forest is thick, mixed with cedar, beech and oak, and the Michelin guide once gave Takao three stars, which tells you how many people come.

Hachioji is also a university city and a hub, where the Chuo Expressway, the Ken-O-Do ring route and several national roads meet, so traffic is a feature. Roads out toward Sagamiko and the Kanagawa border climb into forested valleys with decent curves and little commercial traffic, and these are good routes on a weekday morning. Weekend afternoons are crowded with cars heading home, and the evening rush backs up on the main trunk.

The ordinary comforts are all here, with fuel on every main road and cafes, ramen counters and Hachioji's local specialty of ramen with chopped onions on shoyu broth. Spring brings cherry blossom, autumn colours the hills in late November, and summer is humid and loud with cicadas. Winter mornings can bring frost to shaded bends in the mountains, so check conditions. Park and walk the shopping arcades for an hour if there is light left.
t.tokyo west@35.7,139.5:
The reading of forty metres above sea level tells you the geography: the Musashino plateau, a broad terrace of the Tama River's old floodplain, flat as a table and covered in houses, farms and the long green ribbons of watercourses. Kokubunji, the nearest town, is a commuter hub on the Chuo Line, and the route out toward the west starts here, heading for the mountains that appear as a blue line on clear winter days.

What makes this plateau special is its water engineering. In 1653, the Tamagawa Aqueduct was dug to bring drinking water from the Tama River to Edo, about forty kilometres of open channel running along the ridge line, with minimal slope, and it fed the growing city for centuries. Much of it is now a footpath lined with cherry trees, and stretches near Kodaira and Mitaka are a lovely place to cycle. It was engineered by two brothers of the Tamagawa family, whose names are still remembered, and the surname became the canal's own.

As an exit from the city, the route is anything but wild. Roads are straight, the traffic lights are numerous and the speed limits are strictly enforced, so patience is more useful than a throttle. The reward starts further west, past Tachikawa and Ome, where the road tilts upward and the Chichibu-Tama-Kai mountains come into view. Early morning departures avoid the worst traffic, and Sunday dawns are particularly quiet.

Fuel is easy here, and many stations are self-service. Convenience stores sell hot coffee, rice balls and sandwiches. Spring, with the cherry blossoms along the aqueduct, is the most beautiful time to leave, and late autumn adds yellow ginkgo leaves on the pavements. Summer is hot and humid, so carry water and ride early. A few minutes by the old channel, listening to the passing bicycles, is a nice way to remember how much effort went into the city's water.
t.boso peninsula pacific sweep@35.2,139.7:
Yokosuka is a naval town, and it announces itself with grey warships tied up along the shore, a mix of American and Japanese vessels. The pin sits just offshore, in the water at the mouth of Tokyo Bay, east of Kurihama, so the riding is done on the land to the west, where the city climbs steeply from the harbour into the hills. This is an unusual place: the base has been a centre of Japanese naval power since the nineteenth century, and the Americans have kept a major fleet here since 1945.

In a park by the shore, the battleship Mikasa, the flagship of Admiral Togo at the Battle of Tsushima in 1905, is preserved as a museum, and you can walk along her decks. The street called Dobuita, with its bars and shops, has a lively, slightly rough character, and the town has its own food, Yokosuka naval curry, a recipe that goes back to the Imperial Navy, which served curry on Fridays so sailors would not lose track of the days. A plate of it with a salad and milk is an authentic local lunch.

The riding here is a mixture. Roads in the city are narrow and crowded, with steep hills and sharp turns, but the coast road to the south, towards Kurihama and Miura, is open and scenic, with views of the bay and the ships. The surface is generally good, and speed limits are strictly enforced. The Boso peninsula, on the far side, is a short ferry ride away from Kurihama, a pleasant way to cross the bay and to avoid the traffic around Tokyo.

Yokosuka has more than four hundred thousand people, with fuel, convenience stores and restaurants everywhere. The best seasons are spring and autumn, with clear skies. Summer is hot, humid and crowded, and typhoons can bring strong winds and rain. A short walk along the waterfront at dusk, with the lights of the ships coming on and the smell of the sea, is a good way to end a ride. Bring identification if you want to go near the base entrances, and mind the signs.
t.boso peninsula pacific sweep scenic road:
Otsuki sits in the Kai basin of Yamanashi, at the mouth of a gorge cut by the Katsura river, and it is the gateway from Tokyo to Mount Fuji and the Fuji Five Lakes. The pin sits in the hills just east of the town, where the old Koshu Kaido, the road between Edo and Kofu, runs through a narrow valley between steep wooded ridges. The label mentions the Boso peninsula, which is on the other side of Tokyo, but this ride is a mountain one, with Fuji not far away.

The town has a famous bridge. Saruhashi, the Monkey Bridge, spans the Katsura gorge on the edge of town, and is counted among the three strange bridges of Japan. The present bridge is a replica, built of wood in a cantilever pattern with no piers, and it hangs over a deep, green gorge. According to legend, it was designed by a Korean craftsman who watched monkeys link arms to cross the ravine. It is a handsome piece of engineering, and a short walk through the woods leads to it.

The roads here are the start of the real mountains. Route 139 leaves Otsuki and climbs to the Fuji Five Lakes, with long curves through forests and a stunning view of Fuji as you crest the ridge, and the Koshu Kaido climbs to the Sasago Pass, at about a thousand metres, where the road crosses into Yamanashi from Tokyo. The surface is generally good, with fast bends and steady gradients, and on a clear day the cone of Fuji appears at the end of a straight, a sight that never grows old.

Otsuki has more than thirty thousand people, with fuel, convenience stores and restaurants, and Uenohara, to the east, has more. In the Kai region, local food includes houtou, a hearty noodle stew with pumpkin and vegetables, which is just the thing on a cold day, and fruit, particularly grapes and peaches, in season. The best seasons are autumn, with red maples and clear air, and early summer. In winter, ice and snow can close the passes, and the roads may be icy in the shade.
t.mount haruna and ikaho onsen@35.5,139.4:
Machida is a curious place: it is technically part of Tokyo, yet it pokes into Kanagawa like a thumb, and its streets feel more like Yokohama than like the capital. The pin sits close to the centre, in a dense mix of shopping streets, apartment blocks and the long, straight ribbon of Route 16, the great ring road that circles Tokyo about forty kilometres from the centre and is the logistical spine of the metropolitan region. The label mentions Mount Haruna and Ikaho, far to the north, so consider this the place where the day begins.

The town has an old role as a trading post. In the nineteenth century, silk from the mountains of Yamanashi and Nagano was carried on pack horses along a route that led down to Yokohama, where it was sold to foreign merchants, and the road became known as the Silk Road of Japan. Machida stood at its midpoint, and the merchants' warehouses made it prosperous. Today the road is a busy highway, but its history survives in museums and in the names of shops.

The strength of Machida as a starting point lies in its position. West of here, the Tama hills begin, a ripple of wooded ridges and reservoirs that mark the edge of the plain, and within half an hour you can be on quiet roads with the Tanzawa mountains ahead, the nearest real range to Tokyo. To the north-west is the Okutama valley, and to the west lie Lake Sagami and the road into the Tanzawa. The question is how to get out of town, and the answer is to start early, since Route 16 is jammed with trucks from dawn.

Fuel is plentiful, since Machida has nearly four hundred thousand people and a petrol station at almost every junction, with convenience stores and family restaurants for breakfast. A canned coffee and a rice ball from a convenience store is a Japanese rider's breakfast of choice. The best days are autumn and winter weekdays, when the air is clear and the traffic is light. Weekends are crowded, and the rainy season brings low cloud and damp roads, while summer heat on the asphalt can be fierce.
t.mount haruna and ikaho onsen high point@:
The Tanzawa mountains rise suddenly from the Kanagawa plain, and the country near Lake Miyagase, where this pin sits, is where the urban sprawl finally gives way to forest. Miyagase is a big reservoir, formed by a dam on the Nakatsu river, one of the largest in Kanagawa, and it supplies water to much of the region. Around it, the hills are steep and covered with cedar and cypress, and the roads that wind along the valley sides are among the best near Tokyo.

The surrounding mountains are a prefectural park and a favourite with walkers and riders alike. To the south-west, Mount Oyama, at about 1,250 metres, is an old shrine mountain, whose shrine, Afuri, was a place where people prayed for rain, and the town at its foot is known for its tofu, made with clear mountain water. A cable car climbs part of the way, and the old pilgrim route is lined with shops and inns. The mountain is often in cloud, as it catches the moist air from the sea.

The riding is superb in its way. The roads are narrow, with tight hairpins through the trees, and the surface is smooth but often damp and covered with leaves and moss, so the pace needs to be steady. In the early morning, mist hangs in the valleys, and the smell of wet cedar is strong. Cyclists and other riders are numerous on weekends, and the road to the dam is popular, so care is needed on blind corners. In winter, ice forms on the shaded sections, and some roads are closed for the season.

Fuel is the main thing to plan. Zama and Atsugi, ten kilometres away, are large towns with plenty of stations, while the road beyond the dam has few. Convenience stores and small restaurants serve noodles and rice dishes, and a stop at a mountain cafe with a view of the lake is welcome. Spring brings fresh green and cherry blossom, early summer is cool and misty, and autumn brings red maples, the best season. Midsummer is a cool escape from the heat of the plain.
t.mount haruna and ikaho onsen scenic road:
Ageo and Saitama are part of the great sprawl north of Tokyo, but they have a few unexpected corners, and this pin, on a rural road near the Arakawa river, finds one. The river is wide here, with a broad floodplain of fields, golf courses and cycling paths, and the long bridge across it gives a wide view of the plain, with the mountains of Chichibu on the western horizon, white with snow in winter. It is not a mountain pass, but it has its own openness.

Saitama city, six kilometres away, has a few things worth knowing. In the district of Omiya, the Railway Museum holds a collection of old trains, including steam locomotives and early Shinkansen, a place for anyone who loves machines. Nearby, a quarter known as Bonsai Village was founded in the 1920s by gardeners who moved from Tokyo after the Great Kanto Earthquake, and it still has several nurseries where you can see miniature trees, some of them hundreds of years old. The Hikawa shrine, approached by a long avenue of old zelkova trees, is said to be two thousand years old.

The roads here are crowded and urban, with traffic lights and trucks, but along the river the levee roads offer a quieter alternative, running flat and straight with views across the water. In spring, the banks are covered in rape blossom and cherry trees, and in autumn the pampas grass shimmers in the low light. Wind is a factor, since the open floodplain gives it a free run.

Fuel and food are no trouble in a city of more than a million, with every junction offering a station and a convenience store. The best way to enjoy the area is early in the morning on a weekend, when the traffic is light, and the best seasons are spring and autumn, when the air is clear. In summer, the humidity is heavy, and in winter the dry wind from the mountains brings clear skies and sharp views of the far peaks.
t.bandai azuma skyline weekend high point@:
The pin lies on the flat land where Saitama meets Ibaraki, and there is no pass here, only the long, low line of a levee and the sky. The villages around it, Sakai, Satte and Sugito, sit on the old floodplain of the Tone and the Edo rivers, in a landscape of rice fields, vegetable plots and straight canals, and the highest point for miles is a flood bank, perhaps ten metres above the fields.

The plain has its own attractions. At Satte, the embankment of an old irrigation channel, called Gongendo, is planted with a long avenue of cherry trees, and in early April it is lined with a bright strip of rape flowers, the pink and yellow glowing in the spring sun. A few kilometres south, at Kasukabe, lies one of the strangest sights in Japan, a huge underground flood-control system, with a cathedral-like chamber of giant concrete pillars some twenty metres below the surface, built to protect Tokyo from typhoon floods, and open for guided tours. It is a good reminder of how much of the Kanto plain depends on water control.

Rice and vegetables are the main crops, and the farm stands along the roads sell fresh produce in season, such as strawberries in spring and Japanese pears in late summer. The roads here are almost empty, with long straights and a few right-angled bends, and at harvest time the sight of golden rice drying on racks is lovely. Wind can be a factor, as there is nothing to block it, and in winter the dry northerly can be sharp.

Fuel and food are easy at Satte, with more than fifty thousand people, and in Sugito, with nearly fifty thousand. Convenience stores and family restaurants are common, and some farms offer meals made from their own produce. The best seasons are spring, for cherry blossoms, and autumn, for clear skies and golden rice, and the summer heat is fierce, with humidity and mosquitoes on the riverbanks. In the rainy season, the rivers rise and the sky is grey, but the greens are vivid.
t.bandai azuma skyline weekend scenic road:
The foothills west of Tokyo, around Hanno and Ome, are where the Kanto plain finally crumples into mountains, and the pin sits among low wooded ridges at the edge of Saitama and Tokyo, with the Okutama peaks rising to the west. The label mentions Bandai and Azuma, which are in Fukushima, much further north, so this is the local, softer version: a quiet country of cedar forest, tea fields and small valleys, only an hour from the city.

Hanno has a long history of forestry. Under the name of Nishikawa timber, cedar and cypress from the hills were cut, tied into rafts and floated down the Iruma and Arakawa rivers to Edo, where they were used to rebuild the city after its frequent fires. The old wood merchants' houses in the town still stand. In late September, the Koma river bank near Hanno is covered with millions of red spider lilies, which bloom for a week or two in a vivid scarlet carpet, and draw crowds of visitors.

Ome, a few kilometres to the east, is an old town on the edge of the mountains, once a centre of silk and cloth trade, and later known for hand-painted cinema billboards. It is also the gateway to the Okutama valley and the road to Lake Okutama, one of the best rides near Tokyo. The Ome road winds up the valley of the Tama river, with tunnels, gorges and views of the green water, and in autumn the leaves are splendid.

The roads in the foothills are narrow and twisty, with sharp bends through cedar forest, and the surface is often damp and covered with needles. Traffic is light on weekdays but heavy on weekends, with riders and cyclists. Fuel is plentiful in Hanno and Ome, which have more than eighty thousand and nearly a hundred and fifty thousand people respectively, so fill the tank before heading into the mountains. Convenience stores and small restaurants serve noodles and rice dishes. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with winter bringing ice on the shaded roads.
t.bandai azuma skyline weekend photo pull:
Oiso has a claim that surprises people: in 1885 it opened what is regarded as Japan's first sea-bathing beach, on the idea of a doctor who believed that salt water was good for health. The town on the shore of Sagami Bay became a resort for the rich and powerful, and several prime ministers had villas here, among them Yoshida Shigeru, who shaped postwar Japan. The pin sits a few kilometres inland, in the hills between Oiso, Ninomiya and Hiratsuka, and the label talks about Bandai and Azuma, which are far to the north, so this is a coastal ending.

In the Edo period, Oiso was one of the fifty-three stations of the Tokaido, the great road between Edo and Kyoto, and the old road runs along the coast, lined with pine trees. Today its modern descendant, Route 1, is a busy highway, and the coastal Route 134 is a slow, scenic road along the shore, with long views over the sea and a line of surfers in the waves. On a clear day, Mount Fuji stands across the bay with the Izu peninsula to its left and the island of Oshima out to sea.

Hiratsuka, to the east, is known for its Tanabata festival in July, when huge paper decorations hang from every street, and the Shonan beaches are among the best in Kanto. The hills behind the coast are quiet, with orchards of mandarin oranges and a few tea fields, and narrow roads climb between them, giving views of the sea and Fuji. They are the best place for a photograph at the end of a ride.

Fuel and food are easy in Hiratsuka, with a population of more than two hundred and fifty thousand, and Oiso has cafes and seafood restaurants with views of the sea. Fresh sardines, whitebait and sea bream are the local specialities, eaten with a cold beer. The best seasons are autumn and winter, with clear air and good views of Fuji, and spring brings cherry blossoms. Summer weekends are crowded and hot, with traffic jams on the coast road, so an early start is wise.
t.shosenkyo gorge@35.8,139.9:
Matsudo is a city of nearly half a million people on the Chiba side of the Edo River, the border with Tokyo, and nothing about it says Shosenkyo or mountains. It is a commuter place, an hour or so from the gorge's Yamanashi valleys, and so a natural endpoint when the day's riding has taken you back through the whole sprawl of the Kanto plain. Think of it as the dock where the ship comes in.

The Edo River gives the place its character. It was dug and straightened in the seventeenth century to control the Tone river's floods and to carry goods to Edo, and its broad, grassy embankments now hold cycle paths, sports fields and fishermen. Across from Matsudo, in Tokyo's Katsushika ward, lies Shibamata, the setting of the long-running Tora-san film series, and the Yagiri no Watashi, a small ferry that has crossed the river here since the Edo period. It carries foot passengers and cyclists for a small fare, and it is a charming bit of surviving old Japan in a modern suburb.

For a rider, the roads are urban and dull, laced with traffic lights and trucks serving the logistics parks along the Joban line and the Gaikan expressway. The best moments are along the river embankment roads in the early morning, when the light is soft and the air is cool. Rain and typhoons can flood the low ground, and in summer the humidity is something to be endured, with cicadas shouting from every tree.

You will not struggle for services. Petrol stations line every major road, and ramen, curry and sushi shops are around the station. Matsudo also has a pear story: the Nijisseiki variety, still the classic Japanese pear, is said to have been found as a chance seedling here in the 1880s, and Chiba remains famous for its pears and peanuts. Autumn is the most pleasant season, with clear air and dry weather. Park the bike, walk the embankment at sunset, and let the day wind down slowly.
Few ride days begin in a more ordinary place than this one. The pin lies on the flat, built-over land between Yashio and Sōka, just inside the Saitama border where the Tsukuba Express runs towards Tokyo, and the Nakagawa and Edo rivers draw the edges of the plain. It is a good place for a fuel stop and a coffee, with almost no mountain, forest or sea anywhere in sight, and that is the whole point. The big scenery is a long way south, so the job here is to start with a full tank and a clear head.

Sōka has one genuinely local claim to fame. It is known for senbei, the hard, savoury rice crackers grilled over charcoal and brushed with soy, which were sold to travellers along the old Nikkō road when this was a post town on the way north from Edo. You can still smell the soy drifting from small shops if the wind is right. Nagareyama, just across the river in Chiba, is known for mirin, the sweet cooking wine, and for a short stay by the Shinsengumi in the spring of 1868, when Kondō Isami surrendered there. Not many places can claim both a seasoning and a samurai surrender within a few minutes of a gas station.

The riding from here is a matter of getting out of the city sensibly. Local roads run in strict grids through low-rise suburbs, with traffic lights every few hundred metres and frequent speed cameras on the bigger arteries. The sensible way south is to join the Gaikan ring road or the expressways, and then to cross Tokyo Bay by the Aqua-Line, which dives into a tunnel and surfaces at a mid-bay island before landing on the Chiba side. Early starts pay off, because by nine on a weekday the whole region has woken up and wants to go the same way as you.

Everything you need is within a few streets of the pin, and a town this size has a dozen stations, several that take cards at the pump, plus supermarkets and cafés that open early. Check your ETC card is in the slot and your tank is full, because the first long stretch of toll road runs a good way before the next service area. Japan's expressway service areas are excellent, with proper food and clean washrooms, and they are fine for a second breakfast. Bring layers, since the coast will be cooler and breezier than this baking plain.
t.tanzawa and doshi road@35.9,138.6:
You are a long way up here, and the whole country seems to turn on its side. The pin sits deep in the mountains of Okuchichibu, near the headwaters of the Arakawa and the flanks of Mount Kinpu, where Saitama, Yamanashi and Nagano meet in a tangle of steep ridges and granite pillars. The nearest towns, Hokuto and Enzan, are more than twenty kilometres away down the valleys, so this is a place to arrive with a full stomach or a plan. The mountains are the heart of Chichibu-Tama-Kai National Park, and the air has a thin, cool tang even in summer.

The roads that cross this part of the Japanese Alps are narrow, steep and old, and many of them are closed in winter. Corners are tight and often blind, with sudden stretches of damp or frost in the shade, and the surface can carry gravel and fallen branches. Mist rolls in without warning, and rain in the afternoon is common in summer. On the other side of the divide, the ground falls toward the Kōfu basin, where the ridges give way to orchards of grapes and peaches, the home of Koshu wine, and on a clear day the whole basin shows below you with Mount Fuji beyond.

Food in this country is hearty. The great dish of Yamanashi is hōtō, a thick, flat noodle stew cooked with pumpkin, mushrooms and root vegetables in a miso broth, served bubbling in an iron pot. It is ideal after a cold ride, and it is usually served at roadside restaurants and farm inns across the prefecture. In the Chichibu valleys on the other side, the specialities are miso potatoes and a rich pork cutlet on rice, which riders from Tokyo tend to seek out on weekends.

As for practicalities, fuel is limited. The valley roads have long gaps, and the nearest sure supply is in Enzan, Kōfu or Hokuto, so fill up before climbing. Mobile signal comes and goes. Do not rely on cards in remote places, and carry some cash. Because mountain weather changes quickly, bring a rain layer and gloves even on a sunny morning. If you reach this place in October, the larch and maple turn the slopes red and gold, and the roads are at their quietest after the first snow dusts the peaks.
t.venus line long day@35.8,139.3:
Ōme is where Tokyo stops being Tokyo. The pin sits a few kilometres west of the town centre, on the Tama river terraces where the Chūō commuter line gives way to forest, and the mountains of Okutama begin as a green wall at the end of every street. For a rider heading out on a long day, this is the last proper pocket of petrol stations, bakeries and convenience stores, and it is worth using all three before the road starts to climb. Hannō and Fussa, on either side, are both large enough to have everything a motorbike could need.

The town has a past that explains its look. The Ōme Kaidō, the road that ran from Edo up the Tama valley, carried lime from the quarries here to whitewash the walls of Edo castle, and later the area turned to weaving, producing a striped cotton cloth that was sold across the city. A museum of old film billboards, hand-painted in the style of the 1950s, gives the old centre a nostalgic charm that suits a morning coffee. Every February the Ōme Marathon fills the streets with runners, and the whole town goes quiet and cold around it.

The riding that starts here is the real reason to come. Route 411, the Ōme Kaidō's modern descendant, climbs along the Tama gorge with a mix of tunnels, tight bends and short, fast straights, and it carries a good deal of weekend traffic, both bikes and sightseeing buses. In the early morning, before eight, the road is empty and the air smells of damp cedar and river stone. By midday on a fine Sunday it is a slow procession. Choose your hours and the same road feels like two different roads.

Do not skimp on fuel here. The Okutama valley has pumps, but they are few and close early, and the long climbs eat more than you think. A small cash reserve is also useful, since the mountain cafés and soba shops often take only coins and notes. Fill the tank, check the tyre pressures, buy a rice ball, and then go west with the sun behind you. In the last days of October the maples turn, and the whole valley starts to glow a little at the edges.
Okutama Lake sits at the head of the Tama valley like a cold green bowl, and this pin lies close to its shore, a few kilometres from Itsukaichi on one side and Ōtsuki on the other. The lake is not natural. It was made when the Ogōchi dam was completed in 1957, drowning a number of villages to give Tokyo a drinking-water reservoir, and today it supplies a large part of the capital's taps. The surface is calm and dark, the forested slopes plunge straight into the water, and the roads along the shore have a quiet, reflective quality that surprises people who expect a tourist trap.

Riding here is a mountain pleasure, tempered by a few cautions. The roads around the lake and over the passes into Yamanashi are narrow, with tight hairpins, short tunnels and rough patches where rockfall has been patched. In the dry, bright months of spring and autumn the surface grips well. In the wet it turns slick under the trees, and in winter, ice lingers in the shade long after midday. Because this is catchment land, you will see gates, signs and sometimes closures for maintenance, so check ahead before building a day on a particular road. The route over Matsuhime pass towards Kosuge is the classic way through.

The nature around the lake is worth noticing. Cedar and cypress plantations climb the slopes, with oak, beech and maple higher up, and the autumn colour from late October is one of the best in the Kantō. Deer and Japanese serow live in the forest, monkeys appear on the road, and in the evening, bats skim the surface of the water. The valley below the dam has caves, including the Nippara limestone cave, a long underground passage that is open to the public and noticeably cold.

Practically, you are in a remote place. Fuel is available in the Ōme and Itsukaichi directions, and in Ōtsuki on the Yamanashi side, but nothing in between that you should rely on. There are small cafés and a visitor centre near the dam, which may close on weekdays in winter. Wear warm gloves, because the shade near the water is cold even in May. If you make it for sunrise, the mist rising off the lake is something you will remember for years.
t.gunma three mountain day@35.6,139.4:
Some ride days begin with a good hour of dull riding, and this is where yours starts. The pin lies on the southern edge of Machida, on the border between Tokyo and Kanagawa, in a landscape of low hills, shopping centres and train lines. Machida is a big, practical place of four hundred thousand people, with every kind of petrol station, convenience store and burger counter. For a long day to the mountains of Gunma, it is the sensible place to fill up and gather your thoughts before the northern run.

Machida also carries a bit of history. In the late nineteenth century, silk from the Hachiōji region travelled along a trade route to the port of Yokohama, and the old silk road passed through here. You can still trace some of its course in the line of the Yokohama railway, which was built to carry the same bales. Zama, next door, is known for its sunflower fields and an American army base, and the countryside south of here was once a patchwork of mulberry orchards, replaced now by housing estates and light industry.

The ride north to Gunma's three famous mountains, Akagi, Haruna and Myōgi, is long. From Machida, you work your way up through Route 16 and the expressways, joining the Kan-Etsu or another toll road, and cover a good few hundred kilometres before the hills begin. An early start, ideally before six, is not an indulgence but a necessity. The morning light on the plain is thin and clear, and the riding is easy but dull. Do not plan on stopping often; use the expressway service areas, which have good food and clean toilets.

Fuel and food are no problem here. Stations in the area are numerous, and many take cards at the pump. Check that your ETC card works, that your phone has a charger and that your tyres are properly inflated, since the long expressway stretches punish a soft tyre. The main hazard of the start is traffic, as Route 16 is heavy with trucks. If you leave a little earlier, the roads belong to delivery drivers and a few other bleary riders, and the sun rises over a quiet suburb. That alone is worth getting up for.
t.gunma three mountain day@35.4,139.3:
The pin lies in the Hadano basin, a bowl of flat ground tucked against the southern foot of the Tanzawa mountains, with Ōiso and the sea about five kilometres to the south and the town of Isehara beside it. The big profile above the plain is Mount Ōyama, a squat, rounded peak about twelve hundred metres high that has been a pilgrimage destination since the Edo period. Its shrine, Afuri, was believed to bring rain, and the Edo townspeople made the trip in organised pilgrim bands. Today it is a hiking mountain, with a cable car and a famous road of souvenir shops.

The local food is a reason to stop. Ōyama's speciality is tofu, made with the clear mountain water, served in many forms from simple cold blocks to elaborate multi-course meals in the wooden restaurants along the approach road. Hadano is known for its groundwater, which rises in springs around the basin and is bottled and sold, and in earlier centuries for tobacco. Ōyama also gave Japan its spinning tops, which are still turned and painted by hand. It is a tasteful, quiet little region where lunch is not a chore.

Ōiso, just down the road, is where Japan's first seaside bathing resort opened in the 1880s. A local doctor promoted sea bathing as a cure, and the railway brought Tokyo's well-to-do to the beach. The town still has a charming old-fashioned air, with large villas behind pine trees and a long beach. It makes a pleasant end to a ride, if you are returning toward Kanagawa.

For riders, the corridor along Route 246 and the roads leading toward the Tanzawa foothills are a common route to the mountains. The traffic is heavy on weekends and the roads are busy at rush hour. Fuel is easy: Hadano and Isehara are big towns with several stations. Food stops are plentiful, and the tofu restaurants on the Ōyama approach road offer a good lunch at a relaxed pace. Remember that this is a lunch stop in a day that continues north, and a day that long needs a proper rest at the right moment.
t.tokyo kanto rides@36.3,139.6:
Sano ramen is the first thing to say about this corner of Tochigi. The town is known across Japan for noodles that are flat, springy and kneaded by bamboo poles, served in a clear soy broth that tastes clean and slightly sweet. The pin lies just a few kilometres from Sano, on the flat, farmed floodplain where Tochigi meets Gunma, and any rider arriving at midday should know where lunch is. It also has a famous outlet mall and a temple devoted to warding off bad luck, so the town has a steady flow of visitors.

The terrain is the plain of the Watarase and Tone rivers, marked by drainage channels, levees and rice, with the edge of the Ryōmō hills rising to the north. A few kilometres west, Tatebayashi is known for two things. In spring, the azaleas of Tsutsujigaoka Park bloom in thousands, some of them hundreds of years old, and a festival draws visitors from all over the Kantō. The Morin-ji temple preserves the folk tale of the Bunbuku Chagama, a tanuki that turned into a tea kettle and brought good fortune to a poor priest. It is a cheerful bit of local lore.

South-east of here, the Watarase retention basin is a large wetland where four prefectures meet, built to control flooding and now registered as a Ramsar site, a good place for reeds, herons and migrating birds. In winter, harriers hunt over the reeds and the whole area has a stark beauty. This is not the Japan of mountains and temples but a quiet, productive heartland of vegetables and rice, and the landscape rewards slow looking.

For riders, the roads are flat and straight, which suits an early start from Tokyo before heading to the hills. Fuel is easy, with Sano, Tatebayashi and Fujioka all within a short ride and plenty of stations along the main roads. Ride with attention to crossings, since farm traffic and local drivers do not always look. Pick a hot day and the plain can be oppressive, so take your time and keep water on the bike. In November, when the harvest is done and the air is clear, the views to the mountains are some of the best of the year.
t.okutama and chichibu forest roads@36.1,1:
Nagatoro is one of the places that Tokyoites think of as the countryside, and it earns the title. The Arakawa river cuts through a band of green schist here, polishing the rock into broad, flat terraces known as iwadatami, or rock mats, and for a few kilometres the river runs in a gorge lined with maples. Flat boats poled by boatmen carry visitors downstream in the summer, and the whole place has a holiday air, with small restaurants and souvenir shops lined along the banks. The pin sits a few kilometres east, in the hills near Ogawa and Yorii, on the edge of the Chichibu region.

The nearby town of Ogawa is known for washi, handmade paper that has been produced in the district for over a thousand years and was added to the UNESCO list of intangible heritage with two other Japanese paper traditions. In the same valley, Yorii has a medieval castle site on a hill. Chichibu itself, the large basin to the west, is a town of cement works, textiles and a famous night festival in early December, when huge floats are pulled through the streets under fireworks. Mount Buko, a limestone peak that has been quarried for decades, stands over the town.

The riding is relaxed. Roads such as Route 140, the Chichibu road, and the prefectural roads along the Arakawa run through forested hills with moderate bends and occasional tunnels. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends, when visitors fill the riverside, but on weekdays it is calm. The best seasons are spring, for the cherry blossom, and autumn, for the leaves, and summer riding is hot in the valleys, so start early. Be mindful of leaves and damp patches in shaded corners.

Food is the point of this stop.
