Kamowakeikazuchi, the god worshipped at Kamigamo, is a deity of lightning, and the compound beside the Kamo river in northern Kyoto is thought to be one of the oldest Shinto sites in Japan, with a founding that tradition dates to the seventh century. In the compound, two neat cones of white sand stand in front of the main sanctuary, symbols of purity, imitating the sacred hill where the god is said to have come down. Beyond them, a small stream runs under a bridge in a grove of old trees, and the whole place has a quiet, swept look, like a stage before the performance.

The performances come in May. The Aoi Festival, which links Kamigamo with its sister shrine downriver at Shimogamo, is one of Kyoto's three great festivals, a procession of nobles, ox carts and horses dressed in the style of the Heian court, all wearing leaves of hollyhock, aoi, as emblems. Just before it, in early May, a horse race called Kurabeuma is run on the grass at the shrine, a tradition that runs back more than nine hundred years. The shrine was included in the World Heritage listing of the historic monuments of ancient Kyoto in 1994.

The ride from here goes south to the Nara palace site, which links two capitals, the Heian one at Kyoto and the earlier Heijo one, the first great planned city on the island, founded in 710. The route cuts through Kyoto's outskirts and then southwards through the hills and valleys around Uji, a town famous for green tea, along the Kizu river and over the low ridges that separate the two basins. It is not demanding riding, more a pleasant, rural pace through tea fields and bamboo, with villages in between. North of Kamigamo, by contrast, the Kitayama hills rise quickly into forested valleys, and a short ride up the road toward Kurama and Kibune shows another side of Kyoto, steep, shady and cool even in summer.

Kamigamo is a neighbourhood of the city, so petrol stations, bakeries and noodle counters surround it. The shrine itself is open to walk around freely, though some inner areas have restrictions, and early morning is the best time, when the gravel is raked and the temple priests are sweeping. Parking for motorbikes is limited, so use a nearby lot and walk.
t.tenryu ji@35.0,135.7:
People come to Arashiyama for the bamboo, and they leave with the memory of a garden. Tenryu-ji, the great Zen temple at the foot of the hills on the west side of Kyoto, was founded in 1339 by the shogun Ashikaga Takauji, who built it to console the spirit of the emperor Go-Daigo, his former rival. The garden, designed by the Zen master Muso Soseki, is older than almost every other thing you will see in the area: a pond with rocks arranged like a mountain landscape, with the hills of Arashiyama pulled into the view as borrowed scenery. It has survived fire after fire, though most of the halls themselves are later rebuilds.

Beside the temple's north gate you step directly into the famous bamboo grove, a cool, green corridor where the stems rise far overhead and clatter softly in the wind. It is busy from mid-morning, so the best time to see it is before eight. Beyond, the Katsura river runs wide and slow below the Togetsukyo bridge, and old boatmen still take visitors on the rapids upstream at Hozu. In November the hills around turn red and gold.

For a rider, the interest here lies in the roads that lead out of Arashiyama. Behind the temple, the Kyoto hills rise into forest, and the Shuzan Kaido, now Route 162, climbs north toward Takao and Keihoku, a road that follows a river valley through cedar plantations and tiny villages, with a pleasant mix of bends and gentle gradients. On weekdays it is quiet, and on warm weekends it fills with cyclists and groups of riders heading for the mountain restaurants. This ride, though, heads south to the Fujiwara palace site near Kashihara, crossing the whole of Kyoto and then the border into Nara.

In Arashiyama itself, the main street is lined with cafes, sweet shops, and stands selling tofu, matcha ice cream and pickles. Petrol stations are on the main roads around the district, but within the tourist area, parking for bikes can be hard to find, so try the car parks at the edge. It is a ride best savoured slowly, with a good coffee, because the temple repays attention. Spring and autumn are the most beautiful seasons, but also the busiest, while winter brings a rare quiet and the occasional dusting of snow.
t.historic monuments of ancient kyoto@35.0:
Kyoto sits in a basin with mountains on three sides, a grid of streets laid out in the late eighth century on the model of the Chinese capital, and it remained the imperial seat until 1868. That long continuity explains why the World Heritage list includes seventeen separate places under the name of the historic monuments of ancient Kyoto: temples, shrines and one castle, dotted around the city and across the border into Otsu. The city was spared the worst of the bombing in the Second World War, which is a large part of why so much survives.

For a rider, the city is easier than its reputation suggests, if you leave your expectations at the edge. The grid helps, the avenues run straight, and the big roads around the outer ring let you cross town fast. But the central streets are narrow, one-way and crowded with bicycles, taxis and buses, and parking for motorbikes is limited. A good plan is to leave the machine at the hotel and walk, or to find a dedicated bike park and base yourself there. In the evening, the lanes of Gion and Pontocho glow with paper lanterns, and the smell of grilled fish and charcoal drifts through the alleys.

The ride that begins in Kyoto heads for Yakushi-ji in Nara, an old Buddhist temple founded at the end of the seventh century whose twin pagodas hold some of the finest early architecture in Japan. The route takes you south through the Uji district, where the best Japanese green tea is grown and where you can find a cup of matcha served alongside sweet bean paste in an old tea house. It is also the home of Byodo-in, the Phoenix Hall, an eleventh-century building familiar from the ten-yen coin. From there you follow the Kizu river valley and cross low hills into the Nara basin, a quiet and mildly rolling ride past rice fields, tea terraces and bamboo thickets.

You can fuel in nearly any part of the city, but the busiest areas near Kyoto Station or Gion have fewer stations than the outer districts, so top up when you see one. Food is an art here: tofu cooked in a dozen ways, vegetables pickled in rice bran, and the multi-course meals known as kaiseki. In the hot, damp summer, a cold bowl of noodles by the river is just the thing, and in winter the hills are clean and cold, with bare maples against a pale sky.
t.saiho ji@35.0,135.7:
Saiho-ji has a nickname that tells the whole story: Kokedera, the moss temple. The garden is carpeted by well over a hundred varieties of moss, in shades from emerald to near yellow, spreading between the trees and around the pond in a soft, damp quilt, and a day of rain makes it glow. The effect is accidental in origin, since the moss spread after the temple was neglected in the nineteenth century, but it fits the garden's older bones, which were laid out in the fourteenth century by the Zen master Muso Soseki. Muso also designed the garden of Tenryu-ji, on the other side of the Katsura river, and you can see a family likeness.

The temple is run with great care, and the price of that care is that you cannot simply turn up. Visits require a reservation made in advance, and visitors take part in a short session of sutra copying before walking the garden, with a donation expected. This keeps the numbers low and the atmosphere calm, a very different feeling from the crowded temples in the middle of the city. If you plan a ride around it, sort out the booking first, since slots may fill up, and arrive on time.

The surrounding district, Matsuo, has other things to explore if you have time. Matsuo Taisha, a short distance away, is the shrine to the god of sake brewing, and brewers from across Japan come to pray here. The hills above are wooded and calm, and a stream runs through the shrine grounds. In general this western edge of Kyoto is a quiet residential area, with narrow lanes, bicycles, and the occasional old farmhouse hiding behind a wall.

From here the ride goes to Yakushi-ji, in the south of Nara, across the Kyoto basin and then over the low hills near Uji. It is a steady, mostly flat day, and there is no need to hurry. Roads around Saiho-ji are tight, and parking is limited, so a smaller bike is easier to handle. Fuel stations are along the main roads to the south and east, and the area has small bakeries and noodle shops for lunch. Visit in the rainy season of early summer if you want the moss at its richest, or in the golden light of late autumn, when the maples set the green on fire.
t.oshino hakkai springs@35.5,138.8:
Eight ponds, one hundred yards from the road, and every one of them clear enough to count the pebbles. Oshino Hakkai takes its water from the snow and rain of Mount Fuji, which sinks into the porous volcanic rock of the mountain and takes decades to filter down, so the springs that emerge in the village of Oshino are astonishingly pure and cold. The water holds close to a constant temperature all year, so in winter mist rises from the ponds, and in summer they feel like cool air-conditioning. Carp and trout drift through the plants, water wheels turn quietly, and thatched houses stand behind the ponds, though these days they hold shops selling pickles, soba noodles and sweets.

It is a popular stop, and it feels like it. Tour groups arrive in coaches during the day, and the pathways around the ponds fill up. The trick is to come early or late, when the village returns to being a village, and the hills are quiet. The springs were included in the World Heritage listing of Fuji in 2013, and they were an important place of purification for the pilgrims who climbed the mountain over centuries. It is a good moment to eat a bowl of hot soba and consider how much trouble people once took to prepare for a climb.

The ride continues toward Tokyo and the National Museum of Western Art in Ueno, a building designed by Le Corbusier, and one of the world's few chances to see his architecture in Asia. You can take the Doshi Road, Route 413, which heads south-east from Yamanaka lake, through Doshi village and down to the plains of Kanagawa, a twisting road through forest that motorcyclists have loved for decades. It has speed enforcement in places, so keep your eyes open, and it gets busy on weekends. The fast alternative is the Chuo Expressway, which runs east to Tokyo in under two hours with Mount Fuji visible on a clear day.

Oshino is a small village, but Fujiyoshida, a few kilometres away, has fuel stations, supermarkets and hotels. The best seasons are autumn and winter, when the air is clear and Fuji is likely to be showing. The lake region can be bitterly cold in January, and ice and snow can affect the roads, so check conditions.
t.jizera mountains@50.9,15.2:
The Jizera Mountains sit in the far north of Bohemia, right where the Czech Republic meets Poland and Germany, and they have a stern, quiet character that sets them apart from the better-known Krkonoše to the east. Hejnice, at their foot, is a small town in the valley of the Smědá river, famous for a large Baroque pilgrimage church with a basilica and a Franciscan monastery. Above it, the ridges rise to forested plateaus and open peat bogs, with roads that thread between spruce and beech.

The mountains have a hard recent history. In the 1970s and 1980s the forests of this region were devastated by acid rain from the power stations of the nearby coalfields, a part of Europe sometimes called the Black Triangle. Great swathes of spruce died, and the landscape you see today is partly a result of replanting and natural recovery. Many of the high-altitude areas are protected, and the night skies here are some of the darkest in the country, since the area has been recognised for its low light pollution.

For a motorcyclist, the Jizeras mean quiet, twisty roads through forest, with some fine bends near the passes and an air of seclusion. Surfaces are mixed, with good main roads and rougher forest tracks, some of which are closed to motor vehicles, so check signs and follow them. The weather can change quickly, with mist and cold even in summer, and winter brings snow and ice, so the riding season runs from late spring to early autumn.

Hejnice is small, with fewer than three thousand people, so expect basic facilities, and plan for fuel in larger towns like Frýdlant or Liberec, where you will find plenty of petrol stations and restaurants. In the mountain villages, small guesthouses serve Czech comfort food, and a bowl of garlic soup or a plate of fried cheese will go down well after a chilly ride.

On this ride, the Jizeras link with Herrnhut and the Muskauer Park, which gives a nice picture of Upper Lusatia, a borderland where Czech, German and Polish history overlap. The mountains are a gentle introduction to that world.
t.kutna hora historical town centre with t:
Silver made Kutná Hora. In the late thirteenth century rich veins were found in the hills here, and within a few decades this small town east of Prague had become one of the richest places in medieval Europe. The Bohemian kings minted their silver groschen here, in the building known as the Italian Court, and it was money from these mines that helped finance the reign of Wenceslas II and later Charles IV. The result is a town that has a cathedral's worth of ambition packed into a small hillside setting.

The great landmark is the church of St Barbara, begun in the late fourteenth century by the miners' guilds as a rival to the cathedral in Prague. Its roof is a marvel, a forest of ribs and pinnacles that rises over the town like the sails of a ship, and the interior has fine late Gothic vaulting. It was left unfinished for centuries and completed only much later, but the result is harmonious. The listing also includes the Cathedral of Our Lady at Sedlec, a short distance away, with a Baroque-Gothic interior by the architect Jan Santini Aichel, and nearby is the ossuary chapel, whose chandelier and decorations are made of human bones.

Riding to Kutná Hora from Prague is a pleasant and easy trip, mostly across rolling farmland and low hills, with moderate traffic and a good surface. The roads are not dramatic but they are enjoyable, with long views over fields and orchards, and small villages every few kilometres. The town itself is hilly, with cobbled streets in the centre, so go gently on a loaded bike and leave the machine at one of the car parks on the edge.

With over twenty thousand people, Kutná Hora has all the fuel, food and beds you could want. The restaurants around the old town serve classic Czech dishes, and you can finish with a coffee on one of the squares. Tourists come in large numbers, especially in summer, so arrive early or visit on a weekday.

The ride pairs the town with Průhonice and with the pilgrimage church of St John of Nepomuk at Zelená Hora, another listed Baroque marvel, and together they show how rich this part of Bohemia was.
t.kokorinsko sandstone roads@50.4,15.7:
Hořice is famous for two things: stone and wafers. The town has a school of sculpture, established in the nineteenth century to train carvers in the local sandstone, and statues and fountains in the streets show the skill of its graduates. The other fame is food, the Hořice tubes, thin rolled wafers filled with cream, which are a protected regional product and come in every flavour, from vanilla to hazelnut. Buy a box, and you will understand why people queue for them.

The coordinates lie to the east, in the village landscape around Bílá Třemešná, between Hořice and Dvůr Králové, where the roads wind through farmland with plenty of small climbs and descents. This is the country of the Podkrkonoší, the foothills of the Krkonoše mountains, a part of Bohemia that looks like a model village, with whitewashed cottages, painted church towers and fields in strips of different greens.

For fuel and food, Hořice, with about nine thousand people, is the nearest sizeable town, and has petrol stations, supermarkets and several cafes. The Prachov Rocks, the sandstone towers of the Bohemian Paradise, are some twenty-five kilometres to the west, and make a fine detour, with pathways between the rock walls and viewpoints across the forest. The Bohemian Paradise is a protected landscape, and it is well worth a short walk if you have time.

The riding is relaxed, with quiet back roads, smooth bends and sweeping views across the hills. In summer, the light is long, and the evenings are warm, with the smell of cut hay. The roads are generally well kept, but tractors and farm vehicles can slow progress, and fog can sit in the hollows in autumn. A good place to end a day is a village pub, with a plate of schnitzel, a glass of beer and a view of the hills.
t.odawara coast@35.3,139.2:
Odawara is the gate to Hakone, and it knows it. The city, with two hundred thousand people, sits where the Sagami Bay coast meets the foot of the mountains, about eighty kilometres southwest of Tokyo, and for centuries travellers on the Tokaido highway stopped here before tackling the pass. The castle was the seat of the Hojo clan, who ruled much of the Kanto plain in the sixteenth century until Toyotomi Hideyoshi besieged and took it in 1590. The keep that stands today is a postwar reconstruction, but the stone walls and moats are authentic enough, and the whole thing is worth a short visit on foot.

For a rider, it is a practical place. Fuel stations are everywhere, convenience stores open all night, and the roads out toward the mountains are clearly signed. The coast road, Route 135, runs south along the bay with the Pacific on one side and small fishing towns on the other, and the first light of the day, with the sea turning from grey to pink, is a lovely thing to see if you start early. Odawara is also a good place for breakfast: it is famous for kamaboko, steamed fish paste, and for dried fish, both of which come from the local fishing tradition and are on sale in shops near the station.

Expect traffic. The Tokyo to Hakone corridor is one of the busiest weekend routes in Japan, and on a sunny Saturday the roads fill up with cars, coaches and motorbikes by mid-morning. The best answer is to leave early, or to ride on a weekday, when it is quiet. Japan has its own habits too: speed limits are modest and enforced, tolls are common on the scenic roads, and an electronic toll card makes life easier if you have one. Motorcyclists often gather at roadside stops and convenience stores, and a nod or a wave is usual.

From Odawara the road climbs into the Hakone mountains almost at once, through a forested valley with hot spring villages and old inns, and the temperature drops a few degrees with each bend. On a clear day, Mount Fuji appears over the ridges, but do not count on it, because clouds often hide it in summer. The air is cooler and fresher in autumn, and the leaves are beautiful in November.
t.hakone turnpike high road@35.2,139.1:
Hakone Turnpike is a toll road, one of Japan's famous scenic drives, and it climbs from the coast near Yugawara and Odawara up through the caldera rim into the mountains of Hakone. The turnpike runs through cedar and pine, with views over Sagami Bay behind and the volcanic cone of Mount Kintoki ahead, and it is smooth, well-surfaced and maintained to a very high standard. The bends are broad and flowing, designed for sightseeing as much as for sport, which means the pace is relaxed and the road is wide enough for a bit of enjoyment.

The whole of Hakone sits inside a huge volcanic crater, the rim of which forms the ridges you ride along. Inside the caldera is Lake Ashi, and near it the active volcanic zone of Owakudani, where steam rises from vents and the air smells of sulphur. Eggs boiled in the hot springs turn black and are sold to visitors, and local legend says they add seven years to your life. The volcano erupted in a small way in 2015, and parts of the area were closed for a while, so it is wise to check current conditions before you go.

Hakone was also a barrier. During the Edo period, the Tokugawa shogunate set up a checkpoint here on the Tokaido, the great road between Edo and Kyoto, to control weapons coming into the capital and women, known as irionna, leaving it. A reconstruction stands beside the lake today, and you can still walk a stretch of the old paved path through an avenue of ancient cedars. The place has many hot springs, and a night in an inn with an open-air bath is one of the great pleasures of the region.

The turnpike is a good ride in nearly all seasons, though fog can arrive suddenly and hide the road in a few minutes. Early morning is best, because the road is empty and the light is clear. Autumn colours are bright in late October and November, and in winter the road can have ice in shaded places. The town of Hakone has a population of thirteen thousand, and is the nearest source of fuel and services. Expect to pay a toll on the turnpike, and keep some coins or a card ready.
t.lake ashi viewpoint@35.2,139.0:
Lake Ashi fills the old crater of Hakone, a long, narrow stretch of blue-grey water surrounded by wooded hills, and the viewpoint here gives the postcard version: the lake in front, the ridges behind, and, on the right day, the white cone of Mount Fuji rising over the far shore. The lake is about 723 metres above sea level, cold and clear, and it freezes at the edges only in very hard winters. Sightseeing boats shaped like pirate ships cross it from end to end, which seems silly until you are standing on the shore watching one cross a pool of morning mist.

On the west shore, a red torii gate stands in the water in front of Hakone Shrine, one of the most photographed sights in Japan. The shrine itself is up in the trees, along a quiet path, and dates back to the eighth century according to tradition. The old Tokaido road runs beside the lake here through a long avenue of cedar trees, planted in the early seventeenth century to shade travellers, and some of the trunks are huge and moss-covered. Walking along it for ten minutes is a good way to forget the traffic.

Riding here is more about the setting than the road. The lakeside route is busy and slow, with coaches, taxis and cars looking for parking, and speed limits are low. Early on a weekday, or late in the afternoon, it is quieter. Take time for a stop at one of the cafes by the water, and enjoy the view. Fuji is clearest in winter and early spring, when the air is cold and dry, and in the early morning before clouds build. In summer, haze and cloud often hide it completely, and you may only see the base.

Hakone town, three kilometres away, has about thirteen thousand people and can supply fuel, food and rooms, and Yugawara down the coast has more. There are public toilets and vending machines at the lakeside, and a dozen small shops selling local wooden marquetry, a craft for which Hakone is known. Parking for motorbikes is usually free or cheap, but in peak season it can be hard to find a space. Wear layers, because a cold wind often blows off the water.
t.gotemba fuel window@35.3,138.9:
Gotemba lies on the southeast skirt of Mount Fuji, at the foot of a vast, gently rising slope of black volcanic ash, and the mountain fills the sky to the northwest on any clear day. The city has about eighty thousand people, so fuel is easy, and this is one of the best places to fill the tank before or after the mountain roads of Hakone. Stations are plentiful along the main road, and many are staffed, which in Japan means someone will fill the tank for you and guide you back onto the road.

The town sits at around 450 metres, a modest height, but the air feels cooler than in Tokyo, and the evenings can be fresh even in summer. Gotemba is known for its rice, grown in the fertile volcanic soil with clean water that comes down from the mountain, and for its outlet shopping centre, which draws crowds from Tokyo. To the east lies the Fuji Speedway, one of Japan's most famous circuits, and the area is popular with car and motorbike fans. On race weekends the roads fill up quickly, so check the calendar.

The best thing about Gotemba, for riders, is the road that leaves it. West of the town, a road climbs the slopes of the volcano, through forest and then across barren cinder, to the fifth station where hikers start their climb on the Gotemba trail. East and south, the Otome Pass road climbs toward Hakone, with views of Fuji at its best when the weather allows. The bends are smooth, the gradients easy, and the surface is excellent. Weekday mornings are quietest.

The Fuji Five Lakes lie a short distance to the north, and many riders make a night of it in the area. A hot bath in the evening, followed by a plate of noodles or grilled fish, is hard to beat. The weather around Fuji changes quickly, so carry rain gear, and remember that the summit is often hidden for days at a time. Typhoon season, from late summer into autumn, can bring heavy rain and strong winds, so it is worth checking forecasts. Spring and autumn are the most reliable times for clear views of the mountain.
t.lake yamanaka fuji view@35.4,138.9:
Lake Yamanaka is the largest of the Fuji Five Lakes and the one closest to Tokyo, a broad sheet of water lying at around 980 metres on the north side of Mount Fuji's lower slopes. On a calm morning the mountain reflects in it, and the view of the cone, with its snow cap in winter and spring, is one of the great scenes of Japan. Wind often blows across the lake in the afternoon, so windsurfers and sailors use it, and the water can be choppy.

The area has grown into a holiday district, with campsites, holiday homes and a scattering of hotels around the shore, and it can be crowded in summer. On weekdays and out of season, however, it is quiet, and the walk along the shore at dusk is lovely. The temperature here is lower than at sea level, with cool nights even in August, and in winter the lake can freeze at the edges. It is worth stopping for a photograph, even if the mountain is hiding behind a cloud.

Fujiyoshida, eight kilometres to the north, has about forty-nine thousand people and the kind of services riders need, including fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. It is known for its Yoshida udon, a thick, firm noodle served with cabbage and a rich sauce, and for the Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen shrine, which stands at the old start of the pilgrim path up Fuji. Many centuries of pilgrims, dressed in white, made the climb from here, and the old inns along the street recall that time. Gotemba, to the south, is a larger alternative.

For riders, the road around the lake is easy and pleasant, with gentle bends and good surfaces, and the route over the Mount Fuji foothills toward Hakone or Doshi is among the best in the Kanto region. Check the weather before setting out, because clouds can arrive fast. Autumn colours are best in late October and November, and the air is crisp and clear. Fuji is most likely to be visible in the early morning, so an early start is rewarded.
t.doshimichi road@35.5,139.1:
The Doshimichi is a legend among Tokyo motorcyclists. It is Route 413, a mountain road that leaves the Sagami plain near Sagamihara and climbs west into the Tanzawa and Yamanashi hills, following the valley of the Doshi river toward the village of Doshi. The name simply means the road to Doshi, and it has been a favourite for decades, with twisting bends through forest, steep slopes and the occasional tunnel, and a good number of bikers on weekends.

The pin here lies near Uenohara and Otsuki, on the Yamanashi side of the border, which puts you in the area where the Chuo expressway and the old Koshu Kaido run through the valleys of the Sagami and Katsura rivers. This is a landscape of cedar plantations, small farms and narrow valleys, with steep slopes cut by streams. Lake Sagami, a reservoir on the river of the same name, lies nearby, and the roads around it are quiet.

Doshi village is known for its clear spring water, and there are several places where you can fill a bottle from public springs. The water is cold and tastes of stone, and it is a good reason to stop. The village itself is small, with a handful of shops, and there is a park with a stream, popular with families in summer. In winter, snow can fall on the upper part of the road and ice can form in shaded corners, so be careful.

Do not expect to ride fast. Police patrol the Doshimichi regularly, particularly on weekends, speed limits are strict, and fines are high. The best approach is to enjoy the rhythm of the road and the scenery, and to stop for a break at one of the roadside parking areas. Fuel is available in Uenohara and Otsuki, each with around twenty-eight to thirty-one thousand people, and in Sagamihara, and it is wise to fill up before entering the mountains. Early morning is best, when traffic is light, and the forest smells of damp earth and cedar. Autumn brings red and gold leaves, and the air is clear.
t.atami coast@35.1,139.1:
Atami is a hot spring resort built on a steep hillside above Sagami Bay, with streets that tumble toward the sea and hotels stacked on the slopes like steps. Forty thousand people live here, and it has been a resort since the Edo period, when shoguns had hot spring water carried to Edo for bathing. In the twentieth century it became a honeymoon destination, and the town still has a faded, nostalgic charm, with old inns, souvenir shops and a long seafront promenade.

The coastline here is pretty, with a curve of beach, a small harbour and the rocky shore of the Izu peninsula to the south. Atami Castle, a reconstruction built in the 1950s, sits on the hill above the town, and the views from the top are good, taking in the bay and, on clear days, Hatsushima island offshore. The MOA Museum of Art, up the slope, has a fine collection of Japanese art and gardens. Fireworks displays are held here on many evenings through the year, a tradition that is unusual elsewhere in Japan.

Seafood is the star of the table. Fresh fish, caught in the bay, is served in countless small restaurants and at the morning market near the harbour, with horse mackerel, squid and shrimp on the menu. Atami is also known for dried fish, grilled and eaten with rice and miso soup. After a morning in the saddle, a plate of sashimi and a bowl of rice is exactly what is needed.

For riders, Atami is the start of the Izu coast road, Route 135, which runs south along the shore with sea views the whole way. It is a pleasant, easygoing ride, with gentle curves and small fishing villages, though it can be busy on weekends. The Izu Skyline, a toll road along the ridge above, offers a very different experience, with high views and quiet air. Fuel is easy in Atami, which has plenty of stations, and the nearest bigger towns are Yugawara and Ito. Parking in the town centre is awkward because of the slopes, so look for the designated places.
t.izu skyline high section@35.0,139.0:
The Izu Skyline runs along the backbone of the Izu peninsula, a toll road that follows the high ridge from the Atami area south toward the Amagi mountains, and the section near Ito is among the highest and most open. Here the road runs through grass and low scrub, with views both ways: east to the Pacific and Sagami Bay, west to Suruga Bay, and, on clear days, north to Mount Fuji. The peninsula is narrow, so it is possible to see both seas from one place.

Izu is volcanic in origin, a piece of the Philippine Sea plate that collided with Honshu and is still pushing into it. That collision is responsible for the hot springs, the earthquakes and the steep terrain of the whole peninsula. The ridge itself is made of old volcanic cones, now covered in pampas grass, which turns silver and gold in autumn and is wonderful in low sunlight. In spring, azaleas and wild flowers bloom along the roadside.

The road is well maintained, and the bends are smooth and open, ideal for relaxed riding. Because it is a toll road, traffic is lighter than on the coastal route, and on a weekday morning you may have long stretches to yourself. Cyclists use the road too, so keep an eye out. Fog is common at this height, particularly in spring and early summer, and it can reduce visibility sharply. The road may also close in snow or ice in winter, so check conditions before you go.

Ito, about four kilometres away according to the coordinates, has over seventy thousand people and every kind of shop, including fuel, supermarkets and hot spring baths, and is the obvious place to refuel. Atami lies in the other direction. Bring water and a snack, because the ridge is exposed and the only facilities may be vending machines at parking areas. Ito itself is an old hot spring town, linked to William Adams, the English sailor who became a samurai and built Japan's first Western-style ships here in the early seventeenth century, and a monument to him stands near the harbour.
t.numazu bay photo@35.1,138.9:
Numazu looks out over Suruga Bay, the deepest bay in Japan, and the view from the shore here is one of the better arguments for riding on the Izu side of Fuji. The city has two hundred thousand people and a working port, so do not expect a quiet fishing village; expect fish markets, concrete breakwaters and the smell of the sea. Behind the harbour the land rises toward the Izu hills, and beyond the bay, on a clear morning, Mount Fuji stands over the water with almost nothing between you and its base.

Suruga Bay drops quickly to great depths, which is why deep-sea fish such as shrimp, sakura ebi and various kinds of sea bream turn up on local menus. Numazu has long been known for its dried horse mackerel, split and sun-dried on racks along the shore, and the smell of grilling fish drifts from many a small restaurant. A bowl of rice with raw or lightly seared fish on top, eaten at a counter, is what many riders come here for. The fish market near the port has restaurants that open early, and the portions are generous.

Along the coast to the west runs the Senbon Matsubara, a belt of several hundred thousand pine trees planted centuries ago to shelter the farmland from sea winds, and one of the traditional spots from which to view Fuji. Mishima, a little to the north-east, has a large suspension footbridge across a valley and clear streams running through the old town, fed by snowmelt that has travelled underground from Fuji for decades. Both are an easy hop from Numazu.

For riding, this stop is more about the mood than the road. The streets around the port are flat and urban, with traffic lights and trucks, and a good deal of care is needed. Out along the coast, Route 414 and the smaller roads to the south wind through villages with views across the bay and up toward Fuji. Fuel and food are plentiful here, with stations all over the city. The best light is early in the morning, when the sea is calm and the mountain sharp, or at sunset, when it turns pink. In summer, haze often blurs the view, and typhoons in autumn can bring big waves.
t.hakone turnpike rhythm@35.2,139.1:
Rhythm is the right word for the Hakone Turnpike, because the road does not so much challenge you as set a tempo. Near Hakone, with Yugawara down the hill and Odawara on the coast, it climbs through broad bends that follow the shape of the old volcano, and after a few kilometres you find a steady pace in which gear changes and lean angles settle into a pattern. It is a road for enjoying rather than attacking, with smooth tarmac, clear sightlines and a limit that police take seriously.

What makes it memorable is the changing light. Cloud often rolls up from the coast and fills the valleys, so that the road climbs out of grey into sunshine, with the ridges standing like islands in a white sea. At other times the whole thing is wrapped in fog, the bends appear from nowhere, and the engine sounds louder. Take it slowly when visibility is low, and use your lights. In winter, the shaded sections can hold ice into the late morning.

Near the top, the open grassland of Sengokuhara, on the northern rim of the caldera, is covered in silver pampas grass in autumn, and the whole slope seems to glow when the sun is low. The Hakone Open-Air Museum, with its sculptures on a hillside, and the many small museums and shrines in the area, give you reasons to stop. Hot spring inns are everywhere, and the baths, often outdoors and facing the forest, are the best way to finish a day.

Yugawara, six kilometres away, is a small hot spring town of twenty-seven thousand people on the coast, with fuel and a good selection of places to eat. It is quieter than Hakone and less touristy, and a good alternative if the main town is crowded. Odawara, further along, offers all the services of a city. In peak season, particularly on weekends in autumn, the Hakone roads can be very busy, and traffic crawls. If you can, ride on a weekday and start early. A slow ride on a good road, with views and baths at the end of the day, is among the great pleasures of Japan.
t.fuji five lakes food window@35.5,138.8:
Fujikawaguchiko and Fujiyoshida stand a few kilometres either side of this stop, and between them the northern face of Mount Fuji dominates everything. The Fuji Five Lakes, strung along the foot of the volcano, are the usual base for people who want a view of the mountain, and the whole district has grown up around tourism, with inns, restaurants and shops catering to hikers, photographers and bus tours. It is a busy place in season, but the food is worth the crowds.

The speciality is hoto, a thick, flat noodle stewed in a miso broth with pumpkin and vegetables, served bubbling in an iron pot. It is the signature dish of Yamanashi prefecture, said to have been eaten by the warlord Takeda Shingen's soldiers, and it is a warming meal after a cold ride. Fujiyoshida has its own noodle, a firm, chewy udon served with cabbage and a spicy paste, that is cheap and filling. Both are worth trying, and there is usually no need to book, though lunchtime queues are common.

The landscape here is shaped by the volcano. The forest of Aokigahara, to the west, grew on lava that flowed from Fuji in the ninth century, and the ground beneath is a maze of caves and tubes. Some of the caves are open to visitors, and the cold, dark interiors make a strange contrast to the sun outside. The lakes themselves were formed when lava dammed river valleys, and each has its own character, from the busy shore of Kawaguchi to the quiet waters of Motosu, which appears on the Japanese 1000 yen note.

For riders, the lakes offer easy touring, with good roads and many places to stop. The best views of Fuji come in winter and early spring, and in the early morning, when the air is cold and clear. In summer, cloud often hides the mountain from midday. Fuel is plentiful in both towns, which have twenty to fifty thousand people. On a weekend in cherry blossom or autumn colour season, the roads around the lakes become very crowded, and parking near the popular viewpoints is difficult. Weekdays are far better, and a late afternoon visit can be lovely, with golden light on the water.
t.izu skyline high road@35.1,139.0:
At the high end of the Izu Skyline, with Atami five kilometres away and the Tanna basin tucked in the valley to the west, the road runs along a grassy ridge where the wind is a constant companion. Gusts can be strong enough to push a bike sideways, particularly at the exposed corners, so keep a firm grip and reduce speed when the grass starts to bend. On the ridge the air is cool and clean, and even in July the temperature can be ten degrees below that on the coast.

The Izu Skyline links the Atami Pass with the Amagi mountains to the south, and the high section is a place of long views. To the west, across the Tanna basin, a quiet farming district with dairy cattle and green fields, the white peak of Fuji sometimes appears, and to the east the Pacific lies spread out like a sheet of metal. In the evening, the lights of Atami and the coast glow below, and the sky turns deep violet.

The Tanna basin is worth knowing about. It is a bowl of farmland pocketed in the hills, home to a well-known dairy industry whose milk and ice cream you can try in the small shops around the area. Beneath it, a long railway tunnel, dug in the early twentieth century with great loss of life, carries the Tokaido line toward Numazu and was one of the hardest tunnelling projects in Japanese history. It is a reminder of how steep and difficult the geology of this region is.

Practically, there are no services on the ridge, and fuel must be bought in Atami or Mishima before you start. Atami has forty thousand people, and Mishima over a hundred thousand, with stations all over. Pack water and a snack. The road is a toll road, and the toll is paid at a booth, so keep coins ready. Quite a few cyclists and other motorbikes use it, and on a fine weekend the car parks at the viewpoints fill up with sightseers. The best time to ride is on a weekday morning, when the road is quiet and the light is crisp, and the best season is autumn, when the pampas grass is silver and the air clear.
t.shuzenji onsen food@35.0,138.9:
Shuzenji sits in a narrow valley in the middle of the Izu peninsula, on the Katsura river, and it is the oldest hot spring resort on Izu. The onsen town grew around a temple, Shuzen-ji, founded according to tradition by the monk Kobo Daishi in the early ninth century, and it has an old-fashioned, quiet charm that the busier resorts on the coast have lost. Hot water comes from springs beneath the town, and an open-air bath in the middle of the river, called Tokko no Yu, is the symbol of the place.

History here is dramatic. In 1204, Minamoto no Yoriie, the second shogun of Kamakura, was confined at Shuzenji after being removed from power by his mother's family, the Hojo, and was killed in a bath by assassins. His grave lies in the temple grounds, and the story is told with some relish by local guides. The whole episode is an example of the ruthless politics of medieval Japan, and Shuzenji's quiet setting makes it all the more striking.

Walking through the town is pleasant. A path through a small bamboo grove, the Chikurin no Komichi, leads along the river, and small shops sell local specialities. Izu is famous for wasabi, grown in cold, clear streams on terraced fields in the hills, and the fresh root, grated on a sharkskin board, tastes far milder and sweeter than the paste from a tube. Soba noodles with grated wasabi, wild vegetables and mushrooms, or a bowl of rice topped with fish from the coast, are good choices for a meal here.

The roads into Shuzenji run through forested valleys, with tight bends, a mix of old and new tarmac, and the occasional tunnel. Traffic is lighter than on the coast, and the route over the Amagi Pass to the south is one of the best rides on the peninsula. Fuel can be found along the main road in town, though the bigger supplies are in Ito and Numazu, fourteen and fifteen kilometres away. Rain falls often in the Izu mountains, and the moss-covered cedar forest is lovely when wet, but take care on the shaded corners. Autumn leaves are splendid in November, and spring cherry blossom lines the river.
t.okutama lake road@35.8,139.1:
Lake Okutama is not a natural lake at all. It is the reservoir behind the Ogouchi dam, completed in 1957 to supply water to Tokyo, and it fills a deep, narrow valley in the mountains at the western end of the city's territory. Several hundred families had to leave their homes to make way for the water, and the drowned villages, together with the old roads, lie somewhere beneath the surface. The lake is still one of the main sources of drinking water for the capital, so it is kept clean, the shores are wooded, and there is little building around it.

The road follows the shoreline, climbing and dropping around the arms of the reservoir, with tunnels, bridges and narrow bends. The altitude is about 530 metres, and in the cedar-shaded sections the air feels damp and cool. Across the water, the slopes rise steeply into forest, with the ridges of the Okutama mountains behind. Mount Kumotori, the highest point in Tokyo at 2,017 metres, lies farther on, and much of the surrounding country is a national park. In autumn the maples and oaks turn red and gold, and the lake reflects the colours.

This is a long way from the city centre. Itsukaichi and Ome, the nearest large towns, are seventeen kilometres away, and the road to the lake climbs steadily up the valley of the Tama river. Fill your tank before you start, as pumps are scarce in the mountains. Food is available in the small village of Okutama, where there are a few simple restaurants serving soba, grilled river fish and local vegetables, and a handful of inns. There are also vending machines at most parking areas, which is typical in Japan.

Riding here is a pleasure on a weekday and a slow crawl on a fine weekend, when motorcyclists, cyclists and day-trippers all head for the hills. The bends are tight and the road narrow, with limited visibility and some falling rocks after heavy rain, so go carefully. Wildlife is part of the setting: deer, monkeys and wild boar live in the forests, and bears are present, although rarely seen. The best time is early in the morning, when mist hangs over the water and the road is empty, or in late autumn, when the leaves are at their peak.
t.kazahari pass road@35.7,139.0:
Kazahari is a high saddle on the border between Tokyo and Yamanashi, at around 1,150 metres, and the road over it is one of the quietest and prettiest in the Kanto mountains. It climbs from the Okutama lake country through dark cedar forest and then through deciduous woods that glow in autumn, with occasional views through gaps in the trees. The pass is narrow, with a limited number of corners where two vehicles can pass, and the surface is patchy, so a relaxed pace is the sensible choice.

The country around here is steep, forested and thinly populated. Villages are small, many houses stand empty, and the population has declined for decades as young people move to the city. Agriculture has been replaced by forestry, and the slopes are covered in planted cedar and cypress, with some old beech and oak woodland on the upper ridges. Springs run beside the road, and in places the mountains are covered in moss.

Otsuki, the nearest town of any size, lies fourteen kilometres away and has about thirty-one thousand people, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Uenohara and Itsukaichi are the other options, but they are further. A vending machine or a small shop may offer a drink, but do not count on a meal. A packed lunch is a good idea.

Weather changes quickly at this height. Fog is common, and in winter, snow and ice can close the road for days, so check conditions before setting out. In summer, the forest is cool and shady, a welcome relief from the heat of the plain, and thunderstorms can build in the afternoon. Falling branches and small rockfalls are not unusual after rain. Traffic is light, and in places you may not see another vehicle for half an hour. For riders who like quiet roads and forest scenery, it is an excellent route, though it demands attention and is not suited to hurry.
t.akiruno@35.7,139.3:
Akiruno is a young name on an old place. The city was created in the 1990s by merging Itsukaichi and Hikawa, two towns at the western edge of Tokyo, and the name comes from the Aki river, which runs through a pretty valley of wooded slopes and clear water. At about 180 metres, it is where the mountains of Okutama begin to fall away toward the flat Kanto plain, and it marks the point where Tokyo's suburbs give way to forest. The transition is abrupt: one moment you are among shops and houses, and the next the road is lined with cedar.

The Aki valley, known locally as Akigawa Keikoku, is the main attraction. In summer, families gather on the gravel banks for barbecues and paddling, and the river runs cold and green over rounded stones. Small restaurants along the road serve grilled sweetfish, called ayu, and mountain vegetables, and in winter the stews are warming. Itsukaichi, the old market town, was once a trading post between the mountain villages and the plain, and a few old buildings remain.

North of here, Fussa, just three kilometres away with over sixty thousand people, has several things worth knowing. It is home to a famous sake brewery, Ishikawa, which stands beside the Tama river and is open for visits and tastings. There is also a large American air base, Yokota, whose fences run beside the roads in town. Fussa has fuel stations, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat, so it is a sensible place to refuel before heading into the hills.

For riders, Akiruno is a gateway and a rest stop. Route 411, the Ome Kaido, runs west to Okutama, while smaller roads climb into the Hinohara area and over passes to Yamanashi. The riding is best on weekday mornings, when traffic is light, and the heavy weekend crowds of cyclists, hikers and sightseers are absent. Be careful on the narrow valley roads, especially in damp weather, when moss and leaves make the surface slick. Summer afternoons can bring sudden thunderstorms, and autumn colours peak in mid-November. Eat early, because many small restaurants close by mid-afternoon.
t.yokohama@35.4,139.6:
Yokohama is where modern Japan met the outside world. After the arrival of Commodore Perry's black ships in 1853 and the treaty signed here the following year, the little fishing village of Yokohama was chosen as a treaty port, and when it opened in 1859 foreigners settled on the Bluff and traders built warehouses along the waterfront. Today it is Japan's second-largest city, with more than three and a half million people, and the old brick warehouses by the harbour, now shops and restaurants, stand next to the high towers of Minato Mirai.

At sea level, this is the flattest of starts, and the stop is mostly about logistics. Fuel stations are everywhere, many open around the clock, and the roads are wide and well signed. It is also worth knowing that Yokohama has a number of expressways that carry traffic across the bay and around the port, among them the Bay Bridge, a double-deck structure completed in 1989, with a viewing parking area at Daikoku, where motorbikes and cars gather on weekend evenings. The atmosphere is relaxed and friendly, and you will see all kinds of machines.

Food in Yokohama is an experience of its own. Chinatown, the biggest in Japan, has hundreds of restaurants, many offering steamed buns, noodles and dim sum, and it is lively until late in the evening. Ramen is another local obsession, and the district around Shin-Yokohama has a museum devoted to it with a recreated street from the 1950s. Seafood from the bay and the nearby Miura peninsula is fresh and varied, and a morning at one of the fish markets can be fun.

The ride from here goes south toward Kamakura and the Miura peninsula, a lovely stretch of coast with views of Fuji on clear days. Be ready for traffic on weekends, when day-trippers fill the roads, and take care at the many tolls and junctions. The air has a salt tang, the breeze is steady, and the quiet hours before dawn are the best for riding. In summer the humidity can be heavy and typhoons can bring strong winds and rain in early autumn. Parking for motorbikes in the central district is limited, so look for designated areas, and remember that illegal parking is quickly ticketed.
t.kamakura@35.3,139.6:
Kamakura is a small town with the weight of a capital, because for about a century and a half, from the end of the twelfth century, it was the seat of the shoguns. Minamoto no Yoritomo founded the military government here in the 1180s, far from the imperial court at Kyoto, and the city was chosen for its natural defences: hills on three sides and the sea on the fourth, with narrow passes cut through the rock as the only land entrances. Those passes, the Kiridoshi, can still be seen, and they are part of what gives the town its enclosed, intimate feel.

The Great Buddha, a bronze figure thirteen metres high, sits in the open air at Kotoku-in, the hall that once sheltered it having been swept away by a tsunami in the fifteenth century. It has watched over the town for about seven centuries, and the calm expression and the weathered green patina are moving. The main shrine, Tsurugaoka Hachimangu, stands at the end of a long approach lined with cherry trees, and its steps and halls climb the hillside above.

For a rider, though, Kamakura is a place for coffee and patience. The streets are narrow, the traffic is heavy at weekends and holidays, and finding parking for a motorbike can take time, so look for the designated areas near the station. The reward is a good cup of coffee in one of the many small cafes tucked into old houses, a walk along the shopping street of Komachi-dori, and a feeling of calm in the temple gardens. The Enoden, a little tram-like railway that runs along the coast to Enoshima, rattles past the houses and is worth a look.

It stands about eight metres above sea level and the sea is close, so the air carries a faint saltiness. Zushi and Hayama lie to the south, both smaller seaside towns, and the coast road leads on toward the Miura peninsula. Fuel is available in Kamakura, but the town is busy, and it may be easier to fill up in Yokohama or on the main road outside. Early mornings are the best time to visit, when the streets are empty, the shops are still shuttered and the temples are quiet. In June, the hydrangeas bloom along the temple paths and attract large crowds, so avoid that month if you dislike company.
t.hayama coastal road@35.3,139.6:
Hayama is a small town on the sea with a reputation for being quietly rich. For more than a century, Hayama has been a retreat for Tokyo's elite, and the imperial family still has a villa on the shore, a simple wooden house in a pine grove, guarded and not open to visitors. Thirty thousand people live here, and the coast road runs straight through the middle of the town, along the cliffs and beaches, with yachts in the harbour and pines clinging to rocks.

The road is Route 134, the Shonan coast road, and the stretch between Zushi and Hayama is its prettiest, with the sea close on one side and low wooded hills on the other. The surface is good, the bends are gentle, and the pace is slow, thanks to traffic lights and a limit that does not allow for much speed. On weekends in summer, the road is jammed with cars, surfers and cyclists, and a ride along it can take twice as long as expected. A weekday morning or a winter dawn is a different experience.

Sunset is the best moment. Mount Fuji, which is visible across the bay on clear days, appears as a dark silhouette against the red sky, and the beaches fill with people who have come to watch. The Morito coast and the beaches of Isshiki are especially good, and small cafes along the shore serve coffee and cake to the sound of the waves. In winter, the air is cold and clear and Fuji appears with a white cap, while in summer, haze and humidity often hide it.

Food in Hayama has a good reputation. The town is known for its beef, raised locally and served in a few restaurants, and for a café culture that has grown up around the beach. The Miura peninsula as a whole is famous for fresh seafood, tuna in particular, and for its radishes and cabbages, grown in fields on the plateau behind. Fuel is available in Hayama, but the choice is wider in Zushi, two or three kilometres away, which has sixty thousand people. In busy periods, parking is difficult, so be prepared to circle. The salt air is hard on chains and metal, and a rinse after a coastal ride is good practice.
t.jogashima@35.1,139.6:
Jogashima is an island at the very southern tip of the Miura peninsula, joined to the mainland by a short bridge, and the end of the road in a literal sense. A narrow lane drops through fields of cabbage and radish and a scatter of fishing houses, passes the small town of Misaki, and crosses the bridge to a rocky islet with a lighthouse, a headland path and a view of the open Pacific. On a clear day, the low shape of Izu Oshima appears on the horizon, and freighters slide across the mouth of Tokyo Bay below.

The lighthouse, first lit in the early Meiji years, was one of several built by the British engineer Richard Henry Brunton for the new government, which wanted to make the dangerous waters around Japan safe for foreign ships. The tower on the island today is a later rebuild, but the site is the original. A walk around the rocky shore leads to a sea arch and cliffs of layered sandstone, carved by waves into curious shapes, and the tide pools are full of small crabs and anemones.

Misaki, close to the bridge, is among Japan's best-known tuna ports. The harbour lands fish from far-flung fleets, and the town's restaurants serve tuna in every form: raw, grilled, fried, and as rice bowls with thick slices of dark red flesh. A meal at one of the small places near the harbour is the high point for many riders, and the price is generally fair. Fresh fish is the rule, so do not expect elaborate dishes, just very good ingredients. The fish market opens early, and the best time to visit is in the morning.

Miura has about fifty thousand people and its fuel stations lie along the main road, so fill up there before crossing to the island. Parking on Jogashima is limited and tends to fill up quickly at weekends, but motorbikes are usually squeezed in. Wind blows constantly and can be strong, so be careful on the exposed bridge. Drinking water and toilets are available near the lighthouse, and the shops sell cold drinks and ice cream. In autumn and winter, the light is clear and the air cool, and a late-afternoon visit gives you the sun setting over the sea.
t.lake chuzenji water view@36.7,139.5:
Lake Chuzenji lies at about 1,270 metres in the mountains above Nikko, and it was born in violence. Some twenty thousand years ago, an eruption of Mount Nantai, the cone that now rises above the northern shore, sent lava across the Daiya river and dammed the valley, and the water that built up behind it became the lake. The result is a deep, cold, clear body of water, shaped like a crescent, with wooded slopes plunging into it and no real beach.

For many years the lake was a summer retreat for foreign diplomats, who escaped the heat of Tokyo by travelling up to Chuzenji in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and the British, Italian and other embassies built villas on the shore. A few have been restored and are open to visitors, and the sight of wooden houses in a Western style, with verandas looking over the water, gives the lake a faintly colonial air. Boats and a few small cruise vessels operate in summer, and fishermen cast for trout from the shore.

The way up is the Irohazaka, the famous road of forty-eight hairpin bends, named after the forty-eight characters of the old Japanese syllabary. Today two one-way roads climb and descend the same slope, so you either climb or drop, and the bends come one after another with a drop on the outside and forest on the inside. It is a thrilling ride, though demanding, and best taken at a steady, controlled pace. In mid-October, the maple and birch trees on the slope turn red, orange and gold, drawing crowds, and the road can be slow and busy.

Nikko, twelve kilometres below, has sixteen thousand people and all the usual services, including fuel, and Imaichi, a little farther, has more. At the lake itself, there is a village with restaurants, shops and inns, and fuel is limited, so fill up in the valley. Temperatures here are well below those in the lowlands, with frost in October and snow in winter. When the weather is clear, the view from the shore, with the mountains reflected in still water, is among the most beautiful in Japan, and in morning mist it takes on an almost Chinese ink-painting quality. Bring layers, because the wind off the water is cold.
t.kegon falls@36.7,139.5:
Kegon Falls drops ninety-seven metres from the edge of Lake Chuzenji into a rocky gorge, and it is counted among the three great waterfalls of Japan. The lake's outflow, the Daiya river, simply runs to the lip of an ancient lava flow and falls straight down, creating a white column in a dark basin of volcanic rock. Around the main fall, smaller streams seep from the cliff face, and in winter some of them freeze into long icicles, a magnificent sight if you can bear the cold.

An elevator carries visitors down inside the rock to a viewing platform at the base, where the roar of water is deafening and the spray soaks anyone who stands too close. A free viewing platform higher up gives a more distant but still spectacular view. After heavy rain, the volume increases and the water turns brown, and on a sunny afternoon, rainbows form in the mist. Early morning is quieter and the light softer, and in autumn the surrounding maple forest turns bright red.

The waterfall sits at the top of the Irohazaka, so riders who have just come up the forty-eight bends often stop here first. A cable car, the Akechidaira ropeway, runs to a viewpoint on a nearby ridge, with an overview of both the lake and the fall, and it is a good choice if you have time. A short distance north, the Senjogahara marsh and the Ryuzu falls are further stops in a beautiful area, and the hot spring village of Yumoto lies at the far end.

The place is tourist-heavy, so expect souvenir shops, ice cream stands and noodle restaurants near the viewing area, which cater to tour groups arriving by the busload. Prices are higher than in the valley, but the food is acceptable. Parking for motorbikes is available, and there is a charge at some lots. It is best to fill up there. On a cold day, a hot drink from a vending machine, which comes in a can and warms the hands, is a small pleasure, and a good use of the time.
t.nikko food@36.7,139.7:
Imaichi is the quiet partner of Nikko, a working town of sixty thousand people on the plain where the mountain roads meet the Kanto lowlands, and a very good place to eat after the climb to Chuzenji. The pin sits a kilometre from the middle of Imaichi, on the old road that runs toward the shrines, and it is here that you pick up the Nikko cedar avenue, a line of enormous trees planted in the seventeenth century along the roads that led to the Tokugawa mausoleum. Some of the trunks are as thick as a small car, and the shade under them is deep and green even at noon.

The mausoleum is Toshogu, the shrine to Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the shogunate who died in 1616 and was enshrined at Nikko the following year. His grandson Iemitsu rebuilt it on a vast scale in the 1630s, and the result is a riot of gold leaf, carved animals and lacquered gates, including the famous three wise monkeys and a sleeping cat. It stands in the forest with the cedars around it, and is a UNESCO World Heritage site along with its neighbours. Whatever you think of its taste, it is certainly unforgettable.

The local food is simple and good. Nikko is known for yuba, the skin that forms on heated soy milk, which is lifted off in sheets and served rolled, fried or in soup, a speciality that grew up around the temples and their vegetarian cooking. Soba noodles, made from buckwheat grown in the surrounding hills, and fresh trout from mountain streams are also local favourites. Lunch in a small place with tatami seating and a view of a garden is a restful way to spend an hour.

For riders, Imaichi offers fuel, supermarkets and plenty of rest stops, and the roads from here lead in several directions. To the west lie the climbing roads to Lake Chuzenji and Yumoto, to the north the Kinugawa valley and its hot springs, and to the south the long, straight run back toward Utsunomiya and Tokyo. The Nikko-Utsunomiya road is usually busy, and weekend traffic into Nikko can crawl, so aim to arrive early. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, building over the mountains, and the air cools quickly when they arrive. In autumn the colours around Nikko peak in mid to late October, and you will not be alone.
t.gotemba@35.3,138.9:
Coming back through Gotemba after a day in the hills has its own pleasure, because the town sits at the foot of Fuji and the mountain rules the sky above it. The city lies at about 450 metres on a broad, gentle fan of volcanic ash, with the rice fields of the plain below and the black upper slopes of the volcano above, and at the end of a day the setting sun lights the summit in orange and pink. In clear weather, the whole mountain seems to hover over the town.

A return check is also a practical matter. Gotemba is a convenient place to review the day, check the bike and plan the way home. Over the Otome Pass to the east, the road drops toward Hakone and Odawara, a route of smooth bends through forest, and to the south and east the Tomei expressway runs toward Tokyo, which is about a hundred kilometres away. Expect heavy traffic on Sunday evenings, particularly at the Tanzawa section, where the road narrows and queues form for many kilometres. Leaving early or late can save an hour.

Gotemba is known for its rice, which is grown with the cold, clear water filtered through the volcanic soil, and many restaurants proudly serve it plain, with a few pickles and a bowl of miso soup. Local specialities also include a hot pot, grilled river fish and the rich, creamy dairy products of the highland farms. A simple set meal, with rice cooked in an earthenware pot, makes a fine end to a day. The town has more than eighty thousand people and a big outlet shopping centre, so fuel, food and rooms are all easy to find.

The air at this height is cooler than in Tokyo, and temperatures can drop sharply after sunset, even in summer. Mist forms in the evening and rolls across the fields, and the smell of damp grass and woodsmoke gives a feeling of countryside. Typhoons can bring heavy rain and wind in late summer, and winter nights can be near freezing, with frost on the road in the early morning. If Fuji is hidden by cloud, as it often is, be patient: a gap often opens near sunset, and the mountain emerges for a few minutes, glowing, before the light fades.
t.okutama lake road@35.8,139.0:
The Ome Kaido, Route 411, is the road that leads from the western suburbs of Tokyo up into the Okutama mountains, and it follows the Tama river most of the way, with the valley narrowing and the slopes steepening mile by mile. This stop falls on the lake road, with Itsukaichi and Ome some seventeen kilometres behind, and the air at this point is noticeably cooler and cleaner than in the city. The ride out from the suburbs takes an hour or more on a busy day, and the reward is a different world.

Before the road reaches the lake, it passes the foot of Mount Mitake, where a Shinto shrine with a history of more than a thousand years stands among ancient cedars on the summit, reached by a cable car. Pilgrims have climbed here for centuries, and the shrine keeps a tradition of mountain priests and a guardian wolf, a legacy of the belief that wolves protected crops. Farther up the valley, the Nippara limestone cave is Tokyo's largest, a dark, cold cavern that is open to visitors and a surprising thing to find within the city limits.

The village of Okutama lies at the end of the railway, and its station is a small, cheerful place where hikers gather. From here the road continues past the lake and climbs toward the mountain passes and on to Yamanashi, with the valley narrowing until the slopes seem to close overhead. The road is well surfaced but narrow in places, with tunnels, blind corners and occasional rockfalls, so take care. On weekends, groups of cyclists and motorcyclists share the road, and traffic can be heavy in autumn, when the leaves attract visitors.

Fuel stations are few here, and the sensible move is to fill up in Ome or Itsukaichi before leaving the plain. There are small shops and a handful of restaurants in Okutama, serving soba, trout and local wasabi, but opening hours are short and they close by late afternoon. Wasabi grows in the cold streams of the mountains, and the fresh root is mild and aromatic. Wildlife is plentiful, and deer and monkeys often appear at the roadside, so ride with care. Mist often fills the valley in the morning, and the clear, cool air in autumn is a delight.
t.chichibu forest bend core@36.0,139.1:
Chichibu sits in a high basin ringed by mountains, a town of fifty-eight thousand people that feels more like a market town in the Alps than a place two hours from Tokyo. The ground here is limestone, and to the south the bulk of Mount Buko has been quarried for cement for a century, a vast scar on the hillside that is visible from miles away. The industry made the town prosperous, and it also sits beside a river, the Arakawa, that begins in the mountains above and flows down toward the capital.

The great event of the year is the Chichibu night festival, held on 2 and 3 December, when huge, lantern-hung floats are hauled through the streets by crowds of locals, with fireworks bursting overhead in the cold air. It has taken place for more than three hundred years and is recognised by UNESCO as part of the intangible heritage of humanity. If you happen to be here on those days, it is a thrilling sight, though the town is jammed and accommodation is hard to find.

Chichibu is also a place of pilgrimage. A circuit of thirty-four Kannon temples, established in the sixteenth century, winds through the valleys, and walkers, in the traditional white clothes, still follow it, ringing bells and chanting. A short way up the Arakawa lies Mitsumine Shrine, perched high on a ridge in an old cedar forest, where wolves are venerated as messengers of the gods. It is a long, winding ride, but the setting is magnificent, and the air smells of resin and incense.

The forest roads around Chichibu are winding and shaded, with sharp bends, short tunnels and many blind corners, and the surface can be damp and covered in leaves and pine needles. Take it slowly, particularly after rain. Moss grows on the walls, and light filters through the branches in thin shafts. Traffic is light on weekdays and heavier at weekends, when cyclists and sightseers arrive. The town has fuel stations and supermarkets, and the nearest big place is Yorii, seventeen kilometres east. In winter, ice forms on shaded roads and can stay all day, so check the forecast, and carry a warm layer as the temperature can fall quickly after sunset.
t.okutama lake@35.8,139.0:
Few people riding beside Lake Okutama realise that they are looking at the roof of a drowned valley. The lake exists because of the Ogouchi dam, built across the Tama river in the 1950s to give Tokyo more drinking water, and when the gates closed, the rising water covered farms, a shrine and a handful of villages. Several hundred households were moved to higher ground, and old photographs show the fields and houses that vanished. It is a quiet piece of postwar history, and it explains the unusual stillness of the place.

The shoreline is irregular, with many arms and inlets where the original side valleys flooded, and the road runs high above the water through tunnels and across bridges, with views opening between cedar trunks. The water has a deep green-blue colour that changes with the weather, and on calm mornings the mountains reflect so exactly that the lake becomes a mirror. Walking paths lead along the shore, and a floating footbridge across one of the inlets, swaying gently underfoot, is a favourite stop for visitors.

The mountains around are the Okutama range, forested with cedar and cypress, and with beech and oak higher up, and they are home to deer, monkeys, boar and a few Asiatic black bears. The most dramatic part of the year is autumn, when the slopes burn red and gold, and the weeks around early November draw crowds. Spring brings fresh green and cherry blossom, and in winter, snow often dusts the upper slopes and ice forms in the shaded corners of the road.

This is remote country. Otsuki and Itsukaichi, the nearest larger towns, are about twenty kilometres away, and the lake has only small facilities: a few shops, restaurants and vending machines, with limited hours. Fuel is scarce, so fill up before you leave the plain, and bring a spare layer, since the air is chilly even in summer. The best riding is during the week, when traffic is light, and the best time of day is early, when mist hangs on the water and silence fills the valley. On a damp afternoon, the lake has an almost Scottish mood, with cloud low on the ridges and the smell of wet cedar.
t.daibosatsu high line@35.7,138.9:
Daibosatsu, the Great Bodhisattva, gives its name to a pass, a lake and a ridge on the Yamanashi side of the Okutama and Chichibu mountains, and the high line here follows the ridge for much of the way, with broad views to the south and the great dark shapes of the Southern Alps on the western horizon. The pin lies some fifteen kilometres from Otsuki and eighteen from Enzan, in steep, thinly settled country where the road clings to the contours and the villages are small.

The pass has a place in Japanese literature. Daibosatsu Toge, a long novel by Nakazato Kaizan, was serialised from 1913 and remained unfinished at the author's death, and it follows a violent swordsman through the last years of the shogunate, beginning with a murder on the pass. It is one of the longest novels ever written in Japanese, and has been adapted for film many times. The pass itself is a quiet trail crossing, but its name is known across the country.

The country below, on the Yamanashi side, is fruit land. The slopes around Enzan and Katsunuma are covered with vineyards, and the wine from the local koshu grape, a pale, delicate white variety grown here for centuries, is the pride of the region. Peaches and grapes ripen in summer and early autumn, and roadside stalls sell them at fair prices. A glass of koshu with a plate of local mushrooms is a fine way to end a day, though not if you are riding.

The roads in this area are rewarding, with a mix of tight bends and fast, open sections, and the scenery changes from dark cedar forest to open farmland. Surfaces are usually good, though occasional rockfalls and wet leaves call for care. There are very few services on the high ground, so fill up in Otsuki or Enzan beforehand, and take food and water. Weather changes fast, and fog and cold can arrive within minutes, even in summer, while snow and ice may close the high roads from December to March. On a clear day, however, the view of Fuji from the ridge, floating above the clouds, is one of the best in Japan.
t.chichibu valley food@36.0,139.1:
If Chichibu has a signature dish, it is waraji katsudon, a pair of large, flat pork cutlets laid across a bowl of rice and glazed in a sweet soy sauce, named for the straw sandals, waraji, that they resemble in shape. It is a big meal, enough for any hungry rider after a morning in the mountains, and restaurants in the town centre serve it with miso soup and pickles. The portion is generous, and a small amount of sauce and a lot of appetite are all you need.

The town offers more besides. Chichibu soba, made from buckwheat grown in the mountains, is served cold on a bamboo tray with a dipping sauce and grated radish, and in winter in a hot broth. A local snack, miso potato, is a boiled potato skewered, grilled and brushed with sweet miso, sold at roadside stalls and from small shops. Shops sell cured meats, pickles and sake from the valley breweries, and the local water, which runs clear from the surrounding hills, is considered good for brewing.

Chichibu has about fifty-eight thousand people and sits in a bowl of mountains, so that every street seems to end in a ridge. The old streets around the station are a good place for a walk, and the nearby Chichibu Shrine, with its carved wooden panels of dragons and tigers, is a surprise in the middle of town. On Hitsujiyama hill, a slope near the town is planted with moss phlox, which flower in pink, white and purple carpets in April and May, drawing large crowds.

Fuel and groceries are easy to find, and the roads out of town lead in many directions: north to Nagatoro and the Arakawa gorge, west to the mountain passes, and south toward the high peaks. For a late lunch, aim to be at a restaurant before two, since many close for a break in the afternoon, and they may stop serving before the stated closing time when the day's rice runs out. Parking for motorbikes is usually free, but ask before leaving your helmet and gear. In winter, the valley is cold, and a hot meal is welcome, so plan to enjoy the experience at leisure.
t.mnichovo hradiste@50.5,15.0:
The Jizera river flows past Mnichovo Hradiště on its way to the Elbe, and the town sits at the western gate of the Bohemian Paradise, the Český ráj, a landscape of sandstone towers, forest and ruined castles that was the first protected landscape area in the former Czechoslovakia. It is a quiet, orderly town of about eight thousand people with a square, a large baroque castle and the unhurried feel of a place that has been burnt, rebuilt and forgotten several times over.

The castle is the main thing to see. It belonged for centuries to the Waldstein family, the line of Albrecht von Wallenstein, the Thirty Years' War general who was at once the most powerful and the most feared man in Bohemia, and it later passed to the Thun-Hohenstein family. The grounds are formal and the interiors are in an old noble style. The town also has a battlefield from the Austro-Prussian war of 1866, when Prussian troops pushed back Austrian and Saxon forces here in a short, sharp fight on the way to the decisive battle at Königgrätz.

For riding, Mnichovo Hradiště is a good place to start. From here, roads run east through gently rolling country toward Turnov and Jičín, between fields, forests and villages with steep red roofs. They are not fast roads, but they are pleasant ones, with moderate traffic, a handful of tight bends and occasional rough patches. Sandstone outcrops begin to appear as you move toward the rocks, and the landscape becomes more dramatic. Watch for cyclists and for tractors, and be careful on wet days when leaves or mud can cover the surface.

The town has fuel, supermarkets and several places to eat, so it is a sensible place to stock up before entering the quieter villages. Czech inns serve hearty dishes such as svíčková, beef in a creamy vegetable sauce with dumplings, and a glass of local lager goes well with it, although it is best saved for the evening. A pastry and a coffee in the square is a pleasant way to start.

Come in spring, when the orchards flower, or in early autumn, when the light is low and the forests turn gold. Summer weekends can be busy, so mornings are best.
t.hruba skala@50.5,15.2:
Hrubá Skála means rough rock, and the name suits the place. The village and its chateau sit on a spur of sandstone above the forest, with towers and cliffs rising around it, at the centre of the Bohemian Paradise. The chateau, perched on the edge of a rock, was built for the Valdštejn family and is now a hotel, with views over a sea of trees broken by pinnacles of pale stone.
