It looks like something from a children's book, which is not far from the truth, because this whole area is a favourite with Czech families and walkers.

The rocks are the story. Millions of years ago, this was a shallow sea, and the sand that settled in it hardened into sandstone. Wind, rain and frost have carved it into towers, gorges, arches and mazes, some of them more than fifty metres high, with names that Czech children learn early. Pine and birch grow in every crack, and moss covers the damp shaded sides. Climbers come here to scale the pinnacles, which have a long tradition of climbing without metal aids, a local ethic that is still respected. Nearby, the ruined Valdštejn castle stands on a rock nearby, regarded as the ancestral seat of the Wallenstein family.

The ride into Hrubá Skála is slow and beautiful. The roads are narrow and winding, rising and falling through forest and over small hills, with surfaces that vary from smooth to rough, and a number of tight hairpins. Speeds are low, and there is plenty to look at, but wildlife on the road and walkers at the edges mean you should stay alert. The twin basalt towers of Trosky, a ruined castle visible from far away, appear at intervals above the treeline, a landmark for the whole area.

Fuel is not available in the village. The nearest town with services is Turnov, about six kilometres away, which is known for its tradition of gemstone cutting and garnet jewellery, and has shops, fuel and restaurants. Hrubá Skála has a few places to eat, often busy at weekends, and a hearty meal of goulash with dumplings is an excellent reward after a day on the roads.

Visit in spring or autumn when the crowds are thinner and the forest colours are strongest. In winter, ice can make the shaded roads treacherous.
t.prachov rocks@50.5,15.3:
The Prachov Rocks are the most compact and dramatic part of the Bohemian Paradise, a rock city of sandstone towers, ravines and viewpoints packed into a forest a few kilometres from Jičín. Walking paths and stone steps lead between the pinnacles, some of which look like fingers, others like mushrooms, and from the top of the main viewpoint you look out over a sea of spruce and pine with rocks poking through like islands. A small mountain hut near the entrance serves walkers with simple food and drink.

The area was first opened to visitors in the nineteenth century, when the Romantic movement made wild rock scenery fashionable. The formations were made by erosion, as softer layers of sandstone wore away faster than harder ones, leaving columns and gaps. Moss, ferns and trees cling to every ledge, and in the shadows the temperature drops by several degrees. Climbers have used the rocks for generations, and the tradition of climbing on sandstone with ropes and knots, never with metal protection, is part of the area's identity. A small entrance fee covers the main paths, and the car park charges as well.

The riding is gentle. From Jičín the road runs northeast through farmland and then into forest, with easy bends and a good surface. This is a quiet area, with little through traffic, and the slow pace suits the landscape. It is a good place to stop, park and walk for an hour, as the terrain makes it hard to appreciate from the saddle. Wear boots rather than motorbike shoes if you plan to climb the steps, because the stone can be slippery.

Jičín itself is a handsome town with a large square lined with arcades, and a history tied to Wallenstein, who made it the capital of his duchy in the 1620s and rebuilt much of it. It is also the home of Rumcajs, a much-loved fictional robber from Czech children's stories, and statues and souvenirs of him appear everywhere. The town has fuel, supermarkets and many cafes, so you can resupply easily.

The forest can be damp and cool, even in summer. The best light comes in the late afternoon, when the low sun slants between the rocks and lights the pale stone.
t.ojcow@50.2,19.8:
Ojców is a village tucked into a limestone valley so narrow that the road barely has room beside the stream. This is the Prądnik valley, a green slot cut into the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland, and it lies inside Poland's smallest national park, which packs in an astonishing amount of scenery: pale rock towers, caves, beech woods, mossy springs and a ruined castle perched on a crag. After the open farmland north of Kraków, dropping into it feels like entering a different country.

The riding is slow and attentive. The road through the valley is narrow, shaded and twisty, and the limestone walls rise close on either side, so visibility can be limited and you should expect cyclists, walkers and tour groups at weekends. Parking is by the village and is limited at busy times. The best experience comes on weekday mornings in spring or early autumn, when the beeches are fresh green or gold and the valley smells of wet leaves and rock. In deep winter ice on the shaded bends can be treacherous.

History and legend are everywhere here. The castle above the village, a ruin now, was strengthened in the fourteenth century under Casimir the Great as part of the chain of fortresses along this frontier, and the whole route is known as the Eagles' Nests Trail because those castles sat on cliffs like birds' eyes. A cave in the valley is named after Władysław the Elbow-high, the king said to have sheltered there while fleeing enemies, and the village also has a little wooden chapel built over a stream. The valley later became a health resort and still has a gentle, old-fashioned atmosphere.

There is more to see than you might guess, and the nature is excellent: bats overwinter in the caves, and the cliffs and woods shelter many rare plants and insects. A short walk to the rocky formations is worth it, and the trail up to the castle gives good views. The smell of woodsmoke and baking from the village stalls is hard to resist.

For fuel, Skała is the nearest community of a few thousand people, and Kraków itself is not far south. Cafés and simple restaurants in the village serve trout and pancakes, and there is water at the springs. Bring a lock for your helmet if you walk.
t.pieskowa skala@50.2,19.8:
There is a rock here shaped like a club, and everyone calls it Hercules. It stands about twenty-five metres high beside the castle at Pieskowa Skała, a pale limestone pillar that looks hand-carved and is entirely the work of rain and frost. Behind it the valley of the Prądnik winds off between wooded cliffs, and on top of the next ledge sits one of the best-looking castles in southern Poland, its arcaded courtyard and towers floating above the trees.

The castle began in the fourteenth century as a Gothic stronghold under Casimir the Great, part of the line of fortresses along the old border of Lesser Poland that now makes up the Eagles' Nests Trail. Later owners rebuilt it in Renaissance style, and the arcaded court you see today comes from that time. Fire and neglect hit it hard in the following centuries, but it was restored and now works as a museum, with a collection of furniture and paintings and a small café in the grounds. The name means something like Dog's Rock, and nobody seems quite sure why.

For riders the approach matters as much as the sights. The road comes down into the valley through a succession of gentle bends, villages with wooden houses and chapels, and sudden bursts of forest, and it is a lovely road when traffic is light. At weekends in summer the car park and the lane beside it fill with families, so aim for an early start. Spring brings wild garlic and a thick green smell in the woods, and autumn turns the beeches copper and gold. The surface is mostly decent, but watch for leaves and damp patches on shaded bends.

There is a lot of walking if you want it, including a path up to the castle courtyard and trails through the park nearby, but you can see the main sights in an hour. Souvenir stalls and snack bars near the car park sell grilled sausages, waffles and coffee, and there are toilets close by. The nearest towns with fuel are Wolbrom and Olkusz to the north-east, or Krzeszowice to the south, so check your tank before you commit to the valley roads.

Take a moment at the foot of the rock, look up, and try to guess how long it has been standing.
t.ogrodzieniec@50.5,19.6:
Ogrodzieniec Castle is the biggest ruin on the Eagles' Nests Trail, and the first sight of it is a proper surprise: a long, ragged line of walls and towers sitting along a limestone ridge above the village of Podzamcze, with strange pale rocks poking out of the woods all around it. It looks like a film set, and in fact it has been used as one. The Jura upland here is full of such outcrops, which makes the whole hilltop seem to grow out of the stone.

The castle began as a medieval fortress and then grew under the Boner family, rich bankers and royal officials in the sixteenth century, who turned it into a magnificent Renaissance residence. Its decline came with war: in the seventeenth century Swedish troops did heavy damage during the invasion Poles call the Deluge, and the place was never fully rebuilt. Fire and neglect did the rest, and the ruins stood roofless for generations. Today you can climb through the gate, up the towers and around the courtyard, with views over the village and the forest. Legends cling to it, including a black dog said to roam the grounds and a ghost of Boner's wife, and the guides are happy to tell them.

The ride here from the south is a good one, a quiet run across the upland with long open straights, gentle hills and small villages with whitewashed churches, the road hugging the ridge before it drops toward Podzamcze. Surfaces vary on the secondary roads, and heavy trucks use the main routes near Zawiercie, so keep an eye on your mirrors. The best light is late afternoon, when the limestone turns warm and the shadows of the walls stretch across the grass.

Podzamcze has a busy tourist strip at the foot of the castle, with car parks, stalls, grill bars and ice cream, and it can feel crowded in July and August. Arriving early or on a weekday makes the experience better. The village of Ogrodzieniec has a few thousand inhabitants and shops, and Zawiercie, about ten kilometres away, is the larger town if you need a bigger selection of fuel or repairs.

Rock climbers also love this area, and you may see ropes dangling on the cliffs. Bring sturdy boots if you plan to climb the towers.
t.painted canyon@46.9,-103.4:
Painted Canyon is the first thing you see of the North Dakota badlands if you come in from the interstate, and it is a shock. The land is flat, flat, flat, and then the ground falls away into a maze of buttes, ridges and gullies striped in bands of grey, tan, red, orange and cream. The overlook sits on the rim of the Little Missouri River country, in the south unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, and from it you can see the layers of rock and clay running out across miles of broken land.

The stripes tell a story of time. Over millions of years, rivers laid down layers of sand, silt and clay, and swamps added beds of lignite coal. Later, erosion by wind and water carved the soft rock into the shapes you see now. Where the coal seams caught fire, sometimes through lightning, they baked the clay above into hard red rock called scoria, and the red bands that run through the canyon are the result. Some of these coal fires may burn underground for years, and the whole process is slow and ongoing. The light changes the colours constantly, and the best hours are early morning and late afternoon, when the low sun brings out the reds.

The name Roosevelt comes from the future president who came here in 1883 to hunt bison and ended up buying a ranch. He later said that he would never have been president without his time in the Dakota badlands, and the park, created after his death, preserves the landscape that shaped him. Wildlife includes bison, wild horses, prairie dogs, pronghorn, elk and mule deer, and the sky is huge, with larks and meadowlarks singing across the grass.

The riding around here is flat, open and breezy. The interstate approach is fast, but the park roads are quiet, smooth and winding, with gentle gradients and constant views of the buttes. The wind can be strong on the exposed ridges, and summer heat is intense, with thunderstorms building in the afternoon, so mornings are best. Watch for bison on the road and for rattlesnakes in warm weather.

Belfield, about fourteen kilometres away, has a petrol station and basic services, and Medora, further north, has more, so fill the tank before you enter the park. Bring water and sun protection.

Walk to the edge of the rim and look. The silence and the colours make the long drive across the plains worthwhile.
t.buck hill@46.9,-103.4:
Buck Hill is one of the high points on the scenic loop of the south unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, and from its bare knob you can see more of the badlands than almost anywhere else along the road. The land falls away to the Little Missouri River in a tangle of ridges and flat-topped buttes, the prairie rolls off in every direction to a horizon so distant that it curves, and the wind makes sure you remember that you are standing in the open. There is a small car park, a short path and a view, and that is all it needs.

The loop is the thing. Thirty-six miles of paved road wind through the south unit, passing prairie dog towns, hills of grass and cottonwood bottoms, and offering a series of overlooks over the canyon country. Bison graze beside the road, often walking along it as if they own it, which they do, and wild horses wander in bands across the prairie. Prairie dogs bark from their mounds, golden eagles circle overhead, and in spring the meadowlarks sing from every fence post. The park honours Theodore Roosevelt, who ranched here in the 1880s, and the landscape remains much as he knew it.

The riding is a joy because it is so unpressured. The road is smooth, with gentle gradients and long, easy bends, and the speed limit is low, since the animals have right of way. Heat in July and August can be fierce, with thunderstorms common in the afternoon, so mornings and evenings are the best times for riding and for seeing wildlife. Wind is almost constant, and gusts can be strong near exposed ridges, so hold the bars firmly. Stay well away from bison, which are bigger and faster than they look, and never approach a wild horse.

The park has few services. The visitor centre in Medora sells food and souvenirs, and there are toilets and picnic areas along the loop, but fuel is limited to outside the park, so fill up in Belfield or Medora before entering. Bring water, snacks and a layer, and keep your phone charged, since signal is patchy.

Walk to the top of the hill, face the wind and look out. There is a lot of land here, and not much of it has changed.
t.boicourt overlook@47.0,-103.5:
Boicourt Overlook is a pull-off on the scenic loop of Theodore Roosevelt National Park's south unit, and it gives you a long view down into the valley of the Little Missouri River. The river winds in broad loops through a floor of cottonwoods, with the badlands rising on either side in buttes and ridges banded in grey, tan and rust. From the railing you can often see bison grazing the flats below, their dark shapes small against the pale grass, and prairie dog towns scattered over the slopes.

This is the country that Theodore Roosevelt came to as a young man in the 1880s, when the cattle business boomed along the river. He arrived from New York to hunt bison, grieving after the deaths of his mother and wife on the same day, and the open range and hard life gave him something to hold on to. He ranched here for a few years, until the savage winter of 1886 and 1887 killed much of the cattle on the plains, and he returned east. The experience, he later said, shaped his ideas about conservation, and the park, established in his memory, protects the land he loved. The landscape here is more or less intact, though the bison were nearly wiped out and later reintroduced.

The loop road is a gentle, rolling ride with generous views, and the stretch around the overlook runs along a ridge with long drop-offs to the valley. Speed limits are low, and wildlife is the reason: bison, wild horses, elk, mule deer and pronghorn all use the roadside, and they cross without warning. Summer afternoons are hot and thunderstorms can be violent, so start early. Wind can be strong, and the road surface, though generally smooth, may have frost heaves in spring.

Nothing is sold here. The nearest towns are small: Belfield, some twenty-six kilometres away, has a petrol station and basic supplies, and Medora, near the start of the loop, has more, so fill the tank before you enter. Carry plenty of water and sun protection, and expect little phone signal.

Switch off the engine at the overlook and listen. You will hear wind, birds and maybe the grunt of a bison from the river bottom, which is about all there is, and about all you need.
t.keihoku forest road@35.1,135.6:
North of Kyoto, the city's famous temples and tourist crowds fall away within a few kilometres and the mountains begin. Keihoku is the high, forested country in the northern part of Kyoto's municipal area, reached by roads that follow river valleys up into cedar plantations, and it feels remote in a way that is hard to believe so close to a city of one and a half million. The slopes are covered with straight, tall trees, planted in neat rows, and the light under them is deep green and still.

These are the Kitayama cedars, a type of forestry that has supplied Kyoto's architects for centuries. The trees are pruned and managed with great care to produce slender, uniform, knot-free trunks, which are polished and used as pillars in teahouses and fine homes. The craft goes back to the fifteenth century or so, and it is a living tradition, visible in the carefully tended groves that climb the hillsides. The old road along the river, a branch of the route that carried fresh mackerel from the Sea of Japan to Kyoto, is known as the Mackerel Road, and fish were said to be salted on the way and arrive in time for the evening meal.

The riding is a pleasure. The roads climb through the forest in a series of curves, with a good surface but some narrow sections, and the air is cool and fragrant. Traffic is light, apart from the occasional logging truck, and the pace is slow. In autumn the maples add red and gold to the dark green, and in winter, snow can fall and ice can form on the shaded corners, so check the conditions before you go. Fog in the valleys is common in the morning.

Fuel and food are best handled before leaving the city or in Kameoka, about sixteen kilometres away, or in Arashiyama on the western edge of Kyoto, where the services are plentiful. Small shops and roadside stations in the valleys offer drinks and snacks, but it is wise not to rely on them. Bring a rain layer, because mountain weather changes quickly. Mornings and late afternoons give the best light, and the air carries the clean smell of cedar. It is a quiet, easy way to see the other side of Kyoto.
t.miyama thatched village@35.3,135.6:
Kitamura, the old heart of Miyama, is a hamlet of thatched farmhouses in a green valley in the mountains of northern Kyoto Prefecture, and it looks like a painting of an older Japan. Dozens of houses with steep, deep roofs of reed thatch stand in rows along a stream, among rice paddies and vegetable plots, and the hillsides behind are thick with cedar and oak. The effect, especially in the early morning when mist hangs over the roofs, is of a world that has been left undisturbed.

The village has been designated an Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings, and the roofs are maintained by the community. Re-thatching is a communal job, since a roof needs to be redone every few decades, and the work requires large quantities of reed that must be cut and dried each year. The houses are farmhouses, built by families of the Tamba region, who grew rice and vegetables in the narrow valley, and they were designed to shed snow and rain. Some are now cafes, craft shops, and guesthouses, and a small museum explains the way of life.

The roads to the valley are quiet and pleasant, climbing through forest and farmland on a surface that is generally good, though narrow in places. The ride is gentle, with open bends, a cool breeze, and traffic that is light on weekdays and heavier at weekends and in the autumn colour season. Look out for tour buses on the narrow sections, and keep your speed modest in the village, where visitors wander the street. Winter brings snow, which makes the thatched roofs beautiful and the roads slippery.

Fuel is not available in the village, and the nearest large towns, Obama on the Sea of Japan coast and Arashiyama on the edge of Kyoto, are some distance away, so fill the tank before the climb. Kameoka and the towns on the Keihoku road have stations. In the village, you can find simple lunches of soba noodles, local vegetables, and river fish, and a cup of green tea on a porch is a good way to spend a quiet half hour. Late autumn and winter are especially beautiful, when the hills are gold or white, and the stillness is almost complete.
t.ogose return hills@36.0,139.3:
Ogose is a quiet town at the edge of the Kanto plain, where the flat sprawl of greater Tokyo gives way to the first low hills of the Chichibu and Okutama mountains, and it has the feel of a place that most people pass through without noticing. Its pleasures are modest ones: terraced tea fields, stands of cedar and cypress, small orchards, and a plum grove, the Ogose Baien, that blooms in March and fills the slopes with white and pink. The roads that wind through these hills are the sort that a rider remembers as the pleasant end of a long day.

The hills here are the Musashi ridge, a fringe of old forested ridges that rise to a few hundred metres, and the landscape is a patchwork of woodland, villages and rice paddies, with narrow valleys running between. The area is known for its tea, the Sayama tea that is grown and processed in the nearby hills, and for its small farms, which sell vegetables, eggs and persimmons from stalls by the road. In the autumn, the persimmon trees hang heavy with orange fruit among the bare branches, and the maples on the ridges turn red.

Riding here is a matter of careful pace. The roads are narrow, often with one lane and passing places, and they twist sharply between the houses and the trees, with blind corners, steep ramps and drainage grates at the edges. The surface is generally well kept, but fallen leaves and wet patches in the shade can be slippery, and on weekends, there are many cyclists and other riders. Speed limits are low and strictly enforced, and a patrol car may wait at the bottom of a popular hill. Drive on the left, and watch for traffic coming out of side roads.

Morohongo, only three kilometres away, and Sakado and Ogawa, a bit further, are the towns for fuel, convenience stores and meals, and there are noodle shops and small restaurants by the station. In Japan, you can rely on a vending machine for a hot or cold drink in almost every village, and on a convenience store for a rice ball and a coffee. The best seasons are March, for the plums, and November, for the colour, and the roads are least crowded on weekday mornings.
t.musee national des beaux arts de l occid:
Ueno is where Tokyo keeps its museums, and the National Museum of Western Art sits at the park's southern edge, a few minutes on foot from the station. The building is the point. Le Corbusier drew it in the late 1950s to house a collection of European art that Japan had won back from France after the war, and it later joined the UNESCO list of his works spread across several countries. It is a raised concrete box on pillars with a ramp-like logic inside, meant to grow outward as the collection did. In the forecourt Rodin's Gate of Hell and The Thinker sit in the open air, and on a grey morning the bronze looks wonderfully out of place against the Tokyo sky.

Nobody comes to Tokyo by motorcycle for the corners, so treat this as the calm end of a ride rather than the thrilling middle. The city is a grid of elevated expressways, narrow side streets, bicycles, delivery scooters and traffic lights that cycle slowly. Expressways are tolled and most riders sort out an electronic toll card before arriving. Speeds are low and patient driving is the norm, which makes the whole thing less frightening than the map suggests. The real difficulty is parking. Ueno has paid motorcycle bays, but they fill early, so aim for a weekday morning if you can.

Wander before you ride out. Shinobazu Pond next door is covered in lotus leaves in high summer and crowded with cormorants and ducks in winter, and the old Ueno Park trees give some of the only deep shade in this part of the city. Cherry blossom season turns the park into a slow river of people under pink canopy, lovely and impossible to ride near. The zoo is here too, the oldest in Japan, and the Tokyo National Museum is just up the path if the art has not worn you out.

For fuel and food you are in a city of more than eight million, so this is not a problem. Petrol stations exist but are thinner in the dense centre than in the suburbs, so top up on the ring road before you head in. Around the station there are noodle counters and tiny cafes that are open from early morning, and Ameyoko market, with its shouting fishmongers, is a short walk if you want lunch with some noise. Leave before the evening rush; the expressway out is a lot nicer in daylight.
t.fujisan moutain area@35.4,138.7:
Mount Fuji does not have an edge. From the north side, near Fujiyoshida, it simply grows out of the forest in one long unbroken slope, and on a clear morning it looks too big to be real. The roads around it are better than most people expect. The Fuji Five Lakes sit like a necklace on the northern flank, with Kawaguchiko the busiest and Saiko and Shojiko the quietest, and the road circling them gives long views of the cone over the water. Fujiyoshida, about eleven kilometres away, has the fuel, the noodles, the hot springs and the shrine at Kitaguchi Hongu Sengen, an old pilgrim gateway where climbers once prayed before starting up.

Aokigahara, the lava forest, spreads between the lakes and the mountain. It grows on a basalt flow from the ninth century that is rough and full of caves, and the trees root straight into cracked rock. Compasses are said to misbehave, though what you mostly notice is a hush, the moss and the lack of birds. Walkers should stay on marked trails.

Riding up toward the mountain itself is a decision of the season. The toll road to the Fifth Station on the north side climbs to about 2,300 metres, and the air thins noticeably; by midsummer the access can be restricted when climbing crowds peak, so check before committing. The rest of the year the road is open when snow allows, and winter closes sections. Weather on the mountain is its own business. A warm valley can have a cold, clouded summit, and the wind at the top picks up in an hour.

Fuji is best seen in the cold, clear months, from November to February, when the air is dry and the cone is sharp and white. Summer haze often hides it completely, which surprises first-time visitors. Early morning is the safest bet in any month. On the way south, the road to Fujinomiya passes the Shiraito Falls and the broad, grassy Asagiri plateau, where dairy cattle graze under the cone. Petrol is easy in the towns and thinner on the mountain roads, so fill before you climb.
t.kyoto@35.0,135.8:
Kyoto was the capital of Japan for over a thousand years, from 794 until 1868, and it still carries itself like it. The founders laid the city out on the Chinese model, a rectangular grid with the palace at the north, and the grid is why a tourist can wander straight for ten minutes and know where they are. The old city sits in a basin ringed by low wooded mountains on three sides: Higashiyama to the east, Kitayama to the north, Nishiyama to the west. Seventeen monuments in and around Kyoto make up the UNESCO listing, from the mossy temples to the great castle of Nijo.

On a motorcycle the city asks for patience rather than skill. Streets are narrow, bicycles go everywhere, buses stop without warning, and parking for bikes is a puzzle you solve street by street. Slow is the right speed. The reward is how quickly you leave the city: twenty minutes to the north puts you on the Kurama and Kibune road, winding up a cedar-lined river valley with small shrines and an old mountain temple at the top, and in the evening it smells of woodsmoke and wet stone. Heading southeast, the old road to Nara takes you past tea fields near Uji and into rural lanes where the old province of Yamato begins.

The riding day starting here goes to Toshodai-ji, the temple in Nara that the Chinese monk Ganjin founded in the eighth century after several failed attempts to reach Japan by sea. He arrived nearly blind and brought the first proper ordination ceremonies. That story is worth having in your head as you cross the plain.

The city's food reaches in two directions. There is formal kaiseki, which most riders skip because it takes an evening and a good deal of money, and there is the everyday: tofu, pickles, noodles, matcha, and the covered market of Nishiki, a long narrow lane that starts selling in the morning. Fuel is available everywhere on the outskirts, but central stations are few, so fill on the ring road. The best seasons are late March for blossom and mid November for maples, though they are also the most crowded. February is cold, empty and very beautiful.
t.ainokura village@36.4,136.9:
Ainokura is the smaller, quieter sibling to Shirakawa-go, tucked at the head of a side valley in the Gokayama district of Toyama prefecture. About twenty houses stand in the steep thatched gassho style, a name that means hands pressed in prayer and describes the roofs, which are steeply pitched to shed heavy snow. Inside, big wooden frames are lashed together with rope and not nails, and the top floors were built for silk and, famously, for making gunpowder ingredients. The remote location mattered. The Kaga domain, which ruled the area, valued the saltpetre, and the valley was a quiet place where people could make it out of sight. The village forms part of the UNESCO listing with Ogimachi, which is the bigger one.

The road in is the story. From Fukumitsu or Nanto, you wind up the Sho river valley along Route 156 and then onto smaller mountain roads that thread between cedar slopes and over bridges above blue water. The curves are steady and the gradients mild until the last climb to the village. In the shoulder seasons the road can be wet and shaded all day. Winter closes parts of it, and snow is heavy, often three metres or more in the deepest months, so spring through autumn is the riding season. October brings colour, and June brings rice fields so green they are almost fluorescent.

Nanto, sixteen kilometres away, is the place for fuel. Higher up the valley, stations are few and close early, and the village itself has none. There are a handful of small restaurants and guesthouses in the area, and a local favourite worth ordering is the tofu, which is dense and firm in the mountain style, along with soba and river fish. Toilets and a car park at the entrance cost a small fee.

Come in the late afternoon, once the day-trippers have left. The thatch glows, the light drops into the valley, and a communal folk song named Kokiriko, said to be one of the oldest in Japan, is still sung at festivals in the autumn. The village feels like a place where people actually live, because they do. Walk the paths slowly, keep out of the fields and do not step into private doorways.
t.ogimachi village 2@36.3,136.9:
Ogimachi is the largest of the gassho villages and the one most people picture when they think of Shirakawa-go, a cluster of steep thatched farmhouses in a valley of the Sho river in Gifu prefecture. Some sixty houses survive here, dark with age, their roofs angled at about sixty degrees so that deep snow slides off. Families once lived on the ground floor, kept silkworms in the attic spaces, and shared the work of rethatching in a communal effort called yui, in which the whole village turned out to rebuild a roof in a day or two. The practice carries on in a smaller form, and a roof is replaced every few decades. The village shares its UNESCO listing with Gokayama, 1995.

Getting here from Kanazawa is a fine day out. The Tokai-Hokuriku Expressway runs most of the way through long tunnels, though the older Route 156 follows the river and is more fun, a steady two-lane road beside deep green water, with big cedars and little villages. The curves are easy and the road is rarely busy outside holiday weekends. Be aware that Shirakawa-go's peak days, in autumn and in the winter illumination season, see long traffic queues, and the parking fields fill. Early morning is far better.

The village is best on foot. Wooden walkways follow irrigation channels past rice paddies, small shrines and one or two houses with open interiors, where you can climb narrow ladder stairs and see the bare roof beams lashed with rope. Wada House is the biggest of those open to the public. For a wider view, a viewpoint above the village gives the classic panorama over roofs and fields. In winter the whole scene is under heavy snow, with a pink glow at dawn, but the roads need chains or a car, and this is not a motorcycle season.

Fuel is best taken before you reach the valley, since there are very few stations along Route 156. Takayama, thirty-four kilometres south, has everything, including excellent beef and sake brewed in old merchant houses. The village sells hot soba and river fish, and a freshly made rice cracker costs very little. Rain brings out the colour in the thatch, so a showery day is not the disaster it seems.
t.katowice@50.3,19.0:
Katowice is the capital of Upper Silesia, and for a century it was a place of coal and steel. The region's mines and furnaces made Poland industrial, and the city grew quickly in the nineteenth century from a village into a city of brick, smoke and railway lines. In recent decades much has changed. The mines have closed and a new city has grown from the old industrial land. The Silesian Museum is built into the shafts and buildings of a former colliery, and the concert hall of the Polish National Radio Symphony Orchestra stands beside it, a bold block of red brick and glass. Nearby, the flying-saucer shape of the Spodek arena has been a landmark since the 1970s.

Nikiszowiec, a few kilometres east, is one of the strangest and best places in the city, a settlement of red-brick housing blocks built a century ago for miners and their families around a church, a square and a laundry. The brickwork is handsome, with arcades and courtyards, and the whole district has the feel of a stage set, though people still live there. It is worth stopping for coffee and a slice of cake, and for a look at the work of local artists.

Silesia has its own character. People speak a dialect that includes many German-derived words, and local food is hearty: roulade of beef with dumplings and red cabbage, known as rolada, and kluski slaskie, soft potato dumplings with a dimple for gravy. The region was fought over after the First World War and changed hands between Germany and Poland, and the sense of an in-between place is part of its identity.

For a rider, Katowice is mostly a hub. The motorways, with the A4, tolled on parts, running west toward Wroclaw and east to Krakow, make travel quick. Traffic in the conurbation is dense and tram lines are slippery in the rain. Fuel is everywhere. The day's ride heads east to Oswiecim, about sixty kilometres away, where the Auschwitz-Birkenau memorial and museum stand. It is a place that deserves a quiet, unhurried visit, and a rider should plan time and energy for it. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Winter days are short and damp.
t.gdansk@54.4,18.7:
Gdansk has been a trading port for a thousand years, and the front of its Long Market, the Dluga Targ, shows what the money bought. Tall, narrow merchant houses stand shoulder to shoulder, their facades painted and gilded and carved with figures, around the Neptune Fountain and the Artus Court. In the Second World War, the city was ninety percent destroyed, and what you see today is a painstaking reconstruction from old paintings and photographs, which makes it more remarkable. The Gothic crane on the quay, the Zuraw, was once the largest in Europe, and it hoisted masts and cargo from ships in the Middle Ages.

The city carries a heavy history. The first shots of the Second World War were fired in September 1939 at Westerplatte, at the harbour entrance, where a Polish garrison held out for a week. In 1980 shipyard workers in Gdansk, led by Lech Walesa, went on strike and formed Solidarity, the independent trade union that helped bring down communism in Poland. The European Solidarity Centre, a rust-coloured building near the shipyard gates, tells the story with seriousness and clarity and is worth a couple of hours.

Amber is the local treasure. This part of the Baltic coast has been famous for it since antiquity, and the shops on Mariacka Street, a lovely cobbled lane lined with carved stoops, sell it by the kilo. Fish soup, pierogi and a pale local beer are easy to find. The seafront at Sopot, a few kilometres north, has a very long wooden pier and a lively beach scene.

Riding in the city is easier than it looks, with wide roads and a good ring system, though trams and cobbles call for care. The motorway south, the A1, has tolls, and it leads toward Torun. The ride follows the Vistula valley, a region of flat farmland, brick Gothic towns and castles built by the Teutonic Knights, such as the huge fortress at Malbork. Flat country means wind, and the Baltic brings sudden showers even in summer. Fuel is available everywhere.

Summer, from June to August, is warm, bright and busy, and September is calmer and lovely. Winter is cold and grey, and the roads can be icy.
t.wroclaw@51.1,17.0:
Wrocław is a city of islands and bridges on the Oder, in Lower Silesia, and it has changed hands often enough to carry several names. Under the Habsburgs, then Prussia, then Germany it was Breslau, and after 1945 it became Polish as the borders moved, with nearly the whole population exchanged. Most of today's residents came from the east, from places like Lwów, and brought their own memories and food, which gives the city a layered feel. The old centre was wrecked in the war and carefully rebuilt, so the market square looks as it did in the sixteenth century, with colourful gabled houses and a lacy Gothic town hall.

On a cathedral island upstream, Ostrów Tumski, the lamps along the street are still lit by hand in the evening by a lamplighter, a little ritual that locals like. Dwarf statues, the krasnale, are hidden on pavements and in doorways all over the city, and hunting for them is a pastime for children and adults, a gentle echo of a protest movement of the 1980s. The Oder has flooded the city more than once, notably in 1997, and the riverbanks have been reshaped with parks and walkways since.

The riding starts in an urban sprawl of trams and ring roads, but the countryside to the south opens quickly. The road toward Świdnica and Jawor, home to the great timber churches of peace, crosses fertile farmland with long views, then gradually folds into the foothills of the Sudetes, where the roads become more varied, with gentle curves, small villages, castles and half-timbered houses. The surface is generally decent, though patched, and there are speed cameras at the entrances to villages. In the autumn the beech woods on the hills are rich in colour, and mist lies in the fields at dawn.

Fuel is plentiful on the outskirts and along every major road. Wrocław is also a city for eating, with bakeries selling poppy-seed pastries, pierogi bars that run late, and a thriving craft beer scene around the market. If you want to park the bike, hotels on the edge of the old town are often able to offer a safe space, and it is worth asking. The summer evenings by the river, with students and music, are lively.
t.centennial hall in wroc aw@51.1,17.1:
A concrete dome sixty-five metres across looks like a modest thing to put on a World Heritage list, until you stand underneath it. The Centennial Hall in Wrocław was designed by the architect Max Berg and opened in 1913, to mark a hundred years since the Prussian uprising against Napoleon. At the time it was the largest reinforced-concrete building of its kind, and its ribbed dome, rising above a four-lobed hall and lit by a ring of windows, was a daring leap in engineering. Many early modernists took it as a sign of what concrete could do, and it still has the calm confidence of a building that did not need to apologise.

It sits in the middle of an exhibition park laid out at the same time, on the east side of the Oder, with a long pergola surrounding a fountain that shoots jets of water in choreographed shows on summer evenings. Next door is a Japanese garden from the same period, and the grounds hold a zoo, a botanical garden and a tall steel spire made for an exhibition in 1948. On a fine day the park is full of families and people with dogs, and it is one of the pleasantest places in the city to wander without a plan.

The ride that starts from here takes you south-west to two Churches of Peace at Jawor and Świdnica, timber-framed Lutheran churches built in the mid-seventeenth century. After the Thirty Years' War, the Catholic Habsburg rulers allowed the Protestants of Silesia to build only three churches, outside the town walls, with wood, clay and straw and no towers or bells. The result is astonishing: Świdnica's church, with its galleries and painted ceiling, can hold thousands of people and is among the largest timber religious buildings in Europe. The road there, about sixty kilometres, crosses easy farmland on a decent surface and is a pleasure at a calm pace.

Fuel is easy around the park, with stations on the main roads north and south. Park the bike at the hall and walk, as the grounds are large, and tickets for the hall and the pergola are sold on site. Late afternoon light on the concrete is warm, and the fountain show at dusk is worth waiting for.
t.gdynia modernist city centre@54.5,18.5:
Gdynia is the youngest large city on the Polish coast, and its story is unusually clear. In 1920 Poland regained access to the Baltic after more than a century and found that its main port, Danzig, was a free city under League of Nations control. So the new state built a port of its own at a small fishing village here, and in about fifteen years Gdynia grew from a few thousand people to over a hundred thousand. The architects of the day built in the style they knew, the modernism of the 1930s, with white walls, rounded corners, ship-like balconies and flat roofs, and the city centre still has a streak of that confident, optimistic look.

The best way to see it is on foot around the main avenue, the Świętojańska, and out along the pier at the Kościuszko Square, where the waterfront has been laid out as a promenade. Alongside the pier lie two museum ships, the destroyer Błyskawica, which served with the Royal Navy in the Second World War, and the tall sailing ship Dar Pomorza. Behind the town the wooded hill of Kamienna Góra gives a view over the harbour, and the cliffs and beach of Orłowo to the south are a favourite place for a seaside walk, with a long wooden pier.

As the middle one of the Tricity, with Gdańsk and Sopot, Gdynia sits in a dense strip of urban land, and the roads around it can be congested, particularly in summer. The ride to Malbork leaves along fast main roads, then drops onto quieter lanes across the flat farmland of the Vistula plain. The surface is generally good, with some patched sections and many speed cameras in the villages. Baltic weather is changeable and a stiff onshore wind can make the coast cold even in July.

Fuel is plentiful, and the big stations on the ring road make it easy to leave with a full tank. Smoked fish from the harbour stalls is the local lunch, and the cafes on Świętojańska are good places to rest. If you have time, a short walk along the beach is a fine way to clear the head before you ride.
t.castle of the teutonic order in malbork@:
Seen across the river Nogat on a clear day, Malbork looks almost too large to be real. It is the biggest brick castle in the world by area, built by the Teutonic Knights from the late thirteenth century and made their capital in 1309, when the Grand Master moved here from Venice. They called it Marienburg, in honour of the Virgin, and it served as the fortress, monastery and administrative headquarters of a military state that stretched along the Baltic. The brick walls rise in layer on layer, with a high castle, a middle castle and a lower castle, protected by moats, towers and gates, and it was more of a small city than a single building.

The order's power ended in the fifteenth century after defeat by Poland and Lithuania, and the castle passed to the Polish crown. Prussia took it over in the eighteenth century, and in the nineteenth it was restored with great romantic zeal, then badly damaged in the fighting of 1945. Careful reconstruction has made it whole again, and it earned a World Heritage listing in 1997. Inside, the vaulted halls and the great refectory are impressive in a plain and heavy way, and the museum holds amber and arms. Allow at least half a day, and bring an audio guide if the crowds are heavy in summer.

The countryside around Malbork is the Żuławy, the delta of the Vistula, a flat land of polders, dikes and drainage channels that lies at or below sea level in places. Dutch Mennonite settlers drained it in the sixteenth century, and the farms and the remains of arcaded houses still show their influence. Riding here is easy and fast, with long straight roads under a huge sky, but a strong wind off the Baltic can push a bike around, and in autumn and winter fog and early darkness are a problem. Watch for tractors and cyclists on narrow lanes.

Malbork is a town of nearly forty thousand people and has fuel, food and shops, and the castle is a short walk from the station and the old centre. The riverside gives good views back to the walls, and a bench by the Nogat at sunset, with the red brick glowing, is the best place to end the visit. Gdańsk is about fifty kilometres to the north, and Elbląg and the Vistula Lagoon lie to the east.
t.jelenia gora@50.9,15.7:
The Karkonosze, the Giant Mountains, wall off the south of Lower Silesia, and Jelenia Góra sits in the broad basin at their feet like a market town at the foot of a castle wall. Until 1945 it was Hirschberg, a German linen and glass town, and the arcaded burghers' houses around the rectangular market square still show that prosperity, with Baroque gables and a town hall in the middle. About eighty-seven thousand people live here now, which is enough for a proper centre and not enough to be a headache.

The surrounding valley is a ring of ranges. The Karkonosze rise to Śnieżka at about 1,603 metres, the highest point in Czechia and Poland's border ridge, and lesser ranges close the circle, the Rudawy Janowickie, the Kaczawskie, and the Izera mountains to the west. The basin is dotted with castles and palaces, which is why riders come: Chojnik, a ruined fortress on a granite crag above the village of Sobieszów, Wojanów, Łomnica, and others set among parks. Cieplice, a spa district a few kilometres away, has been bathing people in warm mineral water for centuries, and its old spa houses and park are well worth a slow lap.

The riding around Jelenia Góra is a fine mix. West and south, the road climbs toward Szklarska Poręba, a glass and ski town on the edge of the national park, with forested bends that tighten as the ridge steepens. East, you move through the hills toward Kowary and Karpacz, passing through villages with wooden mountain-style houses. The roads are narrow, often rough, and the weather is changeable, with fog and sudden showers rolling off the ridge, so wet surfaces and gravel after storms deserve respect. Late spring and early autumn are best, when the tourist traffic thins and the beech woods turn.

Practically, this is the largest town for a long way, so fuel, supermarkets and repair shops are easy to find on the main roads. The old town has cafes with outdoor tables on the square, and Polish food is hearty, with pierogi, soups and good cake. Parking for a motorbike is easy near the centre, and a short walk around the market is the right way to reset before pushing on to the hills.
t.shuzenji forest town@35.0,138.9:
Shuzenji is the sort of place where a ride slows down on purpose. It sits in the middle of the Izu Peninsula, in a bowl of cedar-covered hills along the Katsura River, and has been a hot-spring town for well over a thousand years. The name comes from the temple of Shuzen-ji, said to be founded by the monk Kobo Daishi, who is credited with opening up many of Japan's springs. In the middle of the river a small open-air bath, the Tokko no Yu, is the oldest in town, and wooden bridges, ryokan and old shop fronts line the banks.

The history here is darker than the postcard. In 1204, the young shogun Minamoto no Yoriie, who had been forced to resign by his mother's family, the Hojo, was killed in the baths at Shuzenji, and his grave is in the temple precinct. A bamboo grove path, Chikurin no Komichi, runs along the river and gives the whole place its soft, green light.

For motorcyclists, Shuzenji is the crossroads of the peninsula. The Izu Skyline runs along the ridge to the east, the coast road at Itō is about twelve kilometres away, and the mountain roads to the south run through forest, tea fields and plots where wasabi is grown in cold spring water, a speciality of Izu. The roads are twisty, tree-shaded and frequently damp, so go carefully, especially on the shaded corners after rain. Traffic can be heavy on weekends, with tour buses and a long line of cars, so a weekday morning is a much better time to come.

Fuel is available in the town and along the main roads, and Itō, a city of seventy-one thousand, has everything. Try a soba or a bowl of rice with fresh wasabi grated at the table, and, if the weather is cool, take half an hour in one of the public baths. Spring brings cherry blossom, autumn brings maples, and winter brings the best clarity for views of Fuji from the ridges.
t.atami fuel and coast@35.1,139.1:
Atami is where Tokyo comes to forget about Tokyo. It is a hot-spring resort stacked up a steep hillside above Sagami Bay, with concrete hotels, narrow lanes, a small harbour and a long curve of beach, and it has the happy, slightly faded air of a seaside town that was fashionable in the 1960s. The city has fewer than forty-five thousand people, but it feels bigger, because everything is vertical and every street seems to have a view of the water.

Atami has a place in popular culture, too. On the seafront, a statue of a man kicking a woman recalls a scene from the Meiji-era novel Konjiki Yasha, and every Japanese person seems to know the story. There are fireworks over the bay on a number of nights across the year, the town has a castle, a modern reconstruction on the hill, and the plum garden blooms in February, early enough to make the resort worth a winter day trip.

For riders, Atami is a base. It is the doorway to the Izu Peninsula and to the Hakone region, with the coast road toward Itō running south on the one side and the toll roads up to Hakone leading north-west on the other. Fuel is easy in town and on the outskirts, which is just what you need before heading into the hills, where stations are fewer and the roads are long. The streets in town are steep, with sharp turns and a lot of one-way sections, so take it slowly, and park where it is legal, since Japanese enforcement is strict.

The seafront is the right place for a pause. The beach promenade is wide and calm, and cafes around the harbour serve fresh seafood, especially horse mackerel and dried fish, which Atami is known for. An early start makes the best of the day: the morning light on the water is lovely, and the coast road is quieter before the day-trippers arrive.
t.ito ocean@35.0,139.1:
Itō sits on the eastern side of the Izu Peninsula, a city of about seventy thousand strung along a coast of black lava and quiet coves. It is a place of hot springs, fishing boats and gentle roads, and it has an unexpected piece of history. In the early 1600s the English sailor William Adams, who became a samurai advisor named Miura Anjin, supervised the building of Japan's first Western-style ships here, and a small monument by the river recalls it. It is a small but real moment: the beginning of Japan's contact with European shipbuilding.

The coast around Itō is a geological curiosity. Nearby, the Jogasaki Coast is a ragged shoreline of lava, left by the eruption of Mount Omuro, a symmetrical cinder cone just inland that is easy to spot, and a suspension bridge crosses a cove between sea cliffs. The sea here is deep blue, the sunlight is sharp, and in spring the camellias and the cherry trees along the river bloom early. Fishing boats unload squid, sea bream and horse mackerel at the port, and the restaurants close to the harbour serve what has just come in.

The riding is relaxed. The coastal road north toward Atami and south toward Shimoda has plenty of gentle bends and wide views of the water, with islands on the horizon on a clear day. It is also busy at weekends, with traffic backing up through the small towns, so the secret is an early start or a weekday. In summer the beaches fill and the sea breeze is a relief. In winter, the air is clear and the low sun makes the water glitter.

Fuel in Itō is easy, with stations along the main roads, and there is plenty of food and coffee near the station and the river. Take a break at the seaside and watch the boats, and if you are tired, public baths near the centre are an inexpensive way to restore yourself before the ride onward. Rain can make the road surface slick, particularly under the trees.
t.atami fuel and@35.1,139.1:
Coming back to Atami at the end of a long day on the Izu roads has its own pleasures. The town appears first as lights climbing the hillside, hotels glowing up the slope like a stack of lit windows, and the harbour below dark and still. The road drops down a series of tight curves, and the temperature changes as you descend, usually a degree or two warmer at sea level, with a smell of salt and sulphur in the air that is the signature of a hot-spring town.

This is the place to end the loop. From here, the way back toward Tokyo leads along the Sagami Bay coast through Yugawara and Manazuru, past fishing harbours and orange groves, and then either on the toll road around Odawara or onto the Tomei Expressway. The distance is about a hundred kilometres, and on a busy weekend evening the return can be slow, so allow time. Japanese expressways are well maintained, speed is closely policed, and the rest areas are good, with decent noodles, coffee, and clean facilities.

Atami is also a good place to refill and rest before the trip. Fuel is plentiful in town and on the main road at the edge, which is useful because the journey ahead is long. Cafes and small restaurants near the station serve seafood, and many ryokan and hotels offer day-use baths, an inexpensive pleasure after a day of riding. Sitting in hot water is a well-earned reward, and your shoulders will thank you.

If you arrive after dark, take care on the steep, narrow streets, where one-way systems and pedestrians catch out newcomers. Let the evening settle: eat something simple, watch the bay lights, and treat the last forty minutes into the capital as a separate ride with its own concentration. The hills of Izu behind you will still be there next time, and you will have left room to come back.
t.chino@36.0,138.2:
Chino is a town of fifty-six thousand people on the eastern side of Lake Suwa's basin, in Nagano Prefecture, and it has two secrets. One is that the town gave Japan one of its most famous prehistoric treasures: the Jomon Venus, a small, rounded clay figure found at the Tanabatake site and designated a national treasure, which is perhaps five thousand years old. The other is agar, or kanten, a seaweed jelly made in the cold dry winters here, with long frames of it set out to freeze and dry in the open air. Neither is on the usual tourist list, which is part of the appeal.

Chino sits at the foot of the Yatsugatake Mountains, a volcanic range with a long skyline of peaks, and the town is the starting point for the Venus Line, a famous scenic road that climbs into the hills. The road rises in gentle bends through larch woods, past pasture and lakes, toward the Kurumayama highlands, and Lake Shirakaba, a pleasant place to stop. The Venus Line is smooth and well surfaced, with long views of the Southern and Central Alps on a clear day, and in autumn the larches turn golden.

The riding here is among the best in central Japan, but it comes with a few conditions. At altitude the weather changes quickly, mornings can be cold even in summer, and ice is possible from late autumn to spring. Traffic at weekends can be heavy, and a lot of other motorcyclists share the road, so patience helps. Fuel is easy in Chino itself, where there are stations on the main road and shops, and the road ahead has little, so fill up before you climb.

The town has good food, including soba and regional dishes of local mountain vegetables, and the station is a convenient base for a stop. Lake Suwa and its onsen are a short drive to the west, and a hot bath after the mountain road is hard to beat.
t.tanzawa@36.1,139.6:
Kazo sits on the flat floor of the Kanto Plain, in northern Saitama, about seventy kilometres from the centre of Tokyo, and the land here is so level that the horizon is a ruler. It is a town of seventy thousand people with rice fields, vegetable plots and factories, and next to it flows the Tone River, the largest river in Japan by drainage area, which for centuries was a danger and a highway at once. The Tone was moved eastward in the seventeenth century to protect Edo from floods, and its broad embankments are now popular for cycling and fishing.

Kazo has one great spectacle. Every spring, huge carp streamers, koinobori, are strung across the river, some as long as a hundred metres, and they billow in the wind like enormous coloured sleeves. Children's Day, in early May, is the occasion, and the sight of the fish flying above the water is a lovely one. Not far to the north is the Watarase retarding basin, a large wetland of reeds that is protected under the Ramsar convention and home to herons, harriers and many other birds.

The riding here is flat and easy, with long straight roads through farmland and the occasional levee track, so it will not thrill you with corners. What it does give is space, a feeling of being on a plain with the horizon at all points and, on a clear winter morning, a line of snowy mountains far to the north-west: Tanzawa is nowhere near, but Akagi and Nikko's peaks stand on the skyline. Wind can be strong in winter, a dry cold gale coming off the mountains, and in summer the heat and humidity are heavy.

Fuel is plentiful in Kazo, with stations at all the major crossings, and roadside stations sell fresh vegetables and cheap lunches. If you are travelling on the long link through the plain toward the mountains, this is a good place to eat and refill before the road begins to rise. Stay out of the city's rush hours, and give yourself time.
t.nikko shrine@36.8,139.6:
The shrines at Nikko are among the most lavish in Japan, and they are there because of a single man. Tokugawa Ieyasu, who unified the country and founded the shogunate that ruled for over two and a half centuries, died in 1616 and was enshrined here the following year, in a mountain setting selected for its sacred character. His grandson Iemitsu rebuilt the complex on a grand scale in the 1630s, and the result is Toshogu, a collection of buildings covered in gold leaf, carved animals, flowers and painted beams, set among very tall cedars.

Some of the carvings are famous. The three monkeys, who see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil, are on a stable building. The Sleeping Cat, over a doorway, is small and easy to miss. The Yomeimon, the gate, is so elaborately decorated that it is sometimes called the gate you could look at until sundown. Nearby are Futarasan Shrine and Rinno-ji temple, and the whole complex has been a UNESCO site since 1999. The famous red bridge, Shinkyo, crosses the Daiya River at the foot of the hill.

For the rider, Nikko is a rewarding place at the right time. The old cedar avenue that leads in from the south, planted over decades, is one of the longest of its kind, and its dark, cool shade is a pleasure on a hot day. Parking near the shrines is limited and at busy times it is crowded, so go early on a weekday, and wear shoes you can take off easily, as some buildings require it. The town has fuel and cafes, and the local specialty is yuba, the skin of soy milk, served in many forms.

The approach is by the Nikko-Utsunomiya road, easy and well kept, or from Tokyo on the expressway, about two hours in light traffic. Beyond the town the Irohazaka road climbs to Lake Chuzenji and the high ground, a short ride that is among the best in the region. Autumn is the most colourful season and the most crowded.
t.suzu@37.4,137.3:
Suzu sits at the very tip of the Noto Peninsula, the thumb of land that pokes into the Sea of Japan from Ishikawa Prefecture, and it is the sort of place where roads end and the sea begins. It is a long way from anywhere: Kanazawa lies about two and a half hours back down the peninsula, and the landscape between is one of terraced rice paddies, small fishing villages, black-tiled farmhouses and cedar windbreaks. The people of Noto have a reputation for quiet resilience, and the cooking is seafood-led, with squid, crab and yellowtail landing in the winter.

The region has a deep tradition of salt-making. In some villages along the coast the old method of drying seawater on sand and boiling it in iron pans has been kept alive, and the salt from here is prized by cooks. The peninsula is also known for lacquerware from Wajima, for the Kiriko lantern festivals, and for a coastline of rock arches and small islands, including the Mitsukejima, nicknamed the Battleship Island, a rocky outcrop beside the shore at Suzu.

It is important to be honest about the present. The Noto Peninsula was struck by a powerful earthquake on New Year's Day in 2024 and Suzu was among the worst-hit places, with roads damaged, landslides, and a long period of rebuilding. Some sections of the coast road have been closed or repaired, and conditions change, so before you ride here, check current road information, and expect reconstruction work and reduced services. Respect that people are still living with the consequences, and spend a little money locally when you can.

When the roads are open the riding is excellent: the coast road along the outer shore is quiet and curving, with long views of the sea and the sun setting over the water in the evening. Fuel is available in Suzu normally, but confirm before relying on it, and fill up at the larger towns whenever you can. Late spring and early autumn have the best weather.
t.tokyo south west@35.6,139.6:
Getting out of Tokyo is half the ride, and this is where the first half ends. The pin sits on the south-western side of the capital, in the Chofu area close to the Tama River, only a few kilometres from the Chuo Expressway and not far from the Tomei, the two big arteries that carry traffic west out of the city. The land here is almost at sea level, forty metres up, and it is hard to believe the mountains are so close, but on a clear winter morning you can see the Tanzawa hills and sometimes the white shoulder of Fuji from the riverbank.

Two very different rides leave from here. One goes south and west along the Tomei toward Odawara, then up into the Hakone hills by the toll road, and the other crosses the bay to the southern tip of the Boso Peninsula, where the Tomiura district grows loquats and flowers and ends at Nojimazaki, the cape with a white lighthouse designed by the French engineer Leonce Verny and first lit in 1869. Both rides begin with a stretch of suburban driving that rewards patience: traffic lights, expressway ramps, and cars changing lane without warning.

The golden rule of leaving Tokyo is timing. Weekday rush hours choke the expressways, and the weekend flood of day-trippers can make the Tomei slow from early morning, so the best departure is before dawn or after nine, and you should check the traffic boards at service areas. Tolls are paid by electronic card or cash, and the rest areas, with their good coffee and noodles, are an institution. There is fuel at every corner in this part of the city, so top up before you go, because stations in the hills are fewer and close earlier.

If you have a moment before you set off, the Tama riverbank is a pleasant place to sit and study the map. Cyclists and joggers share the path, and a vending machine sells hot canned coffee at every corner. In spring the river embankments are bright with rapeseed flowers and cherry blossom, and in autumn the pampas grass glows in the low sun.
t.hakone turnpike@35.2,139.1:
The Hakone Turnpike is a toll road that climbs from the Pacific side up to the volcanic highlands of Hakone, a mountain district about eighty kilometres south-west of Tokyo. Here the road runs at roughly 850 metres, close to the northern end of Lake Ashi, a crater lake formed in an ancient caldera. On a clear day Mount Fuji rises above the water in a beautiful cone, and a red torii gate stands in the lake at Hakone Shrine, a classic Japanese view that every visitor photographs.

The road is serpentine in the best sense. It winds through cedar and cypress forest in long, smooth bends, with views opening over the lake and hills, and its gradients are friendly, so even a modest motorbike climbs easily. The surface is generally good, but fog and rain are frequent at altitude, and the shade keeps patches of the tarmac damp long after the sun has come out. Weekend traffic is heavy, with a lot of cars, tour buses and other riders, so aim for a weekday or an early start.

Hakone has a long history as a checkpoint on the old Tokaido highway, the main road that linked Edo with Kyoto. The Tokugawa shogunate established a barrier station here in 1619 to control travellers, and a reconstruction at the lakeshore recalls the strict inspections of the time. The old cedar avenue along the Tokaido path, with its massive trees, is still walkable. Near Sengokuhara, pampas grass fills the hillsides in autumn in silver waves, and at Owakudani the volcanic vents steam and smell of sulphur, with eggs boiled black in the hot water sold at the stands.

Fuel is available in the town of Hakone, about five kilometres away, and at stations on the main road, but there are few in the hills, so fill up before you climb. Soba and trout are local specialities, and the hot springs everywhere are a perfect way to relax your shoulders after the ride. Spring and autumn are the finest seasons, and winter can bring ice to the higher road.
t.tokyo@35.6,139.6:
The end of the ride is the beginning of Tokyo again, and it comes in stages. First the hills drop away, and the road widens; then the first signal lights, the first convenience store, the first apartment blocks, and finally the glow of the capital spread across the plain in the dark. Arriving in Chofu at the end of a long day, with the Tama River running quietly beside the road, is a gentle way to come home.

Chofu is an ordinary city of two hundred thousand, quiet in the evening, with a stadium that hosts football and rugby, a long riverside cycle path, and shopping streets where small restaurants serve grilled chicken and cold beer. After a day in the mountains, a plate of yakitori and a noodle soup in a place with a steamed-up window is about as good as it gets. The locals are used to bikers returning in the dusk, and the hospitality is easy.

A few practical points make the last hour smoother. Japan drives on the left, and speed enforcement is strict, with fixed cameras and patrol cars, particularly on the expressways. Rain makes painted lines and manhole covers slippery, and in the city, taxis and delivery vans stop and start without warning. Tolls are charged on most expressways, and an electronic card saves time at the gates. The Chuo Expressway can back up for many kilometres on Sunday evenings, with the Kobotoke tunnel as a notorious bottleneck, so plan to leave the mountains early or accept a slow crawl.

The pin sits close to the river, and there is fuel, food and coffee within a few minutes. This is also a good place to check the bike over after a long day, look at your tyres, and wipe the bugs from the visor. Park in the places marked for motorcycles, because the rules about street parking are tight and fines can be steep. Then take a deep breath, and let the ride settle.
t.nagatoro river bends@36.1,139.1:
Nagatoro is a small town of seven thousand people in Saitama Prefecture, at the point where the Arakawa River squeezes through a gorge of layered rock, and it has been a day-trip destination for Tokyoites for more than a century. The name means something like long rock bed, and it describes the scene accurately: the river runs over broad shelves of crystalline schist, worn into smooth steps and pools, with cliffs of dark green stone along the bank. In the nineteenth century, geologists came to study the rock; now people come to float on it.

The river bends are the draw. In season, flat-bottomed boats carry passengers down the rapids, steered by boatmen with long poles, and the shouts and splashes echo off the gorge. Above the town, Hodosan, a sacred mountain, has a shrine that can be reached by walking path or a ropeway, and the views over the valley and the Chichibu mountains are excellent. In April the cherry trees along the river bloom in clouds, and in autumn the maples turn red.

The riding in the area is fun without being demanding. The roads follow the river and climb into the hills, with a mix of straight sections, gentle curves and old bridges, and the traffic can be heavy at weekends in good weather. Nagatoro itself has a station that looks like a country railway halt, and a main street of shops selling grilled rice cakes, shaved ice and local sake. The town is a convenient place to park, take a break and watch the boats.

Fuel is available in Nagatoro and in the surrounding villages, though stations are small and close early, so fill before the late afternoon. Try the local delicacy, a kind of sweet-and-savoury miso-flavoured skewer, and the cold noodles that are sold at many stands. Watch out for gravel and damp patches under the trees, and take care on the river bridges, which can be slippery after rain.
t.suganuma village@36.4,136.9:
Suganuma is one of the two small villages in Gokayama that kept their thatched farmhouses, and it is the quieter of them. It sits on the bank of the Sho River in the mountains of southern Toyama Prefecture, in a steep, forested valley that for centuries was cut off by deep snow for months at a time. A cluster of about nine gassho-zukuri houses, with steep thatched roofs said to resemble hands pressed together in prayer, stand together on a small terrace above the water, and the effect, particularly in morning mist, is of a village from a woodblock print.

The isolation shaped the economy. In the Edo period, the farmers of Gokayama produced silk and paper, and they also made saltpetre, the ingredient for gunpowder, in pits beneath their floors, a trade that a local lord kept secret. Smoke from the open hearth kept the thatch dry and pest-free, and the great attic floors held silkworms. The valley is also home to Kokiriko, a folk song accompanied by wooden clappers that is thought to be one of the oldest in Japan, and the local paper, washi, is still made by hand. The listing of the villages by UNESCO, in 1995, was shared with Shirakawa-go across the border in Gifu.

The road here is part of the interest. The valley road follows the river through deep cuttings, tunnels and bridges, with gentle bends and a lot of shade, and in winter it is closed or restricted by heavy snow, so check conditions from November to April. From Fukumitsu, a town of nearly twenty thousand with fuel and shops, it is some seventeen kilometres to the village, and the last section is narrow, with limited parking at the edge of the settlement. Fuel in the valley is scarce, so fill in town.

Spring brings fresh green, and autumn is gold and red, but the silence is what stays with you. Walk slowly, keep off the paddies, and remember that these are working homes. A bowl of soba or a cup of tea at a farmhouse cafe suits the place well.
t.historic villages of shirakawa go and go:
Shirakawa-go and Gokayama together form one of the most photographed rural landscapes in Japan, and for once the photographs are not misleading. Across the border between Gifu and Toyama prefectures, in the deep valley of the Sho River, farming families built houses with huge triangular thatched roofs, some of them three or four storeys high, angled at sixty degrees to shed the heavy winter snow. The roofs are made of reeds without a single nail, and they need rethatching every few decades, a task the village does collectively, in a tradition called yui, with the whole community turning out to help.

Ogimachi, in Shirakawa-go, is the largest of the villages, with more than a hundred gassho houses, and it is busy for a reason. Some of the houses are open to visitors, with smoky hearths and attic floors where silkworms were once raised, and a viewpoint on the hill gives the famous panorama of roofs among rice fields. A UNESCO listing in 1995 brought crowds, and in the middle of the day, in high season, the village is very full. Early morning or late afternoon, when the day-trippers have left, is the time to come. In winter, on selected evenings, the village is lit up in the snow, with timed entry.

The ride here from Kanazawa is a good one. You can take the expressway through a long series of tunnels in about an hour and a quarter, or follow the older roads up the Sho River, with its dams, gorges and little onsen villages, and the valley is a place of strong, sudden weather. Snow can close the high roads in winter, and spring is often rainy, while autumn brings the best colour.

Fuel is limited in the valley, and the nearest large town on the north side is Fukumitsu, some seventeen kilometres away, so fill there, or in Kanazawa. In the village you can try Hida beef, grilled over charcoal, or hoba miso, miso cooked on a magnolia leaf, and soba noodles. Parking is at the edge, and you walk in over a long suspension bridge.
t.aus@-26.7,16.3:
Aus sits on the edge of two worlds. Behind you to the west the Namib starts its long slide towards the Atlantic; ahead, the land lifts onto the high plateau of the south, and the village itself perches at roughly 1,400 metres, which means mornings here can bite even in a country that is famous for heat. It is a handful of buildings, a railway that once mattered, and a view over scrubby plains that go orange at sunset.

The history is stranger than the size suggests. During the First World War the South African forces who took the colony from Germany interned German soldiers near Aus, and the camp left foundations and a small cemetery that people still look for in the rocks. The other local celebrity is the herd of wild horses out near Garub, a short way towards the coast on the road to Lüderitz. Nobody agrees entirely on where they came from, with stories involving abandoned military horses and a stud farm, but they have learned to live on very little water and a waterhole is kept for them. They are worth the detour if you have an hour.

For riding, think of Aus as the doorstep rather than the room. The start of the D707 northwards is gravel, graded but loose in patches, with washboard that punishes a fast pace and fine sand in the dips. The scenery is a grand sequence of granite koppies, dry riverbeds and long horizons, and you may go an hour without meeting a vehicle. That is the charm and also the rule: carry water, tell someone your plan, and keep a margin on your tank. Tyre pressure matters more here than horsepower.

Fuel is the practical heart of the stop. Aus is small, but a village on a main route like this does keep a pump in business, and since the next dependable supply on the D707 is a long way north it is sensible to top up here whatever the gauge says. Lüderitz is the larger town to the west, and Keetmanshoop is the real service town to the east if anything goes wrong.

Go early. The light is soft, the gravel is cool, the wind in the afternoon can pick up, and the sun sets fast. Late autumn to spring, the dry season, is kindest; summer thunderstorms can close riverbeds.
t.keetmanshoop@-26.6,18.1:
Keetmanshoop is the capital of the south, which in Namibia means a flat, dry town of some fifteen thousand people where everything useful happens at once. It is the place you buy tyres, groceries and cash, and fill every container you own, before heading for the Fish River Canyon or turning west towards Aus and the coast. Treat it with that respect and it is a perfectly good place to be.

The name carries the story. It was founded as a mission station by Rhenish missionaries in the 1860s and given a name that honours Johann Keetman, a German industrialist who funded the work. The old Rhenish mission church is a solid stone building that has been preserved, and the old railway station from the German colonial era is one of those sturdy buildings that looks as if it were designed to survive a siege. Short walks, a coffee and a look around are plenty.

The surrounding country is the real attraction for a rider. Just outside town, a few kilometres off, lies a quiver tree forest, where Aloidendron dichotomum, the quiver tree, grows in clusters among dolerite boulders. The tree gets its name because San people used the hollowed branches to carry arrows. At sunrise or sunset the shapes against a red sky are some of the best photographs you will take in the south. Close by are the Giant's Playground boulder fields, a landscape that looks like the leftovers of a game played by something large.

The roads out of town are mostly long, straight tarmac, and the challenge is not the corners but the distance. Straight lines run towards horizons, and gusting wind from the side can tire your arms. Watch for livestock and for the odd springbok at dusk, and avoid riding at night, when the animals are hard to see. The B1 is a busy highway by local standards, with trucks, so give yourself room when overtaking.

Fuel is no problem here; there are several stations, and since distances beyond are huge, this is where you fill up. In summer afternoons the heat is fierce and the town basically sleeps between about one and three. Winter mornings can be cold enough for a proper jacket.
