Grab lunch somewhere simple, try the local game meat if you are curious, and enjoy being in a town that knows exactly why you have stopped.
t.santa elena canyon@29.2,-103.6:
At the far south-western end of the Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive, the Rio Grande runs straight into a wall of limestone and cuts through it. Santa Elena Canyon is a gap in the Mesa de Anguila, a long cliff of rock, with sheer walls about fifteen hundred feet high on either side, and the river, wide and brown in the open desert, turns narrow and green and slow inside it. Mexico is on one bank and Texas on the other. A short trail climbs a few steps from the parking area, crosses the mouth of Terlingua Creek, which may be dry or may be a knee-deep wade after rain, and then follows the river into the shade between the cliffs.

The drive that leads here, named for the first superintendent of Big Bend National Park, is about thirty miles of smooth paved road through the Chihuahuan Desert, passing volcanic ridges, dry washes, and the distinctive jagged shape of Cerro Castellan. Colour changes constantly, with rust, cream and grey bands of rock under a hard blue sky. The road is easy riding, with gentle curves and long straights, but it is exposed and the temperature can reach well over a hundred degrees in summer, so carry plenty of water and wear sun protection.

History is layered here. Castolon, on the way, was a cotton farm and military outpost, with an adobe store that still sells supplies, and it recalls the years of border unrest around the Mexican Revolution. The park itself was established in 1944 and covers more than eight hundred thousand acres, an enormous empty territory that includes mountains, desert and river canyon. Black bears, javelinas, roadrunners and many bird species live here, and the night sky is among the darkest in the lower forty-eight states.

Fuel is the main practical issue. There are no stations on the scenic drive, and the nearest in the park are at Panther Junction and Rio Grande Village, with other options outside the park at Study Butte and Terlingua. Fill up before you leave and bring extra water. The best season is November to March, when days are warm and nights cool, while summer is brutally hot. Heavy rain upstream can cause flash floods in the canyon, so pay attention to warnings.
t.arashiyama@35.0,135.7:
Arashiyama is Kyoto's western edge, where the city runs out of temples and begins to climb into forested hills, and the river Katsura slides under the long wooden Togetsukyo bridge with the mountains rising green behind it. It is one of the most visited corners of the city, and with good reason: the famous bamboo grove, the Tenryu-ji temple with its garden, the old villas tucked among the maples and the little steam-era train that runs up the Hozu gorge all sit within a short walk of each other. Muko, a city to the south, belongs to the suburbs rather than the mountains.

That crowd is the thing to plan around. By ten o'clock the streets are jammed with tourists, rickshaws and tour buses, and a rider will spend more time dodging selfie sticks than leaning into corners, so the start of this ride should be early, at the first light if you can manage it, when the bridge is empty and the bamboo whispers. Once you leave the town, the road climbs north through forest and small valleys, with cedar plantations, narrow lanes and tight bends, a surface that is smooth but often damp, and views that open and close between the trees. Autumn colour in November and cherry blossom in early April bring the biggest crowds and the finest scenery.

The ride runs toward Miyama, the thatched village in the hills north of Kyoto, where dozens of farmhouses with deep, steep roofs of straw stand among rice paddies, a preserved landscape of rural Japan. It is a place of unhurried charm, and the road there is a good way to see how quickly Kyoto's city fades into mountain country. Roads in this part of Japan are well maintained, speed limits are modest and enforced, and local drivers are patient but may not expect a motorbike.

Arashiyama has a long history as a retreat for the imperial court. Aristocrats of the Heian period, over a thousand years ago, built villas among the hills and came to admire the moon over the river, and poets wrote about its cherry blossoms and autumn leaves. The Togetsukyo bridge, whose name means moon crossing bridge, is said to have been named by an emperor who saw the moon appear to cross it. The mountain behind the town holds a park with wild macaques, which can be reached by a short, steep climb.

Fuel is easy to find in Kyoto, so fill up before heading into the hills. Pack a light rain jacket, carry some cash for small shops and leave plenty of time to enjoy the ride.
t.jicin@50.4,15.4:
Jičín owes its looks to one very ambitious man. Albrecht von Wallenstein, the general who made a fortune in the Thirty Years' War, took over the estate in the 1620s and set out to turn a modest market town into the capital of his own duchy. He built a palace, a church, a grand arcaded square and a gate, and brought in Italian architects to do it, so the centre of Jičín today has an unexpectedly Renaissance and early baroque air for a town in the middle of northern Bohemia. The great square, Valdštejnovo náměstí, is lined with arcades and pastel house fronts, and the Valdice Gate, a tall tower with a narrow arch, still marks the way out toward the north.

Wallenstein did not live to enjoy it for long; he was murdered in Cheb in 1634. His body was taken to the Carthusian monastery he had founded at Valdice, a few kilometres from town, which later became a prison, and the old monastery buildings can still be seen from the road. Locals have a gentler hero in Rumcajs, the good-natured robber of a Czech children's tale by Václav Čtvrtek, who lived in the forest near here with his wife and son, and the town celebrates him with statues, shops and an annual festival.

Jičín is known as the gateway to the Bohemian Paradise, the Český ráj, a protected landscape of sandstone towers, deep forests and castle ruins perched on rocky crags. The rock formations stand in green woods in all kinds of odd shapes, and the roads between them wind and climb in a way that suits a motorbike. They are narrow and often patched, with farm traffic and cyclists, so keep to a modest pace and expect surprises around the blind corners. Spring and autumn are good times, when the forest is bright and the crowds thin.

The town, with about sixteen thousand people, is a full service stop, with petrol stations, supermarkets and a good choice of cafés and pubs around the square. Czech pub food is hearty, with roast pork, dumplings, and a very decent pilsner. Regional specialities include the sweet Jičín cakes and the fruit orchards that surround the town, and in late summer the plums and cherries are sold at roadside stalls. It is an excellent place to finish a day, and the arcades give shelter if it rains, which in Bohemia it often does.
t.springbok@-29.7,17.9:
Springbok is the capital of Namaqualand, and for most of the year it is a small, dry, dusty town on the N7 in the north-west of South Africa. Then comes the rain, usually in winter, and the surrounding hills turn into a carpet of wildflowers, orange, yellow, white and purple, as millions of daisies and succulents burst into bloom. The show usually peaks in August and September, and the flowers open only in sunshine, turning their faces to the sun at midday and closing again by late afternoon, so plan your timing accordingly.

The town sits in a rocky valley among granite domes, at about 900 metres, and its history is bound up with copper. Mining started in this region in the nineteenth century, and the nearby town of O'okiep was one of the richest copper areas in the world for a while. The old synagogue in the middle of Springbok, a building from the early twentieth century, now houses the tourist office and a small museum, and the stone houses of the main street give the town a frontier look. Goegap Nature Reserve, just outside the town, protects succulent plants and wildlife, with springbok, zebra and a wealth of birds.

For a rider, the Namaqualand roads are long, quiet and open, with wide views of orange earth and rocky hills. The N7 runs north to the Namibian border at Vioolsdrif and south toward Cape Town in long straights, and side roads lead west to the Atlantic coast through scrubby, empty country. Wind is a feature, often strong, and the sun is fierce, so wear sunscreen and drink water. In flower season, traffic increases and vehicles stop without warning to photograph the blooms, so keep your distance.

Springbok has about ten thousand inhabitants and all the services you need, with several fuel stations, shops and restaurants, and it is the last major town before the long distances to the coast and the border. Distances to the next fuel can be considerable, so fill up before leaving. Guesthouses fill up during the flower season, so book early, and carry cash for small villages. The sunsets, with the hills glowing red, make the end of the day special.
t.port nolloth@-29.3,16.9:
Port Nolloth sits where the Namaqualand desert runs straight into the cold Atlantic, and it feels like the edge of everything. This is a small harbour town on the north-west coast of South Africa, close to the Namibian border, with sandy streets, a handful of brightly painted houses, and a rocky shoreline where kelp piles up on the beach. The sea here is fed by the Benguela current, bringing water so cold that fog drifts in on many mornings and swimming is for the very brave.

The town was founded in the 1850s as an outlet for copper mined inland at O'okiep, and for a time ore was hauled to the coast by mule and then by a narrow-gauge railway. Later came diamonds, and today the town is a base for small-scale and offshore diamond divers, whose boats and compressors you may see in the harbour, and for fishermen who catch west coast rock lobster, the local crayfish, in season. A small museum covers the history of the harbour and the mines, and the wreck-strewn coast has claimed many ships over the years.

The ride to get here is long and empty, in the best sense. From the N7, the road runs west across the flat, gravelly plain of Namaqualand, with horizons that go on forever, past small farms and the occasional donkey cart, and in spring the verges may be covered in daisies. There is almost no traffic, so you can settle into a rhythm, though wind and blowing sand can be a nuisance, and a cold sea mist can drop the temperature by ten degrees within minutes. Dress in layers, and keep your visor clean.

Beyond town, roads continue north toward the Richtersveld, a wild landscape of rock and succulents that is part of a transfrontier park, mostly on gravel tracks that need preparation and a capable bike. Port Nolloth has fuel, a couple of guesthouses and restaurants serving fresh fish and crayfish, and a hardware shop, but the nearest large town is far off, so fill up at every chance and carry water. The sunsets over the cold, grey ocean are memorable, and the smell of kelp and salt stays with you.
t.helmeringhausen@-25.9,16.8:
Helmeringhausen is hardly a village at all: a hotel, a farm, a few outbuildings and a lot of sky, set on the gravel road that runs along the edge of the Namib in southern Namibia. It was founded as a farm in the early twentieth century by German settlers who named it after their home village in Germany, and it has changed little since. A small farm museum beside the hotel displays old wagons, ploughs and household objects, giving a picture of what life was like for early settlers in this dry land.

The area is rugged and full of distances. Red dunes and open plains give way to rocky hills and the occasional stand of quiver trees, strange aloes that look like something drawn by Dr Seuss. Not far away stands Duwisib Castle, a fortress-like mansion built in 1909 by a German officer, Hansheinrich von Wolf, with stones hauled from far off and furnishings brought by ox wagon, and now a quirky museum in the middle of nowhere. Distances here are larger than they look on the map, and a stop at the hotel for a cold drink and a slice of cake can be a lifeline.

The D707 is one of the great gravel roads of Namibia, running through a country of grassy plains, rocky outcrops and dune fields at the foot of the Namib-Naukluft. Surfaces are generally graded but can be corrugated or sandy, and loose gravel on bends requires a steady hand. Wildlife is plentiful, with oryx, springbok and ostrich often seen near the road. Sunrise and sunset paint the landscape in warm tones, and the wind can be strong in the afternoon.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There may be a pump at Helmeringhausen, but supplies in remote places are not guaranteed, so do not rely on it, and carry enough to reach the next sure stop. Aus, a long way south, and Solitaire, to the north, are the places with regular supplies. The hotel has a restaurant, bar and basic rooms, as well as a campsite, and it is a popular overnight stop for travellers on the route. Book in advance in the busy season, bring water, and keep a spare tube and tools.
t.aus namibia@-26.7,16.3:
Aus is a village in the stony hills of southern Namibia, at about 1,400 metres, and its job is to watch over the road to the coast. Beyond it, the land drops toward the Atlantic and the old diamond town of Lüderitz, and the desert grows harsher with every kilometre. In the First World War, the South African forces who took the colony from Germany built an internment camp here, where thousands of German prisoners were held, and traces of the camp, including stone foundations, can still be seen among the rocks on the hillside.

The surprise lies a short way west, near the railway halt of Garub: a herd of wild desert horses that live in the Namib without any permanent water other than a trough pumped for them. How they got here is debated, with stories that they descended from horses abandoned by German cavalry or from a farm stud, but they have survived on sparse grass in this dry country for a century. A viewing platform near the trough lets you watch them drink, especially in the morning and evening.

Riding in the region is a pleasure for those who like open space. The B4 highway runs from Aus to Lüderitz in a long, gently dipping line across plains of stone and sand, with ghostly dunes drifting over the road in places, and the wind can blow hard, sometimes carrying sand across the tarmac. The D707 and other gravel roads lead north through the dramatic scenery of the Tsau Khaeb region. Nights are cold at this altitude, with frost in winter, while days can be hot, so layers are a good idea.

Aus has a petrol station, a couple of guesthouses and a small shop, and it is the last reliable stop before the coast, so fill the tank and your water bottles before heading west. Lüderitz, about a hundred and twenty kilometres away, is a quirky town of colonial architecture and cold sea breezes, and Kolmanskop, a ghost town buried in sand, lies on the way. Obey the signs in the diamond restricted area, and do not leave the road. The stars here are superb, and a night in Aus is a good place to see them.
t.fish river canyon@-27.6,17.6:
The Fish River Canyon is one of those places where the map and the eye disagree. On paper it is a crack in the far south of Namibia, in the Karas region, a long way from anything. In person the ground simply stops, and a gorge on the order of 160 kilometres long and well over 500 metres deep drops away in a series of giant hairpin bends carved by a river that only runs properly after the summer rains. It is regularly named as the second-largest canyon on earth, which is a claim worth a shrug, because standing at the rim you are not comparing it with anything.

Getting there is half the point. You come in on gravel, mostly graded and fast enough, across a flat and stony plain of dry grass, dolerite boulders and the odd quiver tree, with the horizon so far off that a bakkie's dust plume is visible for ten minutes before it reaches you. Corrugations are the real enemy. Let some air out, keep your speed honest, and give oncoming trucks the whole road, because they will not give you any of it. Wind can be fierce on the plateau and sand blows across the track in thin snakes.

Time your arrival for the end of the day. The rock turns from grey to rust to something close to purple, and the baboons and rock hyrax come out of the cracks as the heat drops. Midday is harsh, flat and hot enough to make the viewpoints a quick-look affair. The Nama people lived and grazed this country long before German colonial maps put names on it, and the canyon's famous five-day hiking trail is closed through the hottest months, for good reason.

Practicalities are thin, so plan them. Fill up before you leave the tar, in towns such as Keetmanshoop or Grünau, and carry water. Camping and basic accommodation exist near the canyon, and the hot springs at Ai-Ais lie further south at the end of the gorge, a lovely place to soak sore shoulders if you have time. Without a spare tyre and a patched-up sense of patience this is a bad road to ride; with both, it is one of the best silences in Africa.
t.kameoka food@35.0,135.6:
Kameoka is a city in the hills west of Kyoto, in the basin where the Hozu river leaves its mountain gorge and spreads out into the plain. Most visitors know it only as the place where the river boats start, wooden flat-bottomed craft that carry passengers down the Hozu gorge to Arashiyama, steered by boatmen with long poles, and a ride in one is still among the pleasures of the Kyoto area. With about ninety-seven thousand people, it is larger than it first seems, and it makes a very practical place to eat.

History has a dramatic cameo here. Kameyama castle, now long gone, was the base of Akechi Mitsuhide, the general who in 1582 marched his army out of Kameoka toward Kyoto and turned on his lord, Oda Nobunaga, at Honno-ji temple. The remains of the castle site lie within the grounds of a religious organisation, and the memory of the betrayal still colours the town's story. The surrounding hills are quiet, with bamboo and cedar and terraced fields.

For a rider, Kameoka is the gateway to some of the best country roads in the Kyoto region. Heading north-west, the road climbs through forested hills to the thatched-roof villages of Miyama, and west toward the wooded valleys of Tamba, with mostly good surfaces, medium bends and few cars. Along the way there are small farm shops, tea houses and noodle restaurants. The rainy season, in June and early July, brings humidity and mist, summer is hot, and the best months are April, May, October and November, with cherry blossom in spring and autumn leaves in the hills.

As a food stop, the city has a good range: noodle shops, family restaurants, bakeries, convenience stores that are better than they have any right to be, and local specialities such as Tamba chestnuts, black beans and sweet potatoes, depending on the season. Fuel stations are easy to find, and the town centre is compact. Parking is straightforward, with free bike spaces at some restaurants. Have a hot bowl of something, and refill the tank before the hills, where stations are sparser and close early.

t.tokyo@35.7,139.7:
The end of the ride is the beginning of Tokyo again, and it comes in stages. First the hills drop away, and the road widens; then the first signal lights, the first convenience store, the first apartment blocks, and finally the glow of the capital spread across the plain in the dark. Arriving in Chofu at the end of a long day, with the Tama River running quietly beside the road, is a gentle way to come home.

Chofu is an ordinary city of two hundred thousand, quiet in the evening, with a stadium that hosts football and rugby, a long riverside cycle path, and shopping streets where small restaurants serve grilled chicken and cold beer. After a day in the mountains, a plate of yakitori and a noodle soup in a place with a steamed-up window is about as good as it gets. The locals are used to bikers returning in the dusk, and the hospitality is easy.

A few practical points make the last hour smoother. Japan drives on the left, and speed enforcement is strict, with fixed cameras and patrol cars, particularly on the expressways. Rain makes painted lines and manhole covers slippery, and in the city, taxis and delivery vans stop and start without warning. Tolls are charged on most expressways, and an electronic card saves time at the gates. The Chuo Expressway can back up for many kilometres on Sunday evenings, with the Kobotoke tunnel as a notorious bottleneck, so plan to leave the mountains early or accept a slow crawl.

The pin sits close to the river, and there is fuel, food and coffee within a few minutes. This is also a good place to check the bike over after a long day, look at your tyres, and wipe the bugs from the visor. Park in the places marked for motorcycles, because the rules about street parking are tight and fines can be steep. Then take a deep breath, and let the ride settle.
t.hakone@35.2,139.0:
Hakone is where Tokyo goes to get away from itself. The mountain resort sits in the caldera of an old volcano southwest of the capital, about an hour and a half by road without traffic, with Lake Ashi in the middle and Fuji looming to the northwest on a good day. Odawara, on the coast below, is the practical town, with its castle and its fish markets, while the hot-spring villages scattered through the hills have catered to travellers for centuries. The old Tokaido highway crossed these mountains, and you can still walk stretches of its stone-paved surface and see a reconstructed checkpoint beside the lake, where officials of the Tokugawa shogunate once inspected every traveller's papers.

On a bike, the draw is the mountain road. The Hakone Turnpike climbs from the coast in a long run of bends, open and smooth, with good visibility and a toll that keeps heavy trucks away. The Skyline and the roads around the crater rim offer views over the lake and the Pacific. Expect weekend crowds of cars and motorcycles, especially on fine autumn days, and be careful in fog, which rolls into the caldera quickly and can drop the temperature several degrees. Winter mornings can bring ice on the higher sections.

Landscape matters here as much as the road. Owakudani, the steaming valley of sulphur vents above the lake, is the remains of a violent eruption roughly three thousand years ago, and the smell of rotten eggs drifts across the road. Locals boil eggs in the hot pools there until the shells turn black, and tell you each one adds seven years to your life. The pampas grass fields of Sengokuhara turn silver in autumn, and the cedar avenue along the old highway is cool and dark even in midsummer.

Fuel is straightforward, with stations in Odawara and along the main road up the valley, but the mountain sections have fewer, so fill at the bottom. Konbini stores at the lakeside and along the turnpike sell hot drinks and snacks. A cup of coffee at a mountain cafe, with the lake and the trees outside, is a decent reward after the climb.

Come on a weekday if you can, and early. By midday the lake road is slow, and by evening the mist often comes back down.

t.ogrodzieniec@50.5,19.5:
Ogrodzieniec Castle is the biggest ruin on the Eagles' Nests Trail, and the first sight of it is a proper surprise: a long, ragged line of walls and towers sitting along a limestone ridge above the village of Podzamcze, with strange pale rocks poking out of the woods all around it. It looks like a film set, and in fact it has been used as one. The Jura upland here is full of such outcrops, which makes the whole hilltop seem to grow out of the stone.

The castle began as a medieval fortress and then grew under the Boner family, rich bankers and royal officials in the sixteenth century, who turned it into a magnificent Renaissance residence. Its decline came with war: in the seventeenth century Swedish troops did heavy damage during the invasion Poles call the Deluge, and the place was never fully rebuilt. Fire and neglect did the rest, and the ruins stood roofless for generations. Today you can climb through the gate, up the towers and around the courtyard, with views over the village and the forest. Legends cling to it, including a black dog said to roam the grounds and a ghost of Boner's wife, and the guides are happy to tell them.

The ride here from the south is a good one, a quiet run across the upland with long open straights, gentle hills and small villages with whitewashed churches, the road hugging the ridge before it drops toward Podzamcze. Surfaces vary on the secondary roads, and heavy trucks use the main routes near Zawiercie, so keep an eye on your mirrors. The best light is late afternoon, when the limestone turns warm and the shadows of the walls stretch across the grass.

Podzamcze has a busy tourist strip at the foot of the castle, with car parks, stalls, grill bars and ice cream, and it can feel crowded in July and August. Arriving early or on a weekday makes the experience better. The village of Ogrodzieniec has a few thousand inhabitants and shops, and Zawiercie, about ten kilometres away, is the larger town if you need a bigger selection of fuel or repairs.

Rock climbers also love this area, and you may see ropes dangling on the cliffs. Bring sturdy boots if you plan to climb the towers.

t.near otsuki on the way back@35.7,138.9:
Yamanashi is a prefecture of mountains, fruit and wine, and the pin sits in the middle of it, in the steep country north of Ōtsuki, where the Kōshū mountains rise toward the Okutama range. The Katsura river runs below, cutting a gorge near Ōtsuki that is crossed by Saruhashi, the Monkey Bridge, one of Japan's three great strange bridges, a wooden cantilever construction that has been rebuilt many times since the Middle Ages. Enzan, to the north-west, is the gateway to the Daibosatsu mountains and the Chichibu-Tama-Kai National Park.

This is a landscape of terraced orchards, with grapes, peaches and persimmons ripening along the slopes. The Kōshū grape, grown here for over a thousand years, makes the white wine of Katsunuma, and the vineyards have given the area a growing reputation among wine lovers, with tasting rooms open to visitors. The old Kōshū Kaidō, the road from Edo to Kōfu, ran through here, and Sasago Pass, a long climb to the east, was one of its steepest sections, with checkpoints and inns that have mostly vanished. Mount Fuji appears on the southern horizon from many viewpoints, a huge white shape above the lower hills.

The roads are a pleasure. From Ōtsuki, routes climb the valleys toward Kosuge and Lake Okutama, with sharp bends, narrow sections and a thick cover of forest, and the Matsuhime road in particular has a fine reputation among riders. The surface is mostly good, but narrow in places, and rockfalls, wet leaves and fallen branches are common. In winter, ice persists in the shade, and snow can close the higher roads. Autumn is the best time, with the orchards and forests in colour, and spring brings blossom in the valleys.

Fuel and food are easy in Ōtsuki, Enzan and the Kōfu basin, with convenience stores and restaurants along the main roads. The local dish is hōtō, a thick noodle soup of flat wheat noodles, pumpkin and vegetables, served in an iron pot and perfect for a cold day. Fresh fruit is for sale at roadside stands in season.

The pin is marked for swimming, and the mountain streams are clean and cold, but be careful of strong currents after rain. The label mentions Bandai Azuma and Shōsenkyō, but the mountains here have their own appeal, quieter and little known to visitors.
t.near sano on the way back@36.3,139.6:
Sano ramen is the first thing to say about this corner of Tochigi. The town is known across Japan for noodles that are flat, springy and kneaded by bamboo poles, served in a clear soy broth that tastes clean and slightly sweet. The pin lies just a few kilometres from Sano, on the flat, farmed floodplain where Tochigi meets Gunma, and any rider arriving at midday should know where lunch is. It also has a famous outlet mall and a temple devoted to warding off bad luck, so the town has a steady flow of visitors.

The terrain is the plain of the Watarase and Tone rivers, marked by drainage channels, levees and rice, with the edge of the Ryōmō hills rising to the north. A few kilometres west, Tatebayashi is known for two things. In spring, the azaleas of Tsutsujigaoka Park bloom in thousands, some of them hundreds of years old, and a festival draws visitors from all over the Kantō. The Morin-ji temple preserves the folk tale of the Bunbuku Chagama, a tanuki that turned into a tea kettle and brought good fortune to a poor priest. It is a cheerful bit of local lore.

South-east of here, the Watarase retention basin is a large wetland where four prefectures meet, built to control flooding and now registered as a Ramsar site, a good place for reeds, herons and migrating birds. In winter, harriers hunt over the reeds and the whole area has a stark beauty. This is not the Japan of mountains and temples but a quiet, productive heartland of vegetables and rice, and the landscape rewards slow looking.

For riders, the roads are flat and straight, which suits an early start from Tokyo before heading to the hills. Fuel is easy, with Sano, Tatebayashi and Fujioka all within a short ride and plenty of stations along the main roads. Ride with attention to crossings, since farm traffic and local drivers do not always look. Pick a hot day and the plain can be oppressive, so take your time and keep water on the bike. In November, when the harvest is done and the air is clear, the views to the mountains are some of the best of the year.
